steps.desc: Identify every build, environment, or developer machine that resolved and installed the malicious package.

steps.title: Analyze the malicious package's payload
steps.desc: Review the package source or vendor/community analysis to determine what the malicious code does.
steps.outcome: Payload behavior understood for containment planning.

steps.title: Remove the malicious package from all affected systems and pipelines
steps.desc: Uninstall the package and purge it from lockfiles, caches, and CI artifact stores.
steps.outcome: Malicious package removed from all locations.

steps.title: Isolate systems where the package executed
steps.desc: Contain any build or runtime systems where the malicious package's code actually executed, not just where it was present.

steps.title: Rotate credentials/secrets accessible during package execution
steps.desc: Rotate any secrets, tokens, or environment variables reachable by build processes where the package executed.

steps.title: Implement registry scoping and allowlisting controls
steps.desc: Configure package manager scoping, private registry mirroring, or allowlists to prevent resolution of unapproved public packages.

steps.title: Sweep for secondary persistence on affected build/dev systems
steps.desc: Scan affected systems for artifacts left behind by the malicious package execution.

steps.title: Restore clean builds and verify pipeline integrity
steps.desc: Rebuild affected artifacts from clean dependency sets and verify pipeline outputs before redeployment.
steps.outcome: Clean, verified builds restored to production pipelines.

steps.title: Document incident and train developers on typosquat risk
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and conduct developer awareness training on dependency verification practices.

ITID-61322.def: The takeover of a legitimate open-source package maintainer's account (or its publishing credentials) used to push a malicious version of an already-trusted library, which is then automatically ingested by downstream consumers via routine dependency updates.
ITID-61322.purpose: Captures the compromise of a package the organization already trusts and has used for some time, where the attacker hijacks the legitimate maintainer's account rather than publishing a new fake package.
scopeIncludes: A version bump to a long-trusted library found to contain malicious code after maintainer-account compromise is disclosed
Automated dependency-update tooling pulling in a compromised release within hours of publication
scopeExcludes: A brand-new malicious package impersonating a legitimate name (ITID-61321)
Exploitation of package-name resolution precedence rather than maintainer-account takeover (ITID-61323)
ITID-61322.severity: Critical, since an established dependency typically has broad, deeply-embedded usage and higher inherent trust, making blast radius larger than a typosquat.
ITID-61322.priority: P1 immediately upon any advisory naming a maintainer-account compromise for a package present in the organization's dependency tree.
ITID-61322.escalation: Escalate to application security and pin/rollback the affected dependency version fleet-wide while investigation of impact proceeds.
indicators: Security advisory disclosing maintainer-account compromise for a widely-used package
A version release with no corresponding legitimate changelog or commit history
Sudden, unexplained new runtime behavior following an automatic dependency update
vectors: Phishing or credential-stuffing against an open-source maintainer's registry account
Lack of MFA on package-registry publishing credentials
Social engineering to gain co-maintainer status on a popular package
rootCauses: Automated dependency updates applied without a staged validation window
No internal pinning/review gate before a new dependency version reaches production
Overreliance on a small number of unpaid open-source maintainers for critical infrastructure
mitreTechniques: T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
controls: Dependency version pinning with a mandatory staged validation window before promotion
Automated diffing of new package releases against prior known-good versions
Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) tracking to accelerate impact assessment
ITID-61322.detection: Moderate; SBOM and pinning practices allow rapid impact assessment once an advisory is published, but pre-disclosure detection is difficult since the update arrives through a trusted, previously-benign channel.
ITID-61322.response: Roll back to the last known-good version fleet-wide, rebuild affected artifacts, and assess for compromise during the window the malicious version was live.
metrics: Time from advisory publication to internal rollback completion
Percentage of dependencies with SBOM coverage enabling rapid impact lookup
ITID-61322.notes: Differentiated from ITID-61321 by target: this leaf involves takeover of an already-trusted package's identity, not creation of a new deceptive one.

playbook.name: Legitimate Package Maintainer Account Compromised to Push Malicious Update
playbook.description: The account of a legitimate open-source package maintainer is compromised and used to publish a malicious version of a widely used library.

steps.title: Confirm the compromised-maintainer advisory and malicious version
steps.desc: Validate the security advisory identifying the compromised maintainer account and the specific malicious package version published.

steps.title: Determine internal installations of the malicious version
steps.desc: Scan dependency manifests and lockfiles across all repositories for the specific malicious version string.

steps.title: Determine whether the malicious version executed in any environment
steps.desc: Check build and runtime logs to determine whether the malicious version was actually installed and executed, versus merely present in a lockfile.

steps.title: Pin dependencies to the last known-good version and block the malicious version
steps.desc: Update lockfiles/manifests to pin to the pre-compromise version and block resolution of the malicious version at the registry-proxy level.
steps.outcome: Malicious version blocked from further installation.

steps.title: Isolate systems where the malicious version executed
steps.desc: Contain build or runtime systems confirmed to have executed the malicious version.

steps.title: Rotate credentials/secrets accessible on affected systems
steps.desc: Rotate any secrets reachable by processes that ran the malicious version.

steps.title: Verify the maintainer account and package registry restoration
steps.desc: Confirm the package maintainer/registry has revoked the compromised account, removed the malicious version, and restored legitimate publishing control.

steps.title: Sweep affected systems for secondary persistence
steps.desc: Scan systems that executed the malicious version for dropped payloads or persistence.

steps.title: Restore builds on the verified clean version
steps.desc: Rebuild and redeploy affected artifacts using the confirmed clean version.

steps.title: Document incident and adopt dependency-pinning/integrity-verification practices
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and recommend lockfile integrity checks, version pinning, and update-review policies.

ITID-61323.def: A dependency confusion attack in which an attacker publishes a package on a public registry under the same name as an organization's internal/private package, exploiting build-tool resolution precedence so the malicious public package is installed instead of the legitimate internal one.
ITID-61323.purpose: Captures the specific failure mode where an internal, non-public package name is hijacked on a public registry and resolved in place of the intended internal package, producing a critical build or runtime compromise.
scopeIncludes: Build tooling resolving an internal package name to an unexpected public-registry entry
Discovery of a public package registered under a name matching an internal package, regardless of whether it was yet pulled into a build
scopeExcludes: A malicious package under a name resembling a well-known public library (ITID-61321)
Compromise of an existing package's legitimate maintainer account (ITID-61322)
ITID-61323.severity: Critical if the confused package was resolved into a build that reached production; Medium if identified via proactive registry-squatting reservation before exploitation.
ITID-61323.priority: P1 upon confirmation the malicious public package was installed in any build; P3 for proactive reservation-only findings.
ITID-61323.escalation: Escalate to application security and build/release engineering immediately; treat every internal package name as a potential public-registry collision until namespace reservation is confirmed.
indicators: Build logs showing package resolution from a public registry for a name expected to resolve internally
A public registry entry discovered matching an internal package name with no organizational ownership
Outbound network activity from a build agent immediately following dependency installation
vectors: Publishing a public package matching a leaked or guessed internal package name
Misconfigured package-manager scope/registry precedence defaulting to public resolution
rootCauses: Internal package names not reserved on public registries
Package-manager configuration not explicitly scoping internal packages to a private registry
Internal package names disclosed in public build logs, job postings, or open-source contributions
mitreTechniques: T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
controls: Explicit registry scoping in package-manager configuration to prevent public-registry fallback
Proactive reservation of internal package names on public registries
Build-time verification that installed package sources match an approved registry
ITID-61323.detection: Strong when explicit registry scoping and build-source verification are in place; otherwise largely invisible until the malicious package executes.
ITID-61323.response: Correct package-manager scoping immediately, purge and rebuild affected artifacts, and audit for any credential or data exposure during the compromise window.
metrics: Number of internal package names proactively reserved on public registries
Number of dependency-confusion attempts detected by build-source verification
ITID-61323.notes: This ITID and ITID-62321 (Third-Party Software Exploitation domain) describe the same technique; this leaf is scoped strictly to the critical-outage/business-impact consequence when the attack succeeds, while ITID-62321 documents the technical exploitation mechanism itself.

playbook.name: Dependency Confusion Attack (Internal Package Name Hijacked on Public Registry)
playbook.description: An attacker publishes a malicious package under the same name as an internal-only package to a public registry, and internal build systems resolve the malicious public version.

steps.title: Confirm dependency confusion and identify the hijacked internal package name
steps.desc: Validate the report and identify which internal package name was squatted on the public registry.

steps.title: Determine whether internal builds resolved the public malicious version
steps.desc: Review build logs and package manager resolution order configuration to determine if the malicious public package was pulled instead of the internal one.
steps.guidance: Check package manager scoping/priority configuration for the root cause.

steps.title: Analyze the malicious package payload
steps.desc: Review the malicious package's contents to understand what it does upon installation/execution.

steps.title: Fix package manager scoping to prioritize the internal registry
steps.desc: Immediately update package manager configuration to scope internal package names to the private registry, preventing further resolution confusion.
steps.outcome: Scoping fix deployed preventing further confusion.

steps.title: Isolate and remove the malicious package from affected build systems
steps.desc: Purge the malicious package from build caches, artifact stores, and any system where it executed.

steps.title: Rotate credentials/secrets accessible to affected build systems
steps.desc: Rotate any secrets reachable by builds where the malicious package executed.

steps.title: Register placeholder/defensive packages for all internal names on public registries
steps.desc: Claim internal package names on relevant public registries to prevent recurrence, per registry policy.
steps.outcome: Defensive namespace claims completed where supported.

steps.title: Sweep affected systems for secondary persistence
steps.desc: Scan systems that executed the malicious package for dropped payloads.

steps.title: Restore clean builds and verify pipeline resolution behavior
steps.desc: Rebuild affected artifacts and confirm the package manager now correctly resolves internal names to the private registry.
steps.outcome: Verified correct resolution and clean build restored.

steps.title: Document incident and update internal package naming/scoping standards
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and codify registry scoping requirements for all internal package namespaces.

ITID-61324.def: A catch-all classification for a compromised open-source library incident used during initial triage before the specific compromise pattern is determined.
ITID-61324.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for a compromised open-source library incident that has not yet been narrowed to typosquatting, maintainer compromise, or dependency confusion.
scopeIncludes: Newly reported malicious-package incidents pending root-cause determination among the sibling patterns in this group
scopeExcludes: Any case confirmed as typosquatting (ITID-61321)
Any case confirmed as maintainer-account compromise (ITID-61322)
Any case confirmed as dependency confusion (ITID-61323)
ITID-61324.severity: Critical by default, consistent with the sibling leaves, until root cause narrows the classification.
ITID-61324.escalation: Escalate immediately as with any confirmed supply-chain package compromise; reclassification should not delay containment.
indicators: Initial detection of a malicious package with root cause under investigation
vectors: Unknown/unconfirmed pending investigation
rootCauses: Insufficient initial forensic detail to determine the compromise pattern
mitreTechniques: T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
controls: Incident triage workflow requiring reclassification within a defined SLA once root cause is known
ITID-61324.detection: Not applicable as a distinct detection surface; this leaf exists for classification triage, not detection engineering.
ITID-61324.response: Handle with full supply-chain-compromise response urgency while root-cause investigation proceeds; reclassify promptly once determined.
metrics: Number of incidents held in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
ITID-61324.notes: This is an intake/triage leaf; every incident logged here should be reclassified into a specific sibling ITID once root cause is established.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Compromised Open-Source Library
playbook.description: An open-source library used by the organization is found compromised through an unspecified or unclassified mechanism.

steps.title: Confirm the compromised library report
steps.desc: Validate the advisory and identify the specific library and affected version(s).

steps.title: Inventory internal usage of the affected library
steps.desc: Search dependency manifests and SBOMs across all projects for the affected library and version.

steps.title: Determine execution/exposure status
steps.desc: Determine whether the affected version was actually deployed/executed versus merely referenced.

steps.title: Pin to a known-good version and block the compromised version
steps.desc: Update manifests to pin a safe version and block resolution of the compromised version internally.

steps.title: Isolate systems where the compromised version executed
steps.desc: Contain systems confirmed to have run the compromised library version.

steps.title: Deploy the verified clean/patched version
steps.desc: Update all instances to the vendor/community-verified clean version.

steps.title: Sweep affected systems for secondary persistence
steps.desc: Scan systems that ran the compromised version for residual compromise artifacts.

steps.title: Restore clean builds to production
steps.desc: Redeploy affected applications using the verified clean dependency set.

steps.title: Document incident and improve dependency monitoring
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and recommend continuous dependency vulnerability/compromise monitoring.

ITID-61331.def: The exploitation of a vendor-provided API integration such that a single compromise event grants an attacker access across multiple downstream customer organizations that share the vendor's platform, resulting in critical, multi-tenant business disruption.
ITID-61331.purpose: Captures the case where a single vendor's shared API integration is exploited in a way that reaches multiple downstream customer environments at once, producing multi-tenant, critical business disruption.
scopeIncludes: A vendor's multi-tenant API flaw allowing cross-customer data or system access
A single vendor-side compromise event confirmed to have affected multiple customer organizations through the same integration
scopeExcludes: A single leaked API credential affecting only this organization's own integration (ITID-61332)
General technical exploitation of a vendor API vulnerability with no confirmed cross-customer blast radius, tracked under Third-Party Software Exploitation
ITID-61331.severity: Critical, given the multi-tenant nature means the organization's exposure is coupled to the vendor's other customers and outside the organization's direct control.
ITID-61331.priority: P1 immediately upon vendor disclosure of a multi-tenant API compromise or upon internal discovery of unexplained cross-tenant behavior.
ITID-61331.escalation: Escalate to the vendor's incident response team and internal legal/vendor-management simultaneously, since remediation depends heavily on vendor-side action outside the organization's control.
indicators: Vendor breach notification citing a shared API vulnerability affecting multiple customers
Unexpected data or objects belonging to another tenant appearing in the organization's vendor-hosted environment
Threat intelligence reporting a vendor's API platform as actively exploited at scale
vectors: Broken object-level authorization in a vendor's multi-tenant API
Shared API infrastructure with insufficient tenant isolation
Exploitation of a vendor API rate-limiting or authentication flaw affecting the whole platform
rootCauses: Vendor architecture lacking strict tenant isolation at the API layer
Organization's own lack of independent monitoring/alerting on vendor-provided API activity
No contractual requirement for the vendor to disclose cross-tenant security findings promptly
mitreTechniques: T1195.002 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
controls: Independent logging/monitoring of the organization's own activity through the vendor API, not solely reliant on vendor-side logs
Contractual requirement for prompt vendor disclosure of multi-tenant security incidents
Least-privilege scoping of the organization's own API credentials/permissions with the vendor
ITID-61331.detection: Weak from the customer side, since the vulnerable component is entirely within the vendor's infrastructure; detection typically depends on vendor disclosure or anomalies visible only within the organization's own data.
ITID-61331.response: Coordinate with the vendor on scope and remediation, rotate all credentials shared with the vendor, and independently audit the organization's own data for evidence of cross-tenant exposure.
metrics: Number of vendor multi-tenant incidents disclosed per year
Time from vendor disclosure to internal credential rotation completion
detections: Independent anomaly monitoring on vendor-API-sourced data
ITID-61331.notes: Cross-references the parallel Third-Party Software Exploitation domain, which documents the technical exploitation mechanism of vendor API flaws; this leaf is scoped to the confirmed multi-tenant, critical-business-impact consequence.

playbook.name: Vendor API Integration Exploited to Access Multiple Downstream Customers
playbook.description: A vulnerability in a vendor's API is exploited to gain access across multiple downstream customer tenants, including the organization's.

steps.title: Confirm vendor API exploitation notification
steps.desc: Validate the vendor's disclosure regarding the API vulnerability exploited and whether the organization's tenant was among those accessed.

steps.title: Review organizational API usage logs for anomalous activity
steps.desc: Examine the organization's own API call logs and integration audit trails for unusual access patterns during the exploitation window.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether organizational data was accessed via the exploit.

steps.title: Determine data/functions exposed via the exploited API
steps.desc: Establish what data types and functions the exploited API endpoint(s) exposed.

steps.title: Rotate organizational API keys and tokens for the vendor integration
steps.desc: Rotate all API credentials used by the organization to interact with the vendor's API.

steps.title: Disable or restrict the integration pending vendor patch
steps.desc: Temporarily disable or limit the scope of the vendor API integration until the vulnerability is patched.
steps.outcome: Attack surface reduced during remediation window.

steps.title: Escalate to vendor relationship manager and Security leadership
steps.desc: Notify stakeholders and request confirmation of the vendor's patch timeline.
steps.outcome: Stakeholders briefed and vendor patch timeline obtained.

steps.title: Verify vendor's API vulnerability patch deployment
steps.desc: Confirm the vendor has deployed a fix and, where feasible, independently validate the vulnerability is closed.
steps.abort: If unconfirmed, keep integration restricted or disabled.

steps.title: Review affected data for signs of unauthorized use
steps.desc: Monitor for downstream misuse of any organizational data accessed via the exploit.

steps.title: Restore full integration functionality
steps.desc: Re-enable the integration at full scope once the patch and credential rotation are verified.

steps.title: Determine and execute notification obligations
steps.desc: Assess with Legal/Privacy whether affected customers or regulators require notification.
steps.outcome: Notification decision made and executed if required.

steps.title: Document incident and reassess vendor API risk tier
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and update the vendor's risk classification and API-integration review requirements.
steps.outcome: Report filed and risk tier updated.

ITID-61332.def: The exposure of a vendor API key or secret belonging to the organization in a publicly accessible code repository, leading to unauthorized use of that credential and resulting critical disruption to the organization's own vendor-integrated services.
ITID-61332.purpose: Captures the organization's own exposure when a credential or secret used to authenticate to a vendor's API is accidentally published in a public code repository and subsequently abused.
scopeIncludes: A vendor API key committed to a public GitHub/GitLab repository and later abused by a third party
Automated secret-scanning services or threat intelligence reporting an exposed organizational credential for a specific vendor integration
scopeExcludes: A vendor-side multi-tenant API compromise affecting many customers (ITID-61331)
Exposure of internal, non-vendor-related secrets, tracked under general credential-exposure ITIDs outside this domain
ITID-61332.severity: Critical if the exposed key was actively abused before revocation; High if caught and revoked before any confirmed misuse.
ITID-61332.priority: P1 upon any confirmed use of the exposed credential by an unauthorized party; P2 for exposure caught and revoked with no confirmed misuse.
ITID-61332.escalation: Escalate to the credential-owning team and the vendor immediately to revoke and reissue the exposed key, regardless of whether misuse has yet been confirmed.
indicators: Secret-scanning alert on a public repository
Vendor notification of anomalous API usage tied to the organization's key
Unexpected billing/usage spikes on a vendor account
vectors: Developer committing a hardcoded API key to a public repository
Secret left in a public CI/CD configuration file or build log
Key embedded in a public code sample or documentation snippet
rootCauses: No automated secret-scanning on repositories before or after commit
Vendor credentials stored outside of a managed secrets vault
Lack of key rotation policy for long-lived vendor API credentials
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: Automated secret-scanning on all repositories, public and private, with pre-commit hooks where feasible
Centralized secrets vault for all vendor API credentials with no hardcoding permitted
Scheduled rotation of long-lived vendor API keys
ITID-61332.detection: Strong when automated secret-scanning is deployed across repository hosting; weak without it, relying instead on vendor-side anomaly detection or external threat intelligence.
ITID-61332.response: Revoke and reissue the exposed credential immediately, review vendor-side usage logs for the exposure window, and remediate the repository history to remove the secret.
metrics: Number of exposed vendor credentials detected per quarter
Mean time to revoke an exposed credential after detection
ITID-61332.notes: Differentiated from ITID-61331 by direction of impact: this leaf is the organization's own credential being exposed and abused, not a vendor-side platform compromise affecting many tenants.

playbook.name: Vendor API Key/Secret Exposed in Public Code Repository
playbook.description: An organizational API key or secret used to authenticate to a vendor's API is discovered exposed in a public code repository.

steps.title: Confirm the exposure and identify the exact secret and repository
steps.desc: Validate the report (secret-scanning alert, researcher disclosure) and confirm the exact key/secret value and its exposure location.
steps.guidance: Capture the commit history and how long the secret was publicly visible.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exposed secret and exposure window.

steps.title: Determine the scope of access granted by the exposed secret
steps.desc: Identify what vendor systems, data, and permissions the exposed API key/secret grants access to.

steps.title: Review vendor-side usage logs for the exposed key during the exposure window
steps.desc: Request vendor API usage logs for the exposed key to check for unauthorized use.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the key was misused.

steps.title: Revoke the exposed key immediately
steps.desc: Revoke the exposed API key/secret at the vendor immediately, regardless of confirmed misuse.

steps.title: Remove the secret from the repository and its history
steps.desc: Purge the secret from the current codebase and rewrite git history or use provider tooling to scrub it from all commits.
steps.outcome: Secret removed from repository and history.

steps.title: Issue a new key under least-privilege scope and secrets-management practice
steps.desc: Provision a replacement key scoped to only necessary permissions and store it in a secrets manager rather than source code.
steps.outcome: New key issued and stored securely.

steps.title: Scan for other secrets exposed in the same repository
steps.desc: Run a full secret-scanning sweep of the repository and related repositories for additional exposed credentials.
steps.outcome: All exposed secrets identified and rotated.

steps.title: Restore normal integration operation with the new key
steps.desc: Update all systems using the old key to the new, securely stored credential and verify functionality.
steps.outcome: Integration restored with secure credential handling.

steps.title: Document incident and implement pre-commit secret scanning
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and deploy/enforce pre-commit hooks and CI secret-scanning to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Report filed and preventive controls deployed.

ITID-61333.def: A catch-all classification for a vendor API exploitation incident used during initial triage before the specific pattern is determined.
ITID-61333.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for a vendor API exploitation incident that has not yet been narrowed to a multi-tenant platform compromise or a specific organizational credential exposure.
scopeIncludes: Newly reported vendor API abuse incidents pending root-cause determination among the sibling patterns in this group
scopeExcludes: Any case confirmed as a multi-tenant vendor API compromise (ITID-61331)
Any case confirmed as an organizational credential exposure (ITID-61332)
ITID-61333.severity: Critical by default, consistent with the sibling leaves, until root cause narrows the classification.
ITID-61333.escalation: Escalate immediately as with any confirmed vendor API exploitation; reclassification should not delay containment.
indicators: Initial detection of anomalous vendor API activity with root cause under investigation
vectors: Unknown/unconfirmed pending investigation
rootCauses: Insufficient initial forensic detail to determine the exploitation pattern
mitreTechniques: T1552.001 Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
controls: Incident triage workflow requiring reclassification within a defined SLA once root cause is known
ITID-61333.detection: Not applicable as a distinct detection surface; this leaf exists for classification triage, not detection engineering.
ITID-61333.response: Handle with full vendor-API-exploitation response urgency while root-cause investigation proceeds; reclassify promptly once determined.
metrics: Number of incidents held in this bucket beyond the triage SLA
ITID-61333.notes: This is an intake/triage leaf; every incident logged here should be reclassified into a specific sibling ITID once root cause is established.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Vendor API Exploitation
playbook.description: A vendor's API is exploited through an unspecified or unclassified vector, potentially affecting the organization.

steps.title: Confirm the vendor API exploitation report
steps.desc: Validate the report and identify the specific API and exploitation method involved.

steps.title: Review organizational usage of the affected API for impact
steps.desc: Check organizational logs and integration records for exposure via the exploited API.

steps.title: Rotate organizational credentials for the vendor API
steps.desc: Rotate API keys/tokens used to access the affected vendor API.

steps.title: Restrict or disable the integration pending vendor fix
steps.desc: Limit or pause use of the affected API integration until remediated.

steps.title: Verify vendor's remediation of the exploited vulnerability
steps.desc: Confirm the vendor has fixed the exploited API vulnerability.
steps.abort: If unconfirmed, keep integration restricted.

steps.title: Assess for unauthorized data access via the exploit
steps.desc: Determine if organizational data was accessed or altered as a result of the exploitation.

steps.title: Restore full integration functionality
steps.desc: Re-enable the integration once remediation is confirmed.

steps.title: Determine notification obligations
steps.desc: Assess with Legal/Privacy whether notification is required based on impact findings.

steps.title: Document incident and update API integration risk review
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and update vendor API risk review procedures.

ITID-61341.def: The compromise of an organization's or vendor's CI/CD pipeline infrastructure (build orchestrator, pipeline configuration, artifact repository, deployment automation) enabling an attacker to inject malicious code, alter build artifacts, or manipulate deployment targets without going through an individual developer's environment, resulting in critical downstream disruption.
ITID-61341.purpose: Captures a compromise of the automated CI/CD orchestration system itself (as distinct from an individual developer's environment) that leads to malicious code or configuration reaching production, causing critical disruption.
scopeIncludes: Compromise of pipeline-as-code configuration (e.g., a CI YAML file modified to exfiltrate secrets or inject code)
Unauthorized access to a build orchestrator's admin console used to alter build steps or deployment targets
Compromise of an artifact repository allowing substitution of a build output
scopeExcludes: Compromise of an individual developer's workstation or IDE prior to commit (ITID-61312)
Tampering with an already-published distribution artifact after it leaves the pipeline (ITID-61311)
ITID-61341.severity: Critical, since a compromised pipeline can affect every build and deployment that passes through it going forward, not just a single release.
ITID-61341.priority: P1 immediately upon any indication of unauthorized access to pipeline configuration, orchestration, or artifact-repository infrastructure.
ITID-61341.escalation: Escalate to platform/DevOps engineering and security leadership immediately; halt all pipeline activity until the scope of compromise is understood.
indicators: Unexplained changes to pipeline configuration files or scripts
New or modified service-account credentials with pipeline-admin privileges
Build artifacts with hashes that do not match the expected source commit
vectors: Exploitation of an exposed or misconfigured CI/CD administration interface
Compromised service-account credentials with broad pipeline permissions
Malicious pull request merged with pipeline-modifying changes due to insufficient review gates
rootCauses: Pipeline infrastructure not isolated from general corporate network access
Overprivileged service accounts used by the pipeline with no least-privilege scoping
No mandatory review/approval gate for changes to pipeline configuration itself
mitreTechniques: T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
controls: Least-privilege, short-lived credentials for all pipeline service accounts
Mandatory review/approval for any change to pipeline configuration
Build provenance verification (e.g., SLSA-style attestation) comparing artifact hashes to source commits
ITID-61341.detection: Moderate to strong when build provenance verification and pipeline-configuration change monitoring are in place; weak otherwise, since pipeline infrastructure often has broad implicit trust.
ITID-61341.response: Halt and isolate the affected pipeline, rotate all pipeline credentials, and rebuild from a verified known-good source and configuration state before resuming deployments.
metrics: Time to detect unauthorized pipeline-configuration changes
Percentage of builds covered by provenance/attestation verification
ITID-61341.notes: This is the sole leaf under CI/CD Pipeline Attack in this domain and functions as both the specific and general classification for pipeline-infrastructure compromise, distinct from developer-environment or post-build artifact compromise.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General CI/CD Pipeline Attack (Supply Chain Context)
playbook.description: A vendor's or the organization's CI/CD pipeline is attacked, potentially injecting malicious artifacts into software delivered to or built for the organization.

steps.title: Confirm the CI/CD pipeline attack report and scope
steps.desc: Validate the disclosure and determine whether the affected pipeline is vendor-operated or organization-operated, and what stage (build, test, deploy) was attacked.
steps.outcome: Confirmed pipeline attack scope and location.

steps.title: Identify artifacts produced by the compromised pipeline
steps.desc: Determine which build artifacts, container images, or releases were produced during the compromise window.

steps.title: Determine internal deployment of affected artifacts
steps.desc: Identify where the potentially tainted artifacts were deployed internally or delivered to customers.

steps.title: Suspend the affected pipeline
steps.desc: Halt further builds/deployments from the compromised pipeline immediately.

steps.title: Isolate or roll back systems running affected artifacts
steps.desc: Contain or roll back deployments that used artifacts produced during the compromise window.
steps.outcome: Affected deployments contained or rolled back.

steps.title: Rotate pipeline credentials, signing keys, and secrets
steps.desc: Rotate all CI/CD credentials, deployment keys, and code-signing keys accessible to the compromised pipeline.

steps.title: Identify and remove the attack vector from the pipeline
steps.desc: Determine how the pipeline was compromised (compromised plugin, exposed runner, malicious commit) and remove the vector.

steps.title: Rebuild artifacts from a verified clean pipeline state
steps.desc: Rebuild all affected artifacts from a validated, hardened pipeline configuration.

steps.title: Resume pipeline operations with enhanced controls
steps.desc: Restore pipeline operation with added controls such as signed commits, runner isolation, and dependency pinning.

steps.title: Notify downstream consumers of affected artifacts if applicable
steps.desc: If tainted artifacts were distributed to customers or other internal teams, determine and execute notification.
steps.outcome: Notification decision documented and executed if required.

steps.title: Document incident and strengthen CI/CD security posture
steps.desc: File a post-incident report recommending pipeline hardening measures (least-privilege runners, artifact signing, dependency review gates).

ITID-61411.def: The discovery of a firmware-level backdoor embedded in vendor-manufactured hardware, attributed with credible evidence to a nation-state mandate, export-control leverage, or state-directed intelligence requirement, rather than a compromise introduced independently by the contract manufacturer.
ITID-61411.purpose: Classifies confirmed or strongly suspected firmware backdoors deliberately inserted into manufactured hardware at the direction of, or on behalf of, a nation-state.
scopeIncludes: Firmware backdoors discovered in hardware from manufacturers subject to known state intelligence-sharing mandates
Backdoors matching known nation-state tooling or TTPs identified by threat intelligence
Government advisories naming specific hardware as containing state-mandated backdoors
scopeExcludes: Backdoors introduced independently by a contract manufacturer or OEM without state attribution (see ITID-61412)
Unattributed or unclassified firmware backdoors (see ITID-61413)
ITID-61411.severity: Critical, given nation-state capability and intent, and the strategic nature of the targeting.
ITID-61411.priority: P1, with immediate involvement of executive leadership and, where applicable, government/CISA coordination.
ITID-61411.escalation: Escalate immediately to executive leadership, legal, and relevant national cybersecurity authorities; treat as a strategic threat requiring coordinated disclosure handling.
indicators: Government or vendor advisory identifying state-mandated backdoor firmware
Threat intelligence correlating discovered firmware behavior with known nation-state implants
Independent security research publishing reverse-engineered evidence of the backdoor
vectors: Firmware-level implants inserted during manufacturing under state direction
Mandatory compliance backdoors required by local telecommunications/export law
Pre-OS boot-level persistence mechanisms embedded at the factory
rootCauses: Sourcing critical hardware from manufacturers subject to state intelligence-sharing obligations
Lack of firmware integrity verification at hardware receipt
Insufficient hardware supply-chain diversification
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: Firmware integrity verification and attestation at hardware receipt
Hardware supply-chain risk assessment considering vendor jurisdiction
Restricted procurement policy excluding vendors with known state-mandate risk
ITID-61411.detection: Low from internal telemetry alone; detection typically depends on independent security research, government advisories, or specialized firmware forensics.
ITID-61411.response: Isolate and decommission affected hardware, coordinate with government cybersecurity authorities, and reassess hardware sourcing strategy.
metrics: Number of hardware assets from higher-risk jurisdictions in inventory
Time to decommission affected hardware after confirmation
sops: Hardware Supply Chain Risk Assessment SOP
ITID-61411.notes: Differentiated from ITID-61412 by attribution: state mandate/direction versus independent manufacturer-level compromise.

playbook.name: Nation-State-Mandated Firmware Backdoor in Manufactured Hardware
playbook.description: Hardware manufactured or assembled under a nation-state's jurisdiction is found to contain a government-mandated firmware backdoor.

steps.title: Confirm the backdoor disclosure and affected hardware models
steps.desc: Validate the intelligence/vendor/researcher disclosure identifying the specific hardware models and firmware versions containing the mandated backdoor.
steps.guidance: Corroborate with government advisories, security researcher publications, and vendor statements where available.
steps.outcome: Confirmed affected hardware models and firmware versions.

steps.title: Inventory internal deployment of the affected hardware
steps.desc: Search asset management records for every unit of the affected hardware in use across the organization's environment.

steps.title: Assess network exposure and data sensitivity of affected hardware locations
steps.desc: Determine what networks the affected hardware sits on and what sensitive data or functions could be exposed via the backdoor.

steps.title: Network-isolate or restrict affected hardware
steps.desc: Segment affected devices onto isolated network zones with restricted outbound connectivity pending replacement.
steps.outcome: Affected hardware isolated from sensitive network segments.
steps.abort: If isolation is operationally infeasible immediately, apply strict egress filtering as interim compensating control.

steps.title: Escalate to executive leadership, Legal, and government liaison contacts
steps.desc: Given the nation-state nexus, escalate immediately to executive leadership, Legal, and relevant government/regulatory liaison contacts (e.g., CISA).

steps.title: Monitor affected network segments for anomalous outbound traffic
steps.desc: Deploy enhanced monitoring on network segments hosting affected hardware to detect backdoor communication attempts.
steps.outcome: Monitoring in place with alerting configured.

steps.title: Procure and deploy replacement hardware from a trusted supply chain
steps.desc: Replace affected hardware with units from a vetted, trusted supplier rather than attempting to patch/clean the compromised firmware.
steps.guidance: Do not treat firmware reflash as sufficient remediation for suspected hardware-level or persistent backdoors.

steps.title: Securely dispose of or quarantine removed hardware for forensic/legal purposes
steps.desc: Retain removed units in secure evidence custody rather than disposing of them, pending Legal/government guidance.
steps.outcome: Removed hardware securely quarantined with chain of custody documented.

steps.title: Validate replacement hardware supply chain provenance
steps.desc: Confirm the replacement hardware's supply chain and manufacturing provenance meet organizational trusted-sourcing standards.
steps.outcome: Provenance verified before full production reliance.

steps.title: Restore normal operations on replacement hardware
steps.desc: Return the network segment to normal operation using the replacement, verified hardware.

steps.title: Document incident and revise hardware sourcing/vetting standards
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and update procurement standards to restrict sourcing from jurisdictions or vendors of concern.
steps.outcome: Report filed and sourcing standards revised.

ITID-61412.def: The discovery of a firmware-level backdoor embedded in vendor hardware, introduced by a contract manufacturer or original equipment manufacturer (OEM) acting independently — for financial gain, negligence, or unauthorized third-party subcontracting — rather than under state mandate.
ITID-61412.purpose: Classifies firmware backdoors introduced independently at the contract manufacturer or OEM level, without evidence of nation-state direction.
scopeIncludes: Backdoors traced to a specific contract manufacturer's production process
Undisclosed remote-access functionality built into firmware by an OEM for support or monetization purposes
Backdoors introduced by an unauthorized subcontractor in the manufacturing chain
scopeExcludes: Backdoors attributed to nation-state mandate (see ITID-61411)
Unattributed backdoors where the source has not been determined (see ITID-61413)
ITID-61412.severity: High, given the direct compromise of hardware integrity, though generally lower strategic severity than nation-state attribution.
ITID-61412.priority: P1 for affected hardware in production environments.
ITID-61412.escalation: Escalate to procurement and legal to review manufacturer contracts and consider supplier disqualification.
indicators: Security researcher disclosure of undocumented firmware functionality
Vendor admission of an OEM-introduced backdoor following investigation
Firmware analysis revealing hardcoded credentials or hidden remote-access services
vectors: Hardcoded backdoor credentials left in production firmware
Undocumented remote-support functionality with insufficient access controls
Unauthorized code introduced by a subcontracted manufacturing partner
rootCauses: Lack of firmware source-code review requirements in manufacturing contracts
Insufficient oversight of subcontracted manufacturing steps
Absence of independent firmware security testing before deployment
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: Contractual firmware security review and audit rights over manufacturers
Independent firmware security testing prior to deployment
Manufacturer subcontracting disclosure requirements
ITID-61412.detection: Low to moderate; typically discovered through independent security research or targeted firmware analysis rather than routine monitoring.
ITID-61412.response: Patch or replace affected firmware, review manufacturer contracts, and evaluate supplier disqualification.
metrics: Number of manufacturers subject to firmware security audit
Time to firmware remediation after disclosure
detections: Firmware analysis findings from independent security testing
ITID-61412.notes: Differentiated from ITID-61411 by attribution: independent manufacturer action rather than state direction.

playbook.name: Firmware Backdoor Introduced at Contract Manufacturer/OEM Level
playbook.description: A firmware backdoor is discovered introduced during contract manufacturing or OEM assembly of hardware used by the organization.

steps.title: Confirm the OEM-level backdoor disclosure and affected product lines
steps.desc: Validate the disclosure identifying the contract manufacturer, affected product lines, and firmware versions.
steps.outcome: Confirmed affected product lines and manufacturer.

steps.title: Inventory internal deployment of affected products
steps.desc: Identify all units of the affected product deployed internally, including serial number ranges tied to the implicated manufacturing batches.
steps.outcome: Internal deployment inventory with batch traceability completed.

steps.title: Analyze the backdoor's capability and access scope
steps.desc: Review vendor/researcher analysis of what access or control the backdoor grants.

steps.title: Isolate or restrict affected devices from sensitive networks
steps.desc: Segment affected units away from sensitive systems pending remediation guidance.

steps.title: Escalate to the OEM/vendor and Procurement
steps.desc: Notify the OEM/vendor for remediation guidance and involve Procurement for contractual remedy discussion.

steps.title: Apply vendor-issued clean firmware if available and verified
steps.desc: If the vendor provides a verified clean firmware update, evaluate whether reflashing is sufficient or replacement is required based on backdoor persistence characteristics.
steps.guidance: Favor hardware replacement if the backdoor could survive reflash (e.g., embedded in secondary chip).
steps.abort: If clean firmware cannot be verified as fully removing the backdoor, proceed to hardware replacement.

steps.title: Replace or reflash affected units per the determined approach
steps.desc: Execute the chosen remediation (replacement or verified reflash) across all affected units.

steps.title: Verify remediated units before returning to production
steps.desc: Confirm remediated/replaced units are free of the backdoor before restoring to sensitive network segments.

steps.title: Restore normal operations
steps.desc: Return verified units to normal production use.

steps.title: Document incident and reassess OEM/manufacturer vetting requirements
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and update hardware procurement due-diligence requirements regarding contract manufacturers.
steps.outcome: Report filed and vetting requirements updated.

ITID-61413.def: The discovery of a firmware-level backdoor in vendor-supplied hardware where the responsible party has not yet been attributed to either a nation-state mandate or an independent manufacturer action.
ITID-61413.purpose: Provides an intake classification for discovered firmware backdoors in vendor hardware where attribution (nation-state vs. independent manufacturer) has not yet been established.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered firmware anomalies pending attribution investigation
Third-party or researcher disclosures without attribution detail
scopeExcludes: Backdoors confirmed as nation-state mandated (see ITID-61411)
Backdoors confirmed as independent manufacturer/OEM action (see ITID-61412)
ITID-61413.severity: High pending attribution; treat with the same urgency as a confirmed nation-state case until ruled out.
ITID-61413.escalation: Escalate to threat intelligence and executive leadership for attribution assessment while containment proceeds in parallel.
indicators: Firmware analysis revealing undocumented functionality with unclear origin
Initial researcher disclosure lacking attribution detail
vectors: Not yet determined pending attribution
rootCauses: Lack of firmware integrity verification allowing undetected insertion at any supply-chain stage
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: Firmware integrity verification and attestation program
Threat intelligence engagement for attribution support
ITID-61413.detection: Low; discovery typically precedes attribution and relies on external research or forensic firmware analysis.
ITID-61413.response: Contain and isolate affected hardware immediately, pursue attribution in parallel, and reclassify once attribution is established.
metrics: Mean time to attribution after discovery
ITID-61413.notes: This is the intake bucket for Firmware Backdoors in Vendor Hardware; reclassify once attribution is established.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Firmware Backdoor in Vendor Hardware
playbook.description: A firmware backdoor is discovered in vendor-supplied hardware through an unspecified or unclassified vector.

steps.title: Confirm the firmware backdoor disclosure
steps.desc: Validate the report and identify the specific hardware model and firmware version affected.
steps.outcome: Confirmed affected hardware and firmware version.

steps.title: Inventory internal deployment of affected hardware
steps.desc: Identify all units of the affected hardware deployed internally.

steps.title: Assess exposure and criticality of affected device locations
steps.desc: Determine what network segments and functions the affected hardware supports.

steps.title: Isolate affected hardware
steps.desc: Restrict network access for affected devices pending remediation.

steps.title: Notify vendor and request remediation guidance
steps.desc: Engage the vendor for clarification and a remediation plan.

steps.title: Apply vendor patch or replace affected hardware
steps.desc: Remediate per vendor guidance, replacing hardware if the backdoor cannot be reliably removed via firmware update.

steps.title: Verify remediation effectiveness
steps.desc: Confirm through testing or vendor attestation that the backdoor is no longer present.

steps.title: Restore normal operations
steps.desc: Return remediated hardware to normal production use.

steps.title: Document incident and update hardware vetting practices
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and recommend hardware/firmware vetting improvements.

ITID-61421.def: The discovery of a counterfeit IoT device — one falsely branded as a legitimate manufacturer's product — that entered the organization's environment through a legitimate retail or distribution channel, distinct from devices shipped pre-compromised by their actual manufacturer.
ITID-61421.purpose: Classifies incidents where counterfeit IoT devices are discovered to have entered the organization's environment despite being purchased through a legitimate, authorized retail channel.
scopeIncludes: Devices found to be counterfeit despite being purchased from an authorized retailer or distributor
Counterfeit devices identified via serial-number or authenticity verification failures
Devices exhibiting hardware inconsistent with the genuine manufacturer's specifications
scopeExcludes: Genuine devices shipped with malicious firmware pre-installed by the actual manufacturer (see ITID-61422)
Counterfeit devices whose entry channel has not yet been determined (see ITID-61423)
ITID-61421.severity: Medium-High, given uncertain build quality and likely embedded malicious functionality.
ITID-61421.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the device has network connectivity to sensitive systems.
ITID-61421.escalation: Escalate to procurement to review the retail channel's authentication controls, and to security operations to assess network exposure.
indicators: Serial number or authenticity check failure against manufacturer records
Physical inspection revealing inconsistent build quality or components
Manufacturer confirmation that a device is not a genuine product
vectors: Counterfeit devices infiltrating authorized distributor inventory
Grey-market goods mixed into legitimate retail supply
Repackaged counterfeit hardware sold as genuine stock
rootCauses: Retail/distribution channel authenticity verification gaps
Lack of organizational device-authenticity verification at receipt
Procurement prioritizing cost over verified supply-chain provenance
controls: Device authenticity verification at receipt (serial number, manufacturer registration)
Approved-vendor procurement policy limiting purchases to verified channels
Network segmentation isolating IoT devices from sensitive systems
ITID-61421.detection: Low to moderate; typically discovered via physical inspection, authenticity verification programs, or anomalous device behavior on the network.
ITID-61421.response: Remove and quarantine the counterfeit device, notify the retailer/distributor, and review the authenticity-verification gap.
metrics: Number of counterfeit devices detected per year
Percentage of IoT procurement verified against manufacturer authenticity programs
ITID-61421.notes: Differentiated from ITID-61422 by the counterfeit/impersonation angle versus genuine-device-with-malicious-firmware; differentiated from ITID-61423 by confirmed legitimate retail channel entry.

playbook.name: Counterfeit IoT Device Sold Through Legitimate Retail Channel
playbook.description: A counterfeit IoT device is discovered in use, having been procured through what appeared to be a legitimate retail or distribution channel.

steps.title: Confirm the device is counterfeit
steps.desc: Validate suspicion or report through vendor serial-number verification, physical inspection, or vendor authentication tools.
steps.guidance: Contact the legitimate manufacturer's anti-counterfeiting team if available.
steps.abort: If the device cannot be conclusively confirmed as counterfeit, treat as suspicious pending further analysis.

steps.title: Identify the procurement channel and other units from the same source
steps.desc: Trace the purchase order/reseller and identify any other units procured from the same channel that may also be counterfeit.

steps.title: Assess what the counterfeit device had access to
steps.desc: Determine network access, data handling, and functional role of the counterfeit device before its status was known.

steps.title: Quarantine and physically remove all identified counterfeit units
steps.desc: Disconnect and physically remove all identified counterfeit devices from the network and operational use.
steps.guidance: Do not attempt to simply reconfigure counterfeit devices for continued use.

steps.title: Rotate any credentials or network keys the counterfeit device had access to
steps.desc: Rotate Wi-Fi keys, certificates, or credentials configured on or accessible to the counterfeit device.

steps.title: Forensically examine a sample counterfeit unit if warranted
steps.desc: If risk warrants, forensically examine a counterfeit unit for malicious firmware or hidden functionality.

steps.title: Report the counterfeit source to the legitimate manufacturer and retailer
steps.desc: File a report with the legitimate manufacturer's anti-counterfeiting program and the retailer/marketplace where purchased.

steps.title: Procure legitimate replacement devices through verified channels
steps.desc: Replace removed devices with units procured through verified, authorized distribution channels.

steps.title: Document incident and update procurement verification procedures
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and require authorized-channel verification and device authentication checks for future IoT procurement.
steps.outcome: Report filed and procurement procedures updated.

ITID-61422.def: The discovery of malicious or unauthorized firmware pre-installed on a genuine IoT device at the point of manufacture or distribution, rather than a device that is itself counterfeit.
ITID-61422.purpose: Classifies incidents where a genuine, authentic IoT device is discovered to have been shipped from the manufacturer with malicious firmware already installed.
scopeIncludes: Genuine devices found to contain malicious firmware upon initial deployment or analysis
Manufacturer or distributor confirmation that a production batch shipped with compromised firmware
Malicious functionality (e.g., unauthorized beaconing, hidden accounts) discovered in factory-installed firmware
scopeExcludes: Counterfeit devices impersonating a genuine manufacturer's product (see ITID-61421)
Devices whose firmware compromise source has not yet been determined (see ITID-61423)
ITID-61422.severity: High, given the device is genuine and trusted by default, making the compromise harder to detect through authenticity checks alone.
ITID-61422.priority: P1 for devices with network connectivity to production or sensitive environments.
ITID-61422.escalation: Escalate to the manufacturer for batch-level investigation and to security operations to identify all deployed units from the affected batch.
indicators: Unexpected outbound network connections from a newly deployed IoT device
Firmware analysis revealing unauthorized code or hidden accounts
Manufacturer security bulletin identifying an affected production batch
vectors: Malicious firmware inserted during the manufacturer's production process
Compromise of the manufacturer's firmware build/signing pipeline
Malicious code introduced by a firmware supplier upstream of the device manufacturer
rootCauses: Lack of firmware integrity verification prior to device deployment
Insufficient manufacturer supply-chain security for firmware build pipelines
No network behavior baselining for newly deployed IoT devices
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: Firmware integrity verification prior to deployment
Network behavior baselining and anomaly detection for IoT devices
Manufacturer batch/lot tracking for recall purposes
ITID-61422.detection: Moderate: network anomaly detection on IoT segments can surface unexpected behavior; firmware-level confirmation typically requires vendor or forensic analysis.
ITID-61422.response: Isolate affected devices, identify all units from the same production batch, and coordinate with the manufacturer on remediation or recall.
metrics: Number of devices identified from an affected production batch
Time to isolate affected devices after discovery
ITID-61422.notes: Differentiated from ITID-61421 by device authenticity: genuine device with compromised firmware versus counterfeit device.

playbook.name: IoT Device Shipped with Pre-Installed Malicious Firmware
playbook.description: An IoT device is discovered to have shipped from the manufacturer with pre-installed malicious firmware.

steps.title: Confirm the malicious pre-installed firmware finding
steps.desc: Validate the discovery (internal analysis, vendor disclosure, researcher report) identifying the malicious firmware and affected device model/batch.
steps.outcome: Confirmed affected device model and firmware.

steps.title: Inventory all deployed units of the affected model/batch
steps.desc: Identify all internal deployments matching the affected model and manufacturing batch/serial range.

steps.title: Analyze the malicious firmware's behavior and communication patterns
steps.desc: Determine what the malicious firmware does (data exfiltration, botnet C2, backdoor access) and gather network IOCs.

steps.title: Disconnect and network-isolate all affected devices
steps.desc: Immediately remove affected devices from the network or place them on an isolated quarantine VLAN.

steps.title: Block known C2/IOC network indicators
steps.desc: Deploy firewall/DNS blocks for any identified command-and-control infrastructure.

steps.title: Replace affected devices rather than attempting firmware cleanup
steps.desc: Physically replace affected devices with clean units, given firmware-level malicious code may not be reliably removable by reflashing alone.
steps.guidance: Only accept vendor-reflash remediation if vendor provides verifiable evidence of full firmware chain-of-trust restoration.
steps.outcome: Affected devices replaced or verifiably remediated.

steps.title: Preserve a sample of affected devices for forensic/legal purposes
steps.desc: Retain a sample of removed devices in secure evidence custody rather than disposing of all units.
steps.outcome: Evidence samples preserved with chain of custody.

steps.title: Deploy verified clean replacement devices
steps.desc: Return the affected network segment to normal operation using clean, verified devices.
steps.outcome: Normal operations restored with clean devices.

steps.title: Document incident and require pre-deployment firmware verification
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and implement pre-deployment firmware integrity verification for future IoT procurement.
steps.outcome: Report filed and verification process implemented.

ITID-61423.def: The discovery of a rogue or suspicious IoT device in the organization's environment, in a supply-chain context, where whether the device is counterfeit or a genuine device with compromised firmware has not yet been determined.
ITID-61423.purpose: Provides an intake classification for a discovered rogue IoT device before it is confirmed as either counterfeit or a genuine device with malicious firmware.
scopeIncludes: Newly discovered unauthorized or suspicious IoT devices pending analysis
Devices flagged by network monitoring before physical or firmware inspection is complete
scopeExcludes: Devices confirmed as counterfeit via a legitimate channel (see ITID-61421)
Devices confirmed as genuine with malicious pre-installed firmware (see ITID-61422)
Rogue devices connected without any procurement/supply-chain nexus (a general asset-security ITID)
ITID-61423.escalation: Escalate to security operations to isolate the device from the network pending physical and firmware inspection.
indicators: Network access control (NAC) alert for an unrecognized IoT device
Physical discovery of an unaccounted-for device on the network
vectors: Not yet determined pending classification
rootCauses: Incomplete IoT asset inventory
Lack of network access control for IoT device onboarding
controls: Network access control (NAC) for IoT device onboarding
IoT asset inventory management
ITID-61423.detection: Moderate: NAC and network monitoring can surface unrecognized devices, though root-cause classification requires further inspection.
ITID-61423.response: Isolate the device immediately, conduct physical and firmware inspection, and reclassify once the compromise type is confirmed.
metrics: Mean time to reclassify from intake to specific leaf
ITID-61423.notes: This is the intake bucket for Rogue IoT Devices; reclassify once the device's compromise origin is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Rogue IoT Device (Supply Chain Context)
playbook.description: A rogue or compromised IoT device from the supply chain is discovered in the environment through an unspecified vector.

steps.title: Confirm the rogue device finding and its origin
steps.desc: Validate the discovery and determine how the device entered the environment and its supply chain origin.
steps.outcome: Confirmed device origin and rogue status.

steps.title: Identify other units from the same source
steps.desc: Search for additional devices procured from the same source that may share the same issue.

steps.title: Assess network access and behavior of the device
steps.desc: Determine what network segments the device accessed and any anomalous behavior observed.

steps.title: Disconnect and isolate the device(s)
steps.desc: Remove or isolate all identified rogue devices from the network.

steps.title: Rotate credentials/keys accessible to the device
steps.desc: Rotate network keys or credentials the device had access to.

steps.title: Replace or remediate the device per risk assessment
steps.desc: Replace the device or apply verified remediation depending on the nature of the compromise.

steps.title: Verify no residual network impact
steps.desc: Confirm no persistence or residual compromise remains on the network segment.

steps.title: Restore normal operations
steps.desc: Return the affected area to normal operation with verified clean devices.

steps.title: Document incident and improve device procurement verification
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and improve procurement/device-authentication verification procedures.

ITID-61431.def: The interdiction of hardware while in transit through the shipping/logistics chain, during which an adversary installs a malicious physical implant before the equipment reaches the organization, distinct from tampering that is merely indicated by packaging evidence without a confirmed implant.
ITID-61431.purpose: Classifies incidents where hardware is intercepted and physically implanted with malicious components while in transit between manufacturer and destination.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed discovery of a physical implant (e.g., rogue chip, altered component) installed during shipping
Forensic hardware teardown revealing unauthorized components not present at manufacture
Chain-of-custody gaps correlating with a confirmed implant
scopeExcludes: Tampered packaging/seals without a confirmed implant (see ITID-61432)
Firmware-only compromise with no physical hardware modification (see Firmware Backdoors group)
ITID-61431.severity: Critical, given the sophistication required for physical interdiction and the typical association with well-resourced threat actors.
ITID-61431.priority: P1, with immediate hardware quarantine and forensic analysis.
ITID-61431.escalation: Escalate immediately to executive leadership, legal, and (where the threat actor is suspected to be state-sponsored) national cybersecurity authorities.
indicators: Physical teardown revealing an unauthorized component or modified circuit board
Weight or dimensional discrepancies versus manufacturer specifications
Chain-of-custody records showing an unexplained handling gap during transit
vectors: Interception and physical modification of hardware during freight/customs transit
Insider compromise of a logistics or freight-forwarding employee
Extended dwell time at an intermediate transit point enabling tampering
rootCauses: Lack of tamper-evident packaging and chain-of-custody tracking
Extended or unmonitored transit routes for sensitive hardware
No physical/firmware verification process at hardware receipt
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: Tamper-evident packaging and continuous chain-of-custody tracking
Direct-ship/trusted-courier programs for sensitive hardware
Hardware receipt verification including physical and firmware inspection
ITID-61431.detection: Low; detection typically requires deliberate forensic hardware inspection rather than routine monitoring, since implants are designed to evade casual observation.
ITID-61431.response: Quarantine and forensically analyze the affected hardware, review chain-of-custody records, and reassess logistics/shipping controls for sensitive equipment.
metrics: Number of hardware shipments receiving full tamper inspection
Number of confirmed interdiction incidents per year
ITID-61431.notes: Differentiated from ITID-61432 by confirmation: an actual implant is found here, versus indicative-but-unconfirmed tampering evidence in the sibling leaf.

playbook.name: Hardware Interdiction During Shipping (Implant Installed En Route)
playbook.description: Hardware is intercepted during shipping and modified with a covert implant before reaching the organization.

steps.title: Confirm suspicion of interdiction through physical/chain-of-custody anomalies
steps.desc: Review shipping chain-of-custody records, tracking data, and physical inspection reports for gaps, unexpected routing, or delivery delays suggesting interdiction.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference expected carrier route/timeline against actual tracking history.
steps.outcome: Confirmed or ruled out evidence of interdiction opportunity.

steps.title: Physically inspect the hardware for implants or tampering
steps.desc: Conduct physical inspection (visual, X-ray/imaging if available, weight comparison) of the received hardware for unauthorized components.
steps.guidance: Engage a specialized hardware forensics team if internal capability is insufficient.
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence or absence of physical tampering/implant.

steps.title: Determine network/data exposure if hardware was already deployed
steps.desc: If the hardware was already placed into service before discovery, assess what network segments and data it was exposed to.

steps.title: Isolate the affected hardware and preserve it as evidence
steps.desc: Immediately disconnect the hardware from all networks and preserve it intact for forensic analysis, maintaining chain of custody.
steps.guidance: Do not power-cycle or attempt to remove the implant before forensic imaging.

steps.title: Escalate to Legal, Security leadership, and law enforcement as appropriate
steps.desc: Given the deliberate nature of shipment interdiction, escalate to Legal and Security leadership, and involve law enforcement or government partners if nation-state involvement is suspected.

steps.title: Review and isolate any other in-transit shipments from the same supplier/route
steps.desc: Identify other shipments in the same logistics chain and hold them for inspection before deployment.

steps.title: Conduct forensic analysis of the implant
steps.desc: Perform detailed forensic analysis of the physical implant to determine its capability and any network activity it may have conducted.

steps.title: Dispose of or securely destroy compromised hardware per Legal guidance
steps.desc: Once forensic analysis is complete and Legal has approved, securely destroy or retain the compromised hardware.
steps.outcome: Compromised hardware handled per Legal direction.

steps.title: Implement secure logistics controls and redeploy verified hardware
steps.desc: Establish tamper-evident shipping and chain-of-custody verification for future shipments, and deploy replacement hardware verified free of tampering.
steps.outcome: Verified hardware deployed under enhanced logistics security.

steps.title: Document incident and revise supply chain logistics security requirements
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and update requirements for tamper-evident packaging, direct-ship arrangements, and carrier vetting.
steps.outcome: Report filed and logistics security requirements updated.

ITID-61432.def: The discovery of tamper-evident packaging or security seals showing signs of interference on hardware prior to its delivery and acceptance, indicating possible compromise during transit that has not yet been confirmed through forensic hardware analysis.
ITID-61432.purpose: Classifies incidents where physical evidence of tampering (broken seals, altered packaging) is found on equipment before delivery, without yet confirming an actual implant.
scopeIncludes: Broken, re-applied, or mismatched tamper-evident seals discovered at receipt
Packaging inconsistent with manufacturer specifications (weight, dimensions, materials)
Shipping documentation gaps suggesting unauthorized handling
scopeExcludes: Cases where forensic analysis has confirmed a physical implant (see ITID-61431, hardware interdiction)
Routine packaging damage attributable to normal shipping wear with no security indicators
ITID-61432.severity: Medium-High pending forensic confirmation; treat as a potential interdiction until ruled out.
ITID-61432.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if forensic inspection confirms tampering.
ITID-61432.escalation: Escalate to security operations to quarantine the equipment and initiate forensic inspection before deployment.
indicators: Tamper-evident seal showing signs of removal and reapplication
Packaging materials inconsistent with the manufacturer's standard
Shipping chain-of-custody documentation with unexplained gaps
vectors: Unauthorized opening of packaging during an intermediate transit stop
Resealing with counterfeit or mismatched tamper-evident materials
rootCauses: Lack of standardized tamper-evident packaging requirements from vendors
Insufficient chain-of-custody verification at each transit handoff
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: Mandatory tamper-evident packaging with vendor-provided verification codes
Chain-of-custody tracking at every transit handoff
Quarantine-and-inspect procedure for any hardware with seal discrepancies
ITID-61432.detection: Low to moderate; relies on receiving personnel actively inspecting seals and packaging against known-good baselines.
ITID-61432.response: Quarantine the equipment immediately, do not deploy pending forensic inspection, and reclassify to ITID-61431 if an implant is confirmed.
metrics: Number of tamper-evidence incidents flagged at receipt per year
Percentage confirmed as actual compromise upon forensic inspection
ITID-61432.notes: Differentiated from ITID-61431 by confirmation status: indicative packaging evidence here versus a confirmed physical implant in the sibling leaf.

playbook.name: Tampered Packaging/Seal Indicating Equipment Compromise Before Delivery
playbook.description: Equipment arrives with packaging or tamper-evident seals showing signs of tampering prior to delivery.

steps.title: Document the tampering evidence upon receipt
steps.desc: Photograph and document the damaged/broken seals or packaging anomalies immediately upon discovery, before further handling.
steps.guidance: Do not open or power on the equipment before documentation is complete.

steps.title: Verify seal/packaging integrity against vendor's tamper-evidence standard
steps.desc: Compare observed packaging/seal condition against the vendor's documented tamper-evident packaging specification.
steps.outcome: Confirmed deviation from expected tamper-evident condition.

steps.title: Reconstruct chain of custody for the shipment
steps.desc: Review carrier tracking, handoff points, and storage locations to identify where tampering may have occurred.

steps.title: Quarantine the equipment without deploying it
steps.desc: Hold the equipment in a secure, isolated storage location and do not connect it to any network or power it into production use.

steps.title: Notify the vendor and carrier, and escalate to Security and Legal
steps.desc: Report the tampering to the vendor and carrier and escalate internally for a forensic decision.
steps.outcome: Vendor, carrier, and internal stakeholders notified.

steps.title: Conduct physical/forensic inspection of the equipment
steps.desc: Inspect the equipment internally (with specialized help if needed) to determine whether tampering occurred beyond the packaging.
steps.outcome: Determination of whether the equipment itself was compromised.

steps.title: Reject and return the equipment, or approve for use based on findings
steps.desc: Based on inspection findings, decide whether to reject/return the equipment to the vendor or clear it for deployment.
steps.abort: If equipment compromise cannot be ruled out, reject the shipment.

steps.title: Obtain and verify a replacement shipment if rejected
steps.desc: Coordinate with the vendor for a replacement shipment with enhanced tamper-evident controls.

steps.title: Document incident and strengthen receiving-inspection procedures
steps.desc: File a post-incident report and update receiving-dock inspection procedures for tamper-evidence verification.

ITID-61433.def: An initial report of possible tampering with equipment during transit, prior to determination of whether the case involves a confirmed physical implant or only indicative packaging/seal evidence.
ITID-61433.purpose: Provides an intake classification for tampered-equipment-in-transit reports before it is determined whether a physical implant is confirmed or only packaging evidence exists.
scopeIncludes: Initial receiving reports of suspected tampering pending inspection
Reports lacking sufficient detail to classify as confirmed implant or packaging evidence
scopeExcludes: Confirmed physical implants (see ITID-61431)
Confirmed packaging/seal tampering evidence without implant (see ITID-61432)
ITID-61433.escalation: Escalate to security operations for immediate quarantine and inspection.
indicators: Ambiguous receiving report citing possible tampering
Employee report of unusual equipment condition at receipt
vectors: Not yet determined pending classification
rootCauses: Lack of a standardized tamper-inspection process at receipt
