steps.guidance: Check certificate serial number against internal PKI/HSM issuance logs or vendor's published cert list.
steps.outcome: Confirmed whether the private key was misused or the certificate cloned/misissued.

steps.title: Identify all binaries signed with the compromised certificate
steps.desc: Search endpoint telemetry, software inventory, and build artifact repositories for every binary signed with the affected certificate.
steps.guidance: Query EDR file-catalog by signer thumbprint across the fleet.
steps.outcome: Complete inventory of signed binaries in the environment, malicious and legitimate.

steps.title: Revoke the compromised certificate
steps.desc: Request immediate revocation of the compromised code-signing certificate from the issuing CA and publish updated CRL/OCSP responses.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the CA and internal PKI team; notify the vendor if the certificate is theirs.
steps.outcome: Certificate revoked and revocation status propagated.

steps.title: Block execution of binaries signed with the compromised cert
steps.desc: Deploy application-control (allowlisting) rules or EDR blocklist entries to prevent execution of any binary signed by the compromised certificate thumbprint.
steps.guidance: Use AppLocker/WDAC or EDR signer-based blocking rules.
steps.outcome: Malicious signed binaries cannot execute on any endpoint.
steps.abort: If this would block legitimate vendor software still needed, apply targeted hash-based blocks instead of full signer block.

steps.title: Isolate hosts that executed malicious signed binaries
steps.desc: Network-isolate and preserve forensic evidence on any host confirmed to have run a maliciously signed binary.

steps.title: Remove malicious binaries and issue new signing certificate
steps.desc: Remove all identified malicious binaries from the environment and, if the internal signing key was compromised, generate and distribute a new code-signing certificate/key pair (ideally HSM-backed).
steps.guidance: Rotate HSM keys if internal signing infrastructure was the source of compromise.
steps.outcome: Malicious binaries eradicated; new trusted signing infrastructure established.

steps.title: Reimage compromised build/signing infrastructure
steps.desc: If the compromise originated from internal build or signing servers, rebuild those systems from trusted media.
steps.abort: If the compromise was solely at the vendor, this step is not applicable.

steps.title: Re-establish trust and resume signed distribution
steps.desc: Resume software distribution using the new certificate and verify that endpoints correctly trust the new signer and reject the old one.
steps.guidance: Push updated trusted-publisher lists to application control systems.
steps.outcome: Software distribution operating normally under new trusted certificate.

steps.title: Harden code-signing key management
steps.desc: Document the incident and recommend HSM-backed key storage, signing ceremony controls, and certificate transparency monitoring.
steps.guidance: Include periodic signing-key access review and least-privilege access to signing infrastructure.

ITID-62141.def: An incident in which an adversary compromised a third-party vendor's cloud-based software delivery infrastructure — build service, artifact registry, CDN, or SaaS-hosted release pipeline — to distribute tampered software to customers.
ITID-62141.purpose: Captures supply chain compromises that occur specifically within a vendor's cloud-hosted build, packaging, or distribution infrastructure rather than on-premises systems.
scopeIncludes: Compromise of a vendor's cloud CI/CD or build-as-a-service platform used to produce customer-facing releases
Tampering with a vendor's cloud-hosted CDN or download endpoint to serve a modified installer
Abuse of a vendor's cloud service provider account/API credentials to alter released artifacts
scopeExcludes: On-premises vendor build server compromise (route to ITID-62121)
The organization's own internal CI/CD pipeline compromise (tracked under CI/CD Pipeline Attacks, ITID-626xx)
SaaS application exploitation not tied to software distribution (route to Third-Party SaaS Application Exploits, ITID-625xx)
ITID-62141.severity: High to Critical, given cloud infrastructure typically serves the vendor's entire global customer base from a single control point.
ITID-62141.priority: P1 while the compromised cloud distribution point remains live.
ITID-62141.escalation: Escalate to vendor's cloud security team and internal vendor management immediately; request distribution halt.
indicators: Unexpected changes to a vendor's published release hash on a cloud CDN
Vendor disclosure of unauthorized access to its cloud build/release environment
Anomalous API activity in a vendor's cloud account tied to release artifacts
vectors: Compromised cloud API keys or service-account tokens for the vendor's build/release pipeline
Web Services Compromise: Infrastructure — attacker-controlled or hijacked cloud infrastructure inserted into the legitimate distribution path
rootCauses: Vendor cloud build environment with overly broad IAM permissions
Lack of artifact integrity verification between cloud build and cloud distribution stages
mitreTechniques: T1195.002 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
controls: Independent artifact signing/verification step outside the vendor's own cloud pipeline
Monitoring vendor-published checksums against locally cached known-good hashes
ITID-62141.detection: Limited from the customer side; primarily reliant on vendor transparency and independent checksum verification pipelines.
ITID-62141.response: Halt ingestion from the affected cloud distribution point, verify all recently pulled artifacts against last-known-good hashes, and await vendor remediation confirmation.
metrics: Number of artifacts pulled during the compromise window
Time to independent hash re-verification
detections: Checksum drift monitoring against vendor-published hashes
ITID-62141.notes: Sibling differentiator is the location of compromise: cloud-hosted vendor distribution infrastructure specifically, versus on-prem build compromise (ITID-62121) or signing-trust abuse (ITID-62131).

playbook.name: Cloud Software Supply Chain Attack
playbook.description: A cloud-delivered SaaS/PaaS provider's build, deployment, or update pipeline is compromised, propagating malicious changes into the organization's cloud environment.

steps.title: Identify anomalous cloud resource/config changes
steps.desc: Correlate cloud audit logs (CloudTrail/Azure Activity Log) with a suspected upstream provider compromise to detect unauthorized resource creation, permission changes, or data access.
steps.guidance: Look for changes attributable to a service principal or integration tied to the third-party cloud provider.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized activity traced to the compromised cloud provider integration.

steps.title: Review provider's incident disclosure and shared-responsibility scope
steps.desc: Obtain the cloud provider's incident notification/status page and determine which of the organization's tenant resources fall within the disclosed blast radius.
steps.guidance: Request a customer-specific impact statement from the vendor's trust/security team.
steps.outcome: Documented scope of tenant impact per vendor disclosure.

steps.title: Inventory affected integrations and service principals
steps.desc: Enumerate all API keys, service accounts, and cross-cloud integrations tied to the compromised provider.
steps.guidance: Use CSPM tooling to enumerate third-party integrations and their granted permissions.
steps.outcome: Complete list of integration points and associated privilege levels.

steps.title: Revoke or rotate credentials for the compromised integration
steps.desc: Immediately revoke API keys/tokens and rotate secrets used by the affected cloud provider integration.
steps.guidance: Rotate in the correct order to avoid breaking dependent services; coordinate with app owners.

steps.title: Restrict or suspend the third-party cloud integration
steps.desc: Disable or restrict the integration's permissions/network access until the provider confirms remediation.
steps.guidance: Apply least-privilege IAM policy restrictions or fully suspend the integration if business-critical function allows.
steps.outcome: Blast radius of the compromised integration minimized.

steps.title: Remove unauthorized cloud resources/changes
steps.desc: Identify and remove any unauthorized resources, IAM role changes, or backdoor access created during the compromise window.
steps.guidance: Use infrastructure-as-code drift detection to identify unauthorized changes vs. declared state.
steps.outcome: Cloud environment restored to known-good, authorized configuration.

steps.title: Validate vendor remediation before re-enabling integration
steps.desc: Confirm the provider has patched/remediated their pipeline compromise before restoring the integration.
steps.guidance: Request written confirmation and, where possible, third-party attestation (SOC 2 bridge letter, pen test).
steps.abort: If vendor cannot confirm remediation, keep integration disabled and escalate to vendor management/legal.

steps.title: Restore integration and monitor closely
steps.desc: Re-enable the cloud integration with new credentials and heightened monitoring for anomalous activity.
steps.guidance: Apply temporary enhanced logging/alerting thresholds for 30 days.
steps.outcome: Integration restored with no recurrence of anomalous activity.

steps.title: Reassess third-party cloud risk posture
steps.desc: Document the incident and update vendor risk assessment criteria and cloud integration architecture (least privilege, network segmentation) standards.
steps.guidance: Feed findings into vendor risk register and third-party risk management (TPRM) program.
steps.outcome: Updated TPRM criteria and architecture standard for cloud integrations published.

ITID-62211.def: An incident in which an adversary exploited a publicly known, patchable vulnerability in a currently supported third-party application because the organization had not yet deployed the available fix.
ITID-62211.purpose: Intake leaf for exploitation of a third-party application vulnerability for which a vendor patch was already available but not yet applied by the organization.
scopeIncludes: Exploitation of a CVE with a vendor-published patch that was pending deployment in the organization's environment
Exploitation occurring within the organization's patch-management window (before SLA breach) or after it
scopeExcludes: Exploitation of a vulnerability with no vendor patch available at time of attack (route to ITID-62221, Zero-Day Exploits)
Exploitation of software that is end-of-life/unsupported by the vendor (route to ITID-62241, Legacy Software Exploits)
ITID-62211.severity: High if the vulnerability is remotely exploitable and unauthenticated; Medium for vulnerabilities requiring local or authenticated access.
ITID-62211.priority: P1 for actively exploited critical CVEs on internet-facing applications; P2 otherwise.
ITID-62211.escalation: Escalate to vulnerability management and asset owners immediately; expedite emergency patch deployment.
indicators: Exploit attempt matching a known CVE signature in IDS/WAF logs
Application crash or anomalous process spawned from a vulnerable third-party service
Vulnerability scanner flags the exploited CVE as previously known and unremediated
vectors: Exploit Public-Facing Application against an unpatched, internet-reachable third-party service
rootCauses: Patch management SLA breach on the affected application
Lack of compensating controls (WAF/virtual patching) during the patch gap
controls: Patch management SLA with tracked exceptions
Virtual patching/WAF rules for known CVEs pending remediation
ITID-62211.detection: Strong — known CVE exploitation typically has published IDS/IPS signatures and is well covered by vulnerability scanning correlation.
ITID-62211.response: Apply the available patch immediately, isolate the affected system pending patching if actively exploited, and review patch management SLA compliance.
metrics: Mean time to patch for critical CVEs
Number of exploited-but-patchable incidents per quarter
ITID-62211.notes: Sibling differentiator: patch availability existed at time of exploitation, distinguishing this from zero-day (ITID-62221) and end-of-life legacy software (ITID-62241) exploitation.

playbook.name: Unpatched Third-Party Application Vulnerability Exploited
playbook.description: An attacker exploits a known, unpatched vulnerability in a third-party application to gain unauthorized access or execute code.

steps.title: Confirm exploitation of the known vulnerability
steps.desc: Correlate IDS/WAF/EDR alerts against the CVE/vulnerability signature to confirm active exploitation rather than a false positive scan.
steps.guidance: Check exploit indicators (specific request patterns, payloads) against the published CVE proof-of-concept.
steps.outcome: Confirmed active exploitation of the specific vulnerability.
steps.abort: If evidence only shows scanning without successful exploitation, downgrade to monitoring and vulnerability management ticket.

steps.title: Determine patch status and exposure window
steps.desc: Check vulnerability management records to determine why the patch was not applied and how long the system was exposed.
steps.guidance: Review patch management SLA compliance history for the affected asset.
steps.outcome: Documented patch gap timeline and root cause (e.g., missed cycle, compatibility hold).

steps.title: Assess post-exploitation activity
steps.desc: Investigate for evidence of lateral movement, persistence, or data access following initial exploitation.
steps.guidance: Review process trees, new scheduled tasks/services, and outbound connections from the affected host.

steps.title: Isolate the exploited system
steps.desc: Apply network isolation or segmentation to the affected application server/host to halt further exploitation and lateral movement.

steps.title: Apply virtual patch / WAF rule as interim mitigation
steps.desc: Deploy a WAF or IPS signature to block exploit attempts against the vulnerability while the permanent patch is prepared.
steps.guidance: Use vendor or open-source (e.g., OWASP CRS) signature if available.
steps.outcome: Exploit attempts blocked at the perimeter.

steps.title: Apply the vendor security patch
steps.desc: Apply the official vendor patch or update that remediates the vulnerability, testing in staging first if time permits.
steps.guidance: Follow emergency change management process for expedited patch deployment.
steps.outcome: Vulnerability remediated on all affected instances.
steps.abort: If no patch is yet available, escalate to Zero-Day handling procedures.

steps.title: Remove any persistence mechanisms
steps.desc: Remove webshells, backdoor accounts, or scheduled tasks installed during exploitation.

steps.title: Validate and restore service
steps.desc: Confirm the application is patched, clean, and functioning correctly before removing containment.
steps.guidance: Run a follow-up vulnerability scan to confirm remediation.
steps.outcome: Application restored to normal operation with vulnerability confirmed closed.

steps.title: Address patch management gap
steps.desc: Document root cause of the patching delay and drive improvements to patch SLA enforcement for third-party applications.
steps.guidance: Consider automated patch compliance dashboards and exception review process.
steps.outcome: Patch management process improvement implemented and tracked.

ITID-62221.def: An incident in which an adversary exploited a previously unknown or undisclosed vulnerability in a third-party vendor's software, for which the vendor had not yet published a patch or mitigation at the time of exploitation.
ITID-62221.purpose: Captures exploitation of a third-party vendor's software vulnerability for which no patch or public fix existed at the time of the attack.
scopeIncludes: Exploitation of a vulnerability first identified through the attack itself, prior to any CVE assignment
Exploitation occurring in the window between vendor private disclosure and public patch release
scopeExcludes: Exploitation of a vulnerability with an available vendor patch (route to ITID-62211)
Exploitation of unsupported/end-of-life software where no patch will ever be issued (route to ITID-62241)
ITID-62221.severity: Critical. No compensating vendor fix exists at time of discovery, so all instances of the affected application are exposed.
ITID-62221.escalation: Escalate to executive leadership, vendor security team, and (where applicable) CERT/ISAC coordination bodies without delay.
indicators: Exploitation technique with no matching CVE or existing signature
Vendor confirms novel vulnerability following incident reporting
Anomalous crash dumps or memory corruption artifacts inconsistent with known exploits
vectors: Exploitation of Remote Services against a vendor application where no dedicated zero-day ATT&CK technique exists — noted here honestly as the closest general-fit mapping
Novel memory-corruption or logic-flaw exploitation chain
rootCauses: Inherent software defect undiscovered by vendor security testing prior to release
Lack of organizational behavioral/anomaly detection independent of signature-based tools
controls: Behavioral/EDR detection independent of known-signature matching
Network segmentation limiting blast radius of any single compromised application
ITID-62221.detection: Weak by definition until the exploit technique is characterized; relies on anomaly/behavioral detection rather than signatures.
ITID-62221.response: Contain and isolate affected systems, coordinate responsible disclosure with the vendor, and apply interim compensating controls (segmentation, WAF rules) until a patch ships.
metrics: Time from exploitation discovery to vendor patch availability
Number of assets exposed during the zero-day window
sops: Zero-Day Response and Vendor Coordination SOP
ITID-62221.notes: MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise has no dedicated zero-day technique ID; T1210 is used honestly as the closest general fit for remote-service exploitation without an existing patch. Sibling differentiator versus ITID-62211 is absence of any vendor fix at time of attack.

playbook.name: Zero-Day Exploit in Vendor Software
playbook.description: An attacker exploits a previously unknown (zero-day) vulnerability in a third-party vendor application for which no patch yet exists.

steps.title: Confirm exploitation of an unknown vulnerability
steps.desc: Investigate anomalous application behavior that does not match any known CVE, indicating a potential zero-day.
steps.guidance: Compare exploit indicators against existing signature/CVE databases to confirm novelty.
steps.outcome: Confirmed suspected zero-day exploitation with no existing vendor patch.
steps.abort: If a matching CVE and patch already exist, redirect to the standard unpatched-vulnerability playbook.

steps.title: Capture forensic evidence of the exploit chain
steps.desc: Preserve memory, logs, and network captures demonstrating the exploit technique for vendor coordination and internal analysis.
steps.guidance: Engage forensic/reverse-engineering resources to characterize the exploit primitive.
steps.outcome: Documented exploit chain and IOCs suitable for vendor disclosure.

steps.title: Notify vendor and coordinate disclosure
steps.desc: Report the zero-day to the vendor's security team through their responsible disclosure channel and request an ETA for a fix.
steps.guidance: Engage vendor's PSIRT; consider CERT/CC coordination if vendor is unresponsive.
steps.outcome: Vendor acknowledges the report and provides remediation timeline.

steps.title: Deploy virtual patch via WAF/IPS
steps.desc: Create and deploy a custom WAF/IPS signature to block the specific exploit technique as an interim containment measure.
steps.guidance: Test the virtual patch for false positives before broad deployment.
steps.outcome: Exploit attempts blocked without waiting for the vendor fix.

steps.title: Isolate or disable the vulnerable component
steps.desc: Where feasible, disable the specific vulnerable feature/module or isolate the affected system from untrusted networks.
steps.guidance: Weigh business impact of disabling functionality against risk of continued exposure.
steps.outcome: Reduced attack surface pending vendor patch.
steps.abort: If the component cannot be disabled without severe business impact, rely on compensating monitoring and WAF controls.

steps.title: Enhance monitoring for exploit recurrence
steps.desc: Deploy custom detection rules based on the observed exploit signature across the environment.
steps.guidance: Push IOCs/signatures to SIEM and EDR for fleet-wide detection.
steps.outcome: Broad detection coverage for the zero-day technique.

steps.title: Apply vendor patch once released
steps.desc: Apply the vendor's official fix as soon as it is released and validated, following expedited emergency-change procedures.
steps.guidance: Validate the patch closes the specific exploit path before broad rollout.
steps.outcome: Vulnerability fully remediated across the environment.

steps.title: Remove attacker persistence and validate clean state
steps.desc: Remove any backdoors or persistence established via the zero-day and verify systems are clean.

steps.title: Restore normal operations and lift virtual patch if safe
steps.desc: Confirm patched systems are stable and gradually remove interim WAF/IPS virtual-patch rules once the permanent fix is verified.
steps.outcome: Systems fully operational on patched, vendor-fixed software.

steps.title: Document zero-day handling and update vendor coordination process
steps.desc: Capture lessons on detection speed, vendor coordination effectiveness, and virtual-patching response time.
steps.guidance: Update the zero-day response runbook and vendor PSIRT contact registry.

ITID-62231.def: An incident in which an adversary abused a design flaw, authentication weakness, or logic error in a third-party service's API to achieve unauthorized access, data exposure, or functionality abuse.
ITID-62231.purpose: Captures exploitation of a third-party service's application programming interface (API) rather than its traditional user-facing application surface.
scopeIncludes: Broken object-level authorization (BOLA) or excessive data exposure in a third-party API
API rate-limit or business-logic abuse against a third-party service
Exploitation of an undocumented/shadow API endpoint exposed by a third-party vendor
scopeExcludes: Exploitation of the same vendor's traditional web application UI rather than its API surface (route to ITID-62211/62221 as appropriate)
OAuth/SSO token abuse specifically for SaaS account access (route to Third-Party SaaS Application Exploits, ITID-625xx)
ITID-62231.severity: High if the API exposes sensitive data or privileged functionality; Medium for limited-scope logic abuse.
ITID-62231.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if bulk data exposure or authentication bypass is confirmed.
ITID-62231.escalation: Escalate to the vendor's security team and internal application owners; request emergency API access review.
indicators: Abnormal API request volume or sequencing from a single client credential
Vendor security bulletin describing an API authorization flaw
Data exposure inconsistent with the requesting user's expected access scope
vectors: Automated scripted abuse of exposed or under-authenticated third-party API endpoints
API exploitation via scripting/automation to enumerate or exfiltrate records at scale
rootCauses: Third-party API lacking object-level authorization checks
Absence of API rate limiting or anomaly detection at the vendor or organization level
controls: API gateway rate limiting and anomaly detection
Regular third-party API authorization/logic security testing
ITID-62231.detection: Moderate — API gateway and vendor-side logging can reveal abuse patterns, but many organizations lack visibility into third-party API internals.
ITID-62231.response: Request vendor throttling/revocation of the abused credential, assess data exposure scope, and require remediation confirmation before restoring integration.
metrics: Number of records exposed via API abuse
Time to vendor credential revocation
ITID-62231.notes: Mapped technique is deliberately general (T1059) since API abuse mechanisms vary; where a more specific technique clearly applies to a given case, analysts should note it in the case record. Distinguished from SaaS OAuth/SSO abuse (ITID-625xx), which targets identity/session mechanisms rather than API logic itself.

playbook.name: API Exploitation in Third-Party Service
playbook.description: An attacker exploits a vulnerability or design flaw in a third-party service's API (e.g., broken object-level authorization, injection) to access or manipulate data.

steps.title: Detect anomalous API activity
steps.desc: Investigate abnormal request patterns, error-rate spikes, or unusual data-access volumes involving the third-party API integration.
steps.guidance: Review API gateway logs and third-party service audit logs for anomalies.
steps.outcome: Confirmed anomalous or malicious API activity pattern.

steps.title: Identify the specific API vulnerability class
steps.desc: Determine whether the exploitation involves broken object-level authorization (BOLA), injection, rate-limit bypass, or another OWASP API Top 10 category.
steps.guidance: Replay suspicious requests in a test environment to characterize the flaw.

steps.title: Determine data/records exposed
steps.desc: Assess which records, tenants, or data fields were accessed or modified via the exploited API.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference API access logs with data classification to determine sensitivity of exposure.

steps.title: Revoke or throttle the abused API credentials
steps.desc: Revoke API keys/tokens used in the exploitation and apply rate limiting or IP blocking against the attacking source.

steps.title: Disable the vulnerable API endpoint or feature
steps.desc: Temporarily disable the vulnerable endpoint or feature flag it off if the vendor cannot provide an immediate fix.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with vendor/service owner on acceptable downtime.
steps.abort: If the endpoint is business-critical and cannot be disabled, apply strict WAF rules as compensating control.

steps.title: Coordinate vendor remediation of the API flaw
steps.desc: Report the vulnerability to the third-party vendor and track their fix through to deployment and verification.
steps.guidance: Request a written remediation timeline and confirmation of the fix.
steps.outcome: Vendor deploys and confirms the API fix.

steps.title: Rotate affected credentials and re-authorize integration
steps.desc: Rotate all API keys/secrets associated with the integration and reissue with least-privilege scopes.
steps.outcome: Integration re-secured with minimal necessary permissions.

steps.title: Re-enable and validate the integration
steps.desc: Restore the API integration and validate correct authorization behavior and data-access scoping.
steps.guidance: Run authorization test cases (including negative tests) before full re-enablement.
steps.outcome: Integration restored with verified proper access controls.

steps.title: Strengthen third-party API integration review
steps.desc: Document findings and require security review (including authz testing) for all new and existing third-party API integrations.
steps.guidance: Incorporate API security testing into vendor onboarding and periodic reassessment.
steps.outcome: Updated third-party API integration security standard published.

ITID-62241.def: An incident in which an adversary exploited a vulnerability in a third-party application that is no longer supported or patched by its vendor, regardless of whether the vulnerability was previously known.
ITID-62241.purpose: Captures exploitation of third-party software that has reached end-of-life or end-of-support status, such that no vendor patch will be forthcoming.
scopeIncludes: Exploitation of an application version past its vendor-published end-of-life date
Exploitation of software the organization has continued running without a vendor support contract
scopeExcludes: Exploitation of currently supported software with an available patch (route to ITID-62211)
Exploitation of currently supported software with no available patch (route to ITID-62221)
ITID-62241.severity: High. No vendor remediation path exists, so risk persists until the software is replaced or isolated.
ITID-62241.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if the legacy system is internet-facing or holds sensitive data.
ITID-62241.escalation: Escalate to asset owners and IT leadership; require a compensating-control or decommission plan, not just incident closure.
indicators: Exploited application version flagged as end-of-life in the asset inventory
Vulnerability scanner reporting unremediated findings with 'no fix available' status
Exploit technique matching a long-published CVE with no corresponding patch for the installed version
vectors: Exploit Public-Facing Application against long-unsupported software with known, unfixed vulnerabilities
rootCauses: Business dependency preventing timely decommission or upgrade of legacy software
Incomplete asset inventory failing to flag end-of-life status
controls: End-of-life software inventory and forced decommission timelines
Network segmentation/isolation of legacy systems that cannot be upgraded
ITID-62241.detection: Strong for known/long-published CVEs; detection tooling typically has mature signatures for legacy exploitation techniques.
ITID-62241.response: Isolate or decommission the legacy application, apply available compensating controls, and formally document acceptance of residual risk if retention is unavoidable.
metrics: Number of active end-of-life applications in the environment
Time to decommission or isolate after exploitation
ITID-62241.notes: Sibling differentiator versus ITID-62211/62221 is vendor support status: no patch will ever be issued, as opposed to a pending or absent patch on currently supported software.

playbook.name: Legacy Third-Party Software Exploit
playbook.description: An attacker exploits a vulnerability in end-of-life or otherwise unsupported legacy third-party software for which no vendor patch will be issued.

steps.title: Confirm exploitation and legacy/EOL status
steps.desc: Investigate the alert and confirm the affected software is end-of-life or unsupported, ruling out an available vendor patch.
steps.guidance: Check vendor EOL/EOS announcements and internal asset inventory lifecycle status.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exploitation of a legacy/unsupported component with no vendor fix forthcoming.
steps.abort: If the software is still supported, redirect to the unpatched-vulnerability playbook.

steps.title: Assess business justification for continued use
steps.desc: Determine why the legacy software remains in use (compatibility, cost, business criticality) and document any existing risk acceptance.
steps.guidance: Review risk register for prior formal risk-acceptance sign-off on this legacy component.
steps.outcome: Documented business context and any existing risk acceptance.

steps.title: Assess post-exploitation impact
steps.desc: Determine the extent of unauthorized access, data exposure, or lateral movement resulting from the exploit.

steps.title: Isolate the legacy system
steps.desc: Segment or isolate the legacy system to the greatest extent possible while preserving minimum required functionality.
steps.guidance: Apply strict network ACLs limiting the legacy system to only essential communication paths.
steps.outcome: Legacy system's attack surface substantially reduced.

steps.title: Deploy compensating controls (virtual patching, host hardening)
steps.desc: Apply WAF/IPS virtual patching and host-based hardening (disabling unneeded services) since no vendor patch exists.
steps.outcome: Exploit path blocked via compensating controls.

steps.title: Remove attacker footholds
steps.desc: Remove any malware, webshells, or unauthorized accounts installed via the exploit.

steps.title: Initiate accelerated migration/decommission plan
steps.desc: Escalate to application/business owner and IT leadership to accelerate migration off or decommissioning of the legacy platform.
steps.guidance: Set a firm remediation timeline with executive sponsorship given the demonstrated exploitability.
steps.outcome: Formal migration/decommission plan with committed timeline established.

steps.title: Restore service under compensating controls
steps.desc: Return the legacy system to service under the newly applied compensating controls and monitor closely.
steps.guidance: Apply enhanced logging specifically for this system going forward.
steps.outcome: System operational with reduced risk profile and heightened monitoring.

steps.title: Update legacy technology risk management process
steps.desc: Document the incident and reinforce policy requiring formal, time-bound risk acceptance and compensating-control review for any legacy/EOL software in use.

ITID-62311.def: An incident in which an adversary introduced malicious code directly into an open-source library or package that the organization consumes as a dependency, distinct from impersonation-based attacks like typosquatting or dependency confusion.
ITID-62311.purpose: Captures the technical mechanism by which an open-source software library consumed by the organization was deliberately poisoned with malicious code by an attacker.
scopeIncludes: A maintainer account compromise leading to a malicious version being published under a legitimate, long-used package name
A malicious pull request merged into a popular open-source project by a compromised or malicious contributor
Post-install script abuse within a legitimately named package to execute attacker code
scopeExcludes: A confusingly similar or misspelled package name used to impersonate a legitimate one (route to ITID-62321, Dependency Confusion Attacks, and note overlap with the parallel ITID-61321 Typosquatted Package leaf)
Repository takeover via credential theft with no code poisoning yet confirmed (route to ITID-62341, Open-Source Repository Hijacking)
License compliance findings with no malicious code involved (route to ITID-6233x)
ITID-62311.severity: High to Critical depending on the library's dependency-tree reach and the privilege level at which it executes.
ITID-62311.priority: P1 while the poisoned version remains installed anywhere in the environment.
ITID-62311.escalation: Escalate to application security and development leadership immediately; freeze automated dependency updates pending scope assessment.
indicators: Unexpected network calls or obfuscated code in a routine dependency update
Security advisory (GHSA/OSV) flagging a specific package version as malicious
Software composition analysis (SCA) tool flags a new post-install script or hash mismatch
vectors: Compromise of Software Dependencies and Development Tools via maintainer account takeover or malicious contribution
rootCauses: Lack of dependency pinning/lockfile integrity verification
Automated dependency updates deployed without a review or quarantine window
mitreTechniques: T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
controls: Software composition analysis (SCA) with malicious-package feed integration
Lockfile pinning with a review gate before dependency version bumps
ITID-62311.detection: Moderate and improving — SCA tooling and public malicious-package feeds (OSV, GHSA) now catch many cases, though zero-day poisoning still evades initial detection.
ITID-62311.response: Pin back to the last known-good version, rebuild and redeploy affected applications, and hunt for any execution artifacts from the poisoned version.
metrics: Number of builds using a confirmed-poisoned dependency version
Mean time to dependency rollback
ITID-62311.notes: Scoped to the technical exploitation mechanism of direct code poisoning within a legitimately named package. The parallel ITID-613xx group (Critical System Disruption's Software Supply Chain Attacks) tracks equivalent open-source compromise events from a business-continuity/critical-disruption angle — cross-reference when both apply. Distinct from dependency confusion/typosquatting (ITID-62321), which is an impersonation mechanism rather than direct poisoning.

playbook.name: Poisoned Open-Source Library
playbook.description: A malicious payload is introduced into an open-source library (via compromised maintainer account, malicious pull request, or typosquat) that the organization consumes as a dependency.

steps.title: Identify the poisoned dependency via SBOM/scanning alert
steps.desc: Investigate an alert from software composition analysis (SCA) tooling, SBOM diffing, or threat intel flagging a known-malicious package/version in use.
steps.guidance: Cross-check package name/version against public malicious-package advisories (e.g., OSV, npm/PyPI security advisories).
steps.outcome: Confirmed presence of the malicious package/version in the codebase or build.
steps.abort: If the flagged package is not actually present in any build, close as false positive.

steps.title: Determine build and deployment scope
steps.desc: Identify all repositories, build pipelines, and deployed artifacts that pulled in the poisoned dependency version.
steps.guidance: Query artifact repository and SBOM history across all services.
steps.outcome: Complete list of affected repos/builds/deployed artifacts.

steps.title: Analyze the malicious payload behavior
steps.desc: Reverse-engineer or review the malicious code introduced in the package to determine its capability (data exfil, backdoor, cryptominer, etc.).
steps.guidance: Use sandboxed analysis; consult public write-ups if the package is a known incident.

steps.title: Block the poisoned package version at the registry proxy
steps.desc: Add the malicious package/version to the internal package-registry proxy's deny list to prevent further pulls.
steps.guidance: Use Artifactory/Nexus/verdaccio blocklist capability.
steps.outcome: No additional builds can pull the poisoned version.

steps.title: Halt and quarantine affected deployments
steps.desc: Pause deployment pipelines for affected services and, where already deployed, isolate the running instances.

steps.title: Pin to a verified clean version and rebuild
steps.desc: Update dependency manifests/lockfiles to a verified clean version, rebuild, and re-scan before redeployment.
steps.guidance: Verify the replacement version's hash/provenance against the official maintainer or a trusted mirror.
steps.outcome: All affected builds rebuilt on clean dependency versions.

steps.title: Harden package registry scoping
steps.desc: Implement scoped registry configuration (private registry priority, namespace scoping) to reduce future exposure to poisoned public packages.
steps.guidance: Consistent with prior ITID-30000/40000 supply-chain hardening conventions — enforce internal-registry-first resolution.
steps.outcome: Registry scoping configuration hardened across build systems.

steps.title: Redeploy and validate clean artifacts
steps.desc: Redeploy rebuilt, clean artifacts and validate application functionality and absence of malicious behavior.
steps.outcome: Services restored on clean, verified dependencies.

steps.title: Strengthen SBOM and dependency review practices
steps.desc: Document the incident and drive mandatory SBOM generation, continuous SCA scanning, and maintainer-activity monitoring for critical dependencies.
steps.outcome: Updated open-source dependency governance standard published.

ITID-62321.def: An incident in which an adversary published a public package under the same name as the organization's internal/private package, exploiting package-manager resolution order so that the build system pulls the attacker's malicious public version instead of the intended internal one.
ITID-62321.purpose: Captures the specific technical mechanism of dependency confusion, where an attacker exploits package-resolution precedence to substitute a malicious public package for an internal private one.
scopeIncludes: A build or CI process resolving an internally named package from a public registry due to misconfigured scope/registry precedence
A published public package with a version number deliberately higher than the internal package to force resolution priority
scopeExcludes: Direct poisoning of a legitimately and uniquely named open-source package (route to ITID-62311)
Repository access hijacking without a naming/resolution confusion mechanism (route to ITID-62341)
ITID-62321.severity: High — a successful dependency confusion attack can achieve code execution directly within the organization's own build pipeline.
ITID-62321.priority: P1 upon confirmation of any build pulling the malicious public package.
ITID-62321.escalation: Escalate to application security and DevOps leadership; immediately reserve/claim the internal package name on all public registries in use.
indicators: Build logs showing package resolution from a public registry for a name expected to be internal-only
Unexpected outbound network activity originating from a CI/build agent post-dependency-install
Security researcher or bug-bounty report of a claimed internal package name on a public registry
vectors: Compromise of Software Dependencies and Development Tools via public-registry namespace squatting on an internal package name
rootCauses: Package manager configuration lacking explicit registry scoping for internal packages
Internal package names never reserved as placeholders on public registries
mitreTechniques: T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
controls: Explicit registry scoping/pinning for all internal package namespaces
Proactive registration of internal package names as empty placeholders on public registries
ITID-62321.detection: Moderate — build log analysis and registry-source monitoring can catch this, but it requires deliberate configuration since resolution happens silently by design.
ITID-62321.response: Correct registry scoping configuration immediately, purge the malicious package from build caches, and audit all recent builds for exposure.
metrics: Number of internal package names unclaimed on public registries
Number of builds affected before remediation
ITID-62321.notes: This ITID-v2 leaf tracks the technical exploitation mechanism (registry resolution precedence abuse) for the same underlying event family as the parallel ITID-61323 (Dependency Confusion Attack, Internal Package Name Hijacked) and ITID-61321 (Typosquatted Malicious Package), which sit under Critical System Disruption's Software Supply Chain Attacks and track business-impact/critical-disruption consequences of the same technique. Analysts should cross-link both when a single confirmed event spans both angles.

playbook.name: Dependency Confusion Attack
playbook.description: An attacker publishes a malicious package to a public registry using the same name as an internal private package, tricking the build system into pulling the malicious public version.

steps.title: Detect unexpected public package resolution
steps.desc: Investigate a build/SCA alert or anomalous outbound network call indicating a build resolved a package name from the public registry instead of the intended internal one.
steps.guidance: Review build logs for package source/registry URL used during dependency resolution.
steps.outcome: Confirmed dependency confusion — public malicious package pulled instead of internal package.
steps.abort: If resolution correctly used the internal registry, close as false positive.

steps.title: Determine builds and environments affected
steps.desc: Identify every build/pipeline run and deployed environment that resolved the malicious public package.
steps.outcome: Full scope of affected builds and environments documented.

steps.title: Analyze the malicious package payload
steps.desc: Determine what the malicious package executed (e.g., exfiltrating environment variables, secrets, build metadata).
steps.guidance: Assume any secrets present in the build environment at execution time may be compromised.
steps.outcome: Payload behavior and potential data exposure documented.

steps.title: Halt affected build pipelines
steps.desc: Immediately pause CI/CD pipelines that are vulnerable to the same dependency-confusion pattern.
steps.outcome: No further builds execute the malicious package.

steps.title: Rotate secrets exposed to the build environment
steps.desc: Rotate all credentials, API keys, and tokens accessible to the compromised build environment, treating them as potentially exfiltrated.

steps.title: Configure scoped/namespaced package resolution
steps.desc: Reserve internal package names on public registries (where supported) and configure package managers to prioritize the internal registry/scope explicitly, eliminating ambiguous resolution.
steps.guidance: Consistent with ITID-30000/40000 conventions — use scoped packages (e.g., @org/pkg) and explicit registry mapping.
steps.outcome: Build system can no longer be tricked into resolving internal package names publicly.

steps.title: Report and request takedown of the malicious package
steps.desc: Report the malicious package to the public registry maintainers for takedown.
steps.outcome: Malicious package removed from the public registry.

steps.title: Resume builds and validate integrity
steps.desc: Resume CI/CD pipelines with the hardened resolution configuration and validate builds pull only intended internal packages.
steps.outcome: Builds functioning normally with confirmed correct package resolution.

steps.title: Mandate namespace reservation for all internal packages
steps.desc: Document the incident and require namespace reservation/scoping for every internal package name across all languages/registries in use.
steps.outcome: Dependency-confusion prevention control added to secure development standard.

ITID-62331.def: A compliance finding, not a security incident, in which a product the organization has distributed to customers or the public is found to include GPL/copyleft-licensed open-source code without meeting the license's source-disclosure or attribution obligations.
ITID-62331.purpose: Tracks discovery that a distributed organizational product incorporates GPL or other copyleft-licensed open-source code in violation of that license's terms.
scopeIncludes: A shipped binary found to statically link or bundle GPL-licensed code without corresponding source disclosure
Customer, community, or Software Freedom Conservancy-style complaint alleging copyleft license violation
scopeExcludes: Any malicious code or security vulnerability within the open-source component itself (route to the appropriate technical leaf, e.g., ITID-62311)
Unlicensed/unknown-provenance component usage discovered via internal audit rather than external violation claim (route to ITID-62332)
ITID-62331.severity: Low from a security standpoint; Medium-High from a legal/business standpoint depending on distribution scale and licensor assertiveness.
ITID-62331.priority: P3 for SOC tracking purposes; routed to legal/OSS compliance for actual priority-setting.
ITID-62331.escalation: Escalate to legal counsel and open-source program office; SOC role is limited to logging and cross-referencing, not remediation.
indicators: External legal notice or public disclosure alleging license violation
Software composition analysis (SCA) license scan flagging copyleft code in a distributed artifact
vectors: GPL/copyleft-licensed component integrated into a distributed product without legal review, triggering forced-disclosure obligations
No software composition analysis (SCA) step in the build pipeline to flag copyleft license terms before release
rootCauses: Lack of license-compliance scanning in the software release pipeline
Absence of an open-source program office or component approval process
mitreTechniques: T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
controls: SCA license-scanning gate in the release pipeline
Formal open-source component approval and inventory process
ITID-62331.detection: Not a technical detection surface — findings originate from license-scanning tools, audits, or external legal notices, not security telemetry.
ITID-62331.response: SOC logs the finding and hands off to legal/OSS compliance; no containment or technical response action is expected.
metrics: Number of license-compliance findings per release cycle
ITID-62331.notes: Open-source license compliance issue — no ATT&CK Enterprise technique applies; tracked via legal/OSS-compliance review, not a security incident.

playbook.name: GPL/Copyleft License Violation Discovered in Distributed Product
playbook.description: An internal or external audit discovers that a distributed product incorporates GPL/copyleft-licensed open-source code in a manner that violates the license terms, creating legal and IP exposure rather than a security compromise.

steps.title: Confirm the license violation finding
steps.desc: Review the audit/SCA license-scan finding to confirm the specific copyleft component, license type (GPL/AGPL/LGPL), and the nature of the violation (e.g., static linking without source disclosure).
steps.guidance: Engage OSS compliance tooling (FOSSA/Black Duck/Scancode) output and legal counsel to interpret the specific license obligations violated.
steps.outcome: Confirmed, documented license violation with specific clause(s) implicated.
steps.abort: If the scan is a false positive (e.g., component is dual-licensed or used under a compliant exception), close with documentation.

steps.title: Determine distribution scope and affected products
steps.desc: Identify every shipped product version, customer deployment, and distribution channel that contains the non-compliant component.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with product/release management to map component usage across all shipped SKUs.
steps.outcome: Complete inventory of affected products and distribution history.

steps.title: Assess legal exposure and third-party notification obligations
steps.desc: Legal/OSS-compliance team assesses potential exposure (customer contract breach, community/maintainer complaint risk, injunctive risk) and any obligations to notify customers or the license holder.
steps.guidance: Engage Legal and OSS Program Office; this is a compliance discovery, not an attacker-driven incident — no adversary framing applies.
steps.outcome: Documented legal risk assessment and notification decision.

steps.title: Halt further distribution of the non-compliant build
steps.desc: Pause further shipment/release of the affected product version pending remediation decision from Legal/OSS compliance.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with release management to freeze the specific build/version.
steps.abort: If halting distribution is not feasible immediately, document risk-acceptance with Legal sign-off and target remediation date.

steps.title: Identify remediation path (relicense, replace, or disclose)
steps.desc: OSS compliance team and engineering evaluate options: replace the component with a permissively-licensed alternative, isolate it to comply with copyleft boundary (e.g., dynamic linking), or fulfill source-disclosure obligations.
steps.outcome: Selected remediation path documented and approved.

steps.title: Implement the approved remediation
steps.desc: Engineering implements the approved fix — replacing the component, refactoring the integration boundary, or preparing required source-code disclosure packages.
steps.outcome: Product brought into license compliance in a new build.

steps.title: Fulfill any required source disclosure or notice obligations
steps.desc: Where required by the license, publish corresponding source code, attribution notices, or written offers as legally required.
steps.abort: If no disclosure/notice was legally required for the chosen remediation, mark not applicable.

steps.title: Resume distribution of compliant build
steps.desc: Resume shipment of the remediated, license-compliant product version after Legal sign-off.
steps.outcome: Product distribution resumed with confirmed license compliance.

steps.title: Strengthen OSS license review in the SDLC
steps.desc: Document the finding and implement mandatory license-classification gates in the CI pipeline to prevent future copyleft components from reaching distributed builds unreviewed.
steps.guidance: Add automated license-policy enforcement (allow/deny list) to the SCA pipeline.
steps.outcome: OSS license policy and automated enforcement gate implemented.

ITID-62332.def: A compliance finding, not a security incident, in which an internal software composition audit discovers open-source components in use whose license terms are unknown, unverifiable, or were never formally reviewed and approved prior to inclusion.
ITID-62332.purpose: Tracks internal audit discovery of open-source components used without any identifiable or verified license, as distinct from external claims of copyleft violation.
scopeIncludes: Components pulled into a codebase with no discoverable license file or metadata
Components used beyond the scope their license actually permits (e.g., commercial use of a non-commercial-only license), discovered via internal review
scopeExcludes: External third-party claim of a specific copyleft violation already identified (route to ITID-62331)
Malicious code discovered within an unlicensed component (route to ITID-62311)
ITID-62332.severity: Low from a security standpoint; Medium from a legal/business risk standpoint pending license determination.
ITID-62332.priority: P3 for SOC tracking; actual remediation priority set by legal/OSS compliance based on exposure.
ITID-62332.escalation: Escalate to legal counsel and the open-source program office for license determination and remediation planning.
indicators: Software composition analysis (SCA) audit reporting components with 'unknown' or 'unrecognized' license classification
Periodic open-source inventory review surfacing previously unapproved components
vectors: Unlicensed or unauthorized open-source component discovered embedded in production software during an audit
Developers pulled dependencies directly from public repositories without a vetted internal component registry
rootCauses: No component approval gate at time of original inclusion
Incomplete or outdated software bill of materials (SBOM)
mitreTechniques: T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
controls: Maintained, automatically generated software bill of materials (SBOM) for all products
Mandatory license classification step before any new dependency is approved
ITID-62332.detection: Not a technical detection surface — findings originate from SCA/SBOM audits, not security telemetry.
ITID-62332.response: SOC logs the finding and hands off to legal/OSS compliance for license determination; no containment action expected.
metrics: Number of unknown-license components identified per audit cycle
Time to license determination
ITID-62332.notes: Open-source license compliance issue — no ATT&CK Enterprise technique applies; tracked via legal/OSS-compliance review, not a security incident. Sibling differentiator versus ITID-62331: discovery via internal audit of unknown provenance, rather than an external claim of a known license type being violated.

playbook.name: Unlicensed/Unauthorized Open-Source Component Usage Discovered in Audit
playbook.description: An internal audit discovers open-source components in use for which no license terms were reviewed or approved, or which lack any discoverable license at all, creating undefined legal risk.

steps.title: Confirm the unlicensed/unreviewed component finding
steps.desc: Review the audit finding to confirm the component lacks an approved license record or has no discoverable license (all-rights-reserved default).
steps.guidance: Cross-check against the OSS approval registry and the component's repository/package metadata.
steps.outcome: Confirmed list of unlicensed or unreviewed components in use.
steps.abort: If the component does have an approved, documented license that was simply missing from the registry, correct the record and close.

steps.title: Determine usage scope and criticality
steps.desc: Identify which products/services use the component, how deeply integrated it is, and whether it has been distributed externally.
steps.outcome: Documented usage footprint and distribution status.

steps.title: Legal/OSS compliance risk assessment
steps.desc: Legal and OSS Program Office assess the risk of continued use given the license ambiguity, including IP infringement and warranty exposure.
steps.guidance: This is a governance/compliance matter, not a security compromise — frame accordingly with no attacker language.
steps.outcome: Documented risk rating and recommended action (retain with terms clarified, replace, or remove).

steps.title: Restrict further propagation of the unreviewed component
steps.desc: Block the component from being added to new projects via the internal package registry/approval gate until its status is resolved.
steps.outcome: No new usage of the unreviewed component introduced.

steps.title: Contact upstream maintainer to clarify licensing terms
steps.desc: Attempt to reach the component's author/maintainer to obtain explicit licensing terms or written permission for use.
steps.outcome: Either clarified license terms obtained, or determination that no valid license can be secured.
steps.abort: If maintainer cannot be reached within a reasonable timeframe, proceed to replacement.

steps.title: Replace or formally approve the component
steps.desc: Based on legal guidance, replace the component with a properly licensed alternative or formally document and approve its continued use.
steps.outcome: Component either replaced or formally added to the approved OSS registry with documented terms.

steps.title: Validate build integrity after remediation
steps.desc: Confirm the product builds and functions correctly with the replaced/approved component.
steps.outcome: Product functioning normally with resolved licensing status.

steps.title: Close the OSS intake gap
steps.desc: Document how the unreviewed component entered the codebase and reinforce mandatory OSS intake/approval workflow for all new dependencies.
steps.outcome: Updated OSS intake process with enforcement checkpoint in CI.

ITID-62333.def: A compliance finding, not a security incident, covering any open-source license risk in a distributed product that does not fit the more specific GPL/copyleft-violation (ITID-62331) or unlicensed-component (ITID-62332) leaves.
ITID-62333.purpose: Intake leaf for open-source license compliance issues that do not clearly fit the copyleft-violation or unlicensed-component leaves.
scopeIncludes: License compatibility conflicts between two open-source components used together
Ambiguous or evolving license terms (e.g., a dual-license or license-change scenario) pending legal determination
scopeExcludes: Clearly identified GPL/copyleft violations (route to ITID-62331)
Clearly unlicensed/unverified components identified via audit (route to ITID-62332)
ITID-62333.severity: Low from a security standpoint; variable from a legal standpoint pending case specifics.
ITID-62333.priority: P3 for SOC tracking; actual priority determined by legal/OSS compliance.
ITID-62333.escalation: Escalate to legal counsel and the open-source program office.
indicators: Ambiguous SCA license-scan output requiring manual legal review
Vendor or community notice of a license change affecting an in-use component
vectors: Generic insecure or non-compliant open-source license issue not captured by a more specific sub-category
No ongoing license-compliance monitoring as dependencies are updated over the product lifecycle
rootCauses: Lack of periodic re-review of previously approved components as their licenses evolve
mitreTechniques: T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
controls: Periodic re-scan of the open-source inventory against current license terms
ITID-62333.detection: Not a technical detection surface — findings originate from SCA audits and legal review, not security telemetry.
ITID-62333.response: SOC logs the finding and hands off to legal/OSS compliance; no containment action expected.
metrics: Number of ambiguous license findings pending legal review
ITID-62333.notes: Open-source license compliance issue — no ATT&CK Enterprise technique applies; tracked via legal/OSS-compliance review, not a security incident. This is the unclassified/general catch-all for the Insecure Open-Source Licenses group.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Insecure Open-Source License Issue
playbook.description: A general or unclassified open-source licensing compliance issue is identified that does not fit a more specific license-violation category.

steps.title: Triage the reported licensing issue
steps.desc: Review the reported finding (from audit, tooling alert, or external report) to classify the nature of the licensing concern.
steps.guidance: Engage OSS compliance tooling output and Legal to characterize the issue.
steps.abort: If the issue matches a more specific known category (GPL violation, unlicensed component), redirect to that specific playbook.

steps.title: Determine scope of affected products/components
steps.desc: Identify all products, services, and builds affected by the licensing issue.

steps.title: Legal/OSS compliance assessment
steps.desc: Legal and OSS Program Office evaluate the risk and required remediation approach for the specific licensing concern.
steps.guidance: Frame as a compliance/legal governance matter.
steps.outcome: Documented risk assessment and remediation recommendation.

steps.title: Restrict further use pending resolution
steps.desc: Prevent additional adoption of the flagged component/license configuration until the issue is resolved.
steps.outcome: No further propagation of the licensing issue.

steps.title: Implement the agreed remediation
steps.desc: Execute the remediation approach agreed with Legal/OSS compliance (replacement, relicensing, disclosure, or formal exception).
steps.outcome: Licensing issue resolved per approved remediation path.

steps.title: Validate resolution and update records
steps.desc: Confirm the remediation is complete and update the OSS component registry/SBOM accordingly.
steps.outcome: Component registry accurately reflects resolved licensing status.

steps.title: Reinforce OSS license governance
steps.desc: Document the finding and identify any process gap that allowed the issue to occur, feeding improvements into the OSS governance program.
steps.outcome: OSS governance process improvement documented and tracked.

steps.title: Communicate findings to engineering teams
steps.desc: Share sanitized findings and guidance with engineering teams to raise awareness of license compliance requirements.
steps.outcome: Awareness communication delivered to relevant teams.

ITID-62341.def: An incident in which an adversary gained unauthorized control of an open-source project's source repository, maintainer credentials, or package-registry publishing rights, creating the capability to push malicious releases even if no malicious code has yet been distributed.
ITID-62341.purpose: Captures unauthorized takeover of an open-source project's repository or maintainer account, prior to or independent of any confirmed code poisoning.
scopeIncludes: Stolen or phished maintainer credentials granting repository/publish access
A dormant/abandoned project's ownership transferred to an attacker via registry account-recovery abuse
Compromise of a maintainer's registry API token used to publish releases
scopeExcludes: Cases where malicious code has already been published and is the primary concern (route to ITID-62311, Poisoned Open-Source Libraries)
Naming-based impersonation without any actual account/repository takeover (route to ITID-62321, Dependency Confusion Attacks)
ITID-62341.severity: High — repository control represents a standing capability to poison every future release, regardless of whether it has been exercised yet.
ITID-62341.priority: P1 upon confirmation of unauthorized repository/publishing access, even absent a malicious release.
ITID-62341.escalation: Escalate to application security and the open-source project's maintainers/registry operator immediately to revoke access.
indicators: Unexpected maintainer/ownership change on a package registry
Community reports of unfamiliar commits or account activity on a previously stable project
Registry security notification of anomalous publishing activity
vectors: Compromise of Software Dependencies and Development Tools via maintainer credential theft or account-recovery abuse
rootCauses: Maintainer accounts without multi-factor authentication
Abandoned projects with stale credentials and no succession plan
mitreTechniques: T1195.001 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
controls: Mandatory MFA for package registry publishing accounts
Registry-side anomaly detection for ownership/publishing changes
ITID-62341.detection: Moderate — registry operators increasingly alert on ownership changes, but detection still lags real-time in many ecosystems.
ITID-62341.response: Coordinate with the registry operator to freeze publishing rights, verify no malicious release has shipped, and support legitimate maintainer account recovery.
metrics: Time to publishing-rights freeze after takeover confirmation
Number of dependent projects notified
ITID-62341.notes: Sibling differentiator: this leaf captures the access/control compromise itself (the standing capability), distinct from ITID-62311 which tracks confirmed malicious code already poisoned into a package.

playbook.name: Open-Source Repository Hijacking
playbook.description: An attacker takes over a maintainer account or repository of an open-source project the organization depends on, using the hijacked access to publish malicious releases.

steps.title: Confirm the repository/maintainer account compromise
steps.desc: Investigate a threat intel report, community disclosure, or SCA alert indicating the upstream repository or maintainer account was taken over.
steps.guidance: Check the project's GitHub/GitLab security advisories, commit history for anomalous commits, and community discussion threads.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the upstream repository/maintainer account was compromised and malicious content published.
steps.abort: If unconfirmed, continue monitoring and hold off broad response actions.
steps.tool: Threat Intel / Git Platform Security Advisories

steps.title: Determine which versions/releases were compromised
steps.desc: Identify the exact malicious commit range, tag, or release version pushed by the hijacked account.
steps.guidance: Diff the malicious release against the last known-good tagged release.

steps.title: Determine organizational exposure
steps.desc: Identify every internal build/service that pulled the compromised version.
steps.guidance: Query SBOM/artifact history for the affected package name and version range.
steps.outcome: Complete exposure inventory across the organization.

steps.title: Block the compromised version at the registry proxy
steps.desc: Deny-list the malicious package version in the internal package-registry proxy immediately.
steps.outcome: No further internal builds can pull the compromised version.

steps.title: Halt and isolate affected deployments
steps.desc: Pause deployment pipelines using the compromised dependency and isolate any already-deployed instances pending analysis.
steps.outcome: Spread of the compromised dependency halted.

steps.title: Roll back to last known-good version and rebuild
steps.desc: Pin dependency manifests to the last verified clean version (or an official post-incident clean release once published) and rebuild affected services.
steps.guidance: Verify the replacement version's provenance/signature against the recovered maintainer's official channel.
steps.outcome: All affected builds rebuilt on verified clean dependency version.

steps.title: Monitor for upstream project recovery confirmation
steps.desc: Track the open-source project's own incident response (account recovery, revoked malicious releases) before resuming normal update cadence.
steps.outcome: Confirmed the upstream project has regained control and published a clean release.

steps.title: Resume normal dependency updates
steps.desc: Resume pulling updates from the project once trust is re-established, with continued monitoring.
steps.outcome: Normal dependency update process resumed safely.

steps.title: Improve upstream dependency monitoring
steps.desc: Document the incident and implement continuous monitoring for maintainer-account anomalies and unexpected release patterns on critical dependencies.
steps.guidance: Consider pinning critical dependencies and requiring manual review of major version bumps.
steps.outcome: Enhanced dependency monitoring and update-review process implemented.

ITID-62411.def: An incident in which a browser extension installed by an organizational user was found to perform unauthorized or malicious actions, such as data exfiltration, credential theft, or unwanted code injection into browsed pages, pending further classification.
ITID-62411.purpose: Intake leaf for a malicious browser extension incident not yet attributed to a specific compromise pattern within the Third-Party Plugin and Extension Exploits group.
scopeIncludes: A browser extension confirmed to exfiltrate browsing data, cookies, or form data without user consent
An extension performing unauthorized ad injection, redirect hijacking, or session manipulation
scopeExcludes: CMS plugin compromise on a server-side web application (route to ITID-6242x)
Application add-on/macro backdoors within productivity software (route to ITID-6244x)
ITID-62411.severity: Medium-High depending on the sensitivity of data accessible to the extension's granted permissions.
ITID-62411.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if credential or session-token theft is confirmed.
ITID-62411.escalation: Escalate to endpoint security for fleet-wide extension removal and to affected users for credential rotation.
indicators: Endpoint DLP or proxy logs showing unexpected data flows correlated with a specific extension's activity
User reports of unexpected browser behavior (ads, redirects, pop-ups)
Browser vendor or threat-intel takedown notice naming an installed extension
vectors: Browser Extensions installed via app store listing, drive-by prompt, or bundled software
rootCauses: Lack of browser extension allow-listing/management policy
Users granted local admin rights sufficient to install unapproved extensions
controls: Enterprise browser extension allow-listing/management policy
Endpoint DLP monitoring for anomalous browser-originated data flows
ITID-62411.detection: Moderate — browser management consoles and proxy/DLP logs can surface abuse, but many organizations lack centralized extension visibility.
ITID-62411.response: Force-remove the extension fleet-wide, rotate any credentials or sessions the extension had access to, and review extension installation policy.
metrics: Number of hosts with the malicious extension installed
Time to fleet-wide removal
ITID-62411.notes: Intake/unclassified leaf for the Malicious Browser Extensions Tier-4 group; this group has only this single leaf, so it also serves as the group's primary working definition.

playbook.name: Malicious Browser Extension (Supply Chain Context)
playbook.description: A browser extension used within the organization is found to be malicious, either by design or through a compromised update, exfiltrating data or injecting content.

steps.title: Audit browser extension inventory for the flagged extension
steps.desc: Use browser management/MDM inventory or EDR browser-extension telemetry to identify all endpoints with the flagged extension installed.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference against threat intel/vendor advisories naming the malicious extension and its ID.
steps.outcome: Complete inventory of affected endpoints and extension version.
steps.abort: If the extension is not found in the environment, close as not applicable.

steps.title: Analyze extension behavior and permissions
steps.desc: Review the extension's requested permissions and, where feasible, its code/manifest for data-exfiltration or content-injection capability.
steps.outcome: Documented capability and likely impact of the malicious extension.

steps.title: Assess data exposure
steps.desc: Determine what data (cookies, form data, browsing history, credentials) may have been accessed or exfiltrated based on the extension's permissions and observed network activity.
steps.outcome: Scope of potential data exposure documented.

steps.title: Force-remove the extension via policy
steps.desc: Push a browser management policy (GPO/MDM/enterprise browser policy) to force-uninstall or block the extension across all managed endpoints.

steps.title: Reset credentials/sessions potentially exposed
steps.desc: Force password reset and session invalidation for users whose browsers had the extension installed, particularly for sensitive applications.
steps.abort: If the extension had no credential-access capability, skip this step.

steps.title: Blocklist the extension ID/publisher
steps.desc: Add the malicious extension ID and publisher to a persistent enterprise browser blocklist to prevent reinstallation.
steps.outcome: Extension permanently blocked from installation across the fleet.

steps.title: Validate clean browser state
steps.desc: Confirm affected endpoints no longer have the extension installed and browsers are functioning normally.
steps.outcome: Fleet confirmed clean of the malicious extension.

steps.title: Implement browser extension allowlisting/approval process
steps.desc: Document the incident and establish a formal extension approval process (allowlist model) to prevent future unvetted extension installs.
steps.outcome: Browser extension governance policy implemented and enforced via technical control.

ITID-62421.def: An incident in which an adversary exploited a security vulnerability in a third-party CMS plugin — such as a WordPress plugin — to gain unauthorized access to or control over the underlying website or hosting environment.
ITID-62421.purpose: Captures compromise of a public-facing website through exploitation of a known vulnerability in a WordPress (or comparable CMS) plugin.
scopeIncludes: Exploitation of a known CVE in an installed CMS plugin leading to webshell upload, admin account creation, or content defacement
SQL injection or remote code execution via a vulnerable plugin endpoint
scopeExcludes: A malicious update pushed by a compromised plugin developer account (route to ITID-62422)
Exploitation of an abandoned plugin with no vendor fix forthcoming, where staleness rather than a specific CVE is the driving factor (route to ITID-62423)
ITID-62421.severity: High if the compromised site handles customer data or payment processing; Medium for informational/marketing sites.
ITID-62421.priority: P1 for actively exploited critical plugin CVEs on production sites.
ITID-62421.escalation: Escalate to web operations and, if customer data may be exposed, to privacy/legal.
indicators: Unexpected admin user creation in the CMS
Webshell or unfamiliar file detected in the plugin's directory
WAF or CMS security plugin alert matching a known plugin CVE
vectors: Exploit Public-Facing Application via a known vulnerable CMS plugin endpoint
rootCauses: Plugin not updated to the patched version despite vendor advisory
Lack of a web application firewall covering CMS plugin attack surfaces
controls: CMS plugin patch management SLA
Web application firewall tuned for common CMS plugin exploit patterns
ITID-62421.detection: Strong for known CVEs — CMS security plugins and WAFs commonly have signatures for popular plugin vulnerabilities.
ITID-62421.response: Patch or remove the vulnerable plugin, remove any webshells/backdoor accounts, and restore from clean backup if defacement or persistence occurred.
metrics: Number of CMS plugins overdue for patching
Time to plugin patch after CVE disclosure
ITID-62421.notes: Sibling differentiator: exploitation of a specific known plugin vulnerability, as opposed to a malicious update from a compromised developer (ITID-62422) or staleness of an abandoned plugin (ITID-62423).

playbook.name: WordPress Plugin Vulnerability Exploited for Website Compromise
playbook.description: An attacker exploits a known vulnerability in a WordPress (or similar CMS) plugin to compromise the organization's website.

steps.title: Confirm website compromise and identify the vulnerable plugin
steps.desc: Investigate signs of website compromise (defacement, injected content, unexpected admin users) and identify the specific outdated/vulnerable plugin exploited.
steps.guidance: Check plugin change logs, web server access logs for exploit request patterns matching known plugin CVEs.
steps.outcome: Specific vulnerable plugin and exploit vector confirmed.
steps.tool: Web Server Logs / CMS Security Scanner

steps.title: Audit plugin inventory across all CMS instances
steps.desc: Inventory all WordPress/CMS sites in the organization for the same vulnerable plugin/version.

steps.title: Assess extent of compromise (webshells, admin accounts, defacement)
steps.desc: Determine what the attacker did post-exploitation — installed webshells, created backdoor admin accounts, modified content, or pivoted further.

steps.title: Disable the vulnerable plugin immediately
steps.desc: Deactivate the vulnerable plugin across all affected CMS instances to stop ongoing exploitation.
steps.outcome: Exploitation vector removed from active use.

steps.title: Take the site offline or isolate if actively defaced/serving malware
steps.desc: If the site is actively serving malicious content or defaced, take it offline or place behind maintenance mode while remediation occurs.
steps.outcome: Public exposure of compromised content halted.
steps.abort: If business impact of taking the site offline is too severe, apply WAF rules to block malicious content serving instead.

steps.title: Remove webshells, backdoor accounts, and malicious content
steps.desc: Clean the CMS installation of all attacker-planted artifacts, restoring content from known-good backups where needed.
steps.guidance: Compare current file system against a clean backup/baseline to find all modified files.
steps.outcome: CMS installation fully cleaned of attacker artifacts.

steps.title: Update or replace the plugin with a patched version
steps.desc: Apply the vendor's patched plugin version, or remove the plugin entirely if no fix is available.
steps.outcome: Vulnerable plugin patched or removed across all instances.

steps.title: Restore site and validate integrity
steps.desc: Bring the site back online and validate content integrity, functionality, and absence of residual malicious code.
steps.guidance: Run a malware/integrity scan before final go-live.
steps.outcome: Site restored to normal operation, confirmed clean.

steps.title: Establish CMS plugin vetting and patch cadence
