ITID-63111.def: The introduction of non-genuine networking equipment — devices manufactured or re-badged without OEM authorization — into procurement, deployment, or spares inventory, where the equipment is sold or represented as authentic vendor hardware.
ITID-63111.purpose: Captures counterfeit networking hardware (switches, routers, and similar infrastructure devices) entering the organization's supply chain and being represented as genuine OEM equipment.
scopeIncludes: Counterfeit switches, routers, or transceivers purchased through gray-market or unauthorized resellers
Genuine-looking devices with forged labels, serial numbers, or vendor holograms
Refurbished/harvested networking hardware re-sold as new without disclosure
scopeExcludes: Counterfeit servers or non-networking component hardware (ITID-63112)
Hardware that is genuine but has a deliberately implanted backdoor (ITID-63121)

Firmware-level backdoors in otherwise genuine vendor hardware (ITID-61411-61413, a parallel Critical System Disruption category — this leaf is about the physical authenticity of the device itself, not what is running on it)
ITID-63111.severity: Medium-High. Counterfeit networking gear can fail unpredictably, lack security patching support, and may carry undocumented firmware, creating both an availability and integrity risk.
ITID-63111.priority: P2 on discovery in inventory; escalate to P1 if the device is already in production on a sensitive network segment.
ITID-63111.escalation: Escalate to procurement/supply-chain risk and network engineering immediately; quarantine the device and any devices purchased through the same channel pending verification.
indicators: Serial number fails OEM validation/warranty lookup
Physical inconsistencies (weight, port spacing, label print quality, missing security holograms)
Device purchased from a reseller not on the approved/authorized distributor list
Unexpected firmware version or boot behavior inconsistent with the claimed model
vectors: Procurement through unauthorized or gray-market resellers to cut cost or bypass lead-time constraints
Compromised or spoofed vendor invoices and packaging used to pass visual inspection
Counterfeit goods entering via a legitimate distributor's own compromised upstream sourcing
rootCauses: No requirement to purchase only from OEM-authorized channels
Absence of serial number/authenticity verification at receiving
Cost or urgency pressure driving procurement outside approved vendor lists
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: Procurement restricted to OEM-authorized distributors
Serial number/authenticity verification at receiving
Physical and firmware inspection program for new network hardware before deployment
ITID-63111.detection: Detection is largely a procurement/receiving control rather than a SOC telemetry signal; SOC visibility is typically limited to anomalous device behavior once deployed (unexpected firmware, failed integrity checks).
ITID-63111.response: Quarantine the device, verify authenticity with the OEM, identify all other units from the same purchase order/reseller, and replace with verified-genuine hardware before returning to production.
metrics: Number of counterfeit devices identified per quarter
Percentage of network hardware purchased through OEM-authorized channels
Time from discovery to full quarantine of affected purchase batch
sops: Hardware Receiving and Authenticity Verification SOP
detections: OEM serial/warranty validation check at receiving
Firmware integrity baseline comparison on new network devices
ITID-63111.notes: Differentiator within this Tier-4 group: this leaf is specifically networking infrastructure (switches/routers); ITID-63112 covers servers/components; ITID-63113 is the general catch-all for counterfeit hardware not fitting either.

playbook.name: Counterfeit Networking Equipment (Switches/Routers) in Supply Chain
playbook.description: Suspected or confirmed counterfeit switches or routers have entered the organization's inventory or network posing as genuine OEM equipment.

steps.title: Flag suspect device and gather identifying markers
steps.desc: Record model number, serial number, MAC address ranges, packaging, labeling, and firmware/boot banner details of the suspect switch or router.
steps.guidance: Photograph packaging, holograms, labels, and physical ports before handling further. Note the purchase order, vendor, and delivery chain for the unit.
steps.outcome: A documented evidence set (photos, serials, PO trail) exists for the suspect device.

steps.title: Verify authenticity against OEM/vendor database
steps.desc: Submit serial number and model to the OEM's anti-counterfeiting verification portal or account team to confirm manufacture legitimacy.
steps.guidance: Use the vendor's official verification channel, not the reseller who supplied the unit. Cross-check hologram/security label features against published OEM specimens.
steps.outcome: OEM confirms the device as counterfeit, genuine, or indeterminate pending physical inspection.
steps.abort: If OEM cannot confirm status, proceed to physical/forensic inspection rather than closing the case.

steps.title: Assess network exposure of the suspect device
steps.desc: Identify what network segments, VLANs, and traffic the device handles or has handled since installation.
steps.guidance: Pull configuration backups, syslog, and traffic flow records associated with the device's uptime.
steps.outcome: Scope of potential exposure (segments, data flows) is documented.

steps.title: Isolate and power down the suspect device
steps.desc: Remove the device from active network service without destroying evidence, routing traffic through verified-genuine equipment.
steps.guidance: Preserve the device in its current configuration state where possible; avoid factory reset before forensic imaging.
steps.outcome: Suspect device is out of the production path with no service impact.
steps.abort: If removal would cause a critical outage, implement compensating monitoring on the segment until a maintenance window is available.

steps.title: Quarantine remaining stock from same batch/vendor
steps.desc: Locate and hold all other units from the same purchase order, lot, or reseller pending verification.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with procurement and warehouse teams to freeze distribution of the batch.
steps.outcome: All related units are quarantined and inventory-tagged as under investigation.

steps.title: Forensically image and inspect confirmed counterfeit units
steps.desc: Perform hardware teardown and firmware extraction on confirmed counterfeit devices to identify malicious modifications.
steps.guidance: Engage hardware forensics specialists to check for backdoored firmware, non-standard chipsets, or beaconing behavior.
steps.outcome: Forensic report documenting whether the counterfeit units contain functional or malicious deviations from genuine hardware.

steps.title: Remove and replace all confirmed counterfeit units
steps.desc: Physically remove all confirmed counterfeit equipment from the environment and replace with verified-genuine hardware from a trusted channel.
steps.guidance: Source replacements only through OEM-authorized distributors; re-verify serials on arrival.
steps.outcome: No confirmed counterfeit units remain in active use.

steps.title: Report counterfeit goods to vendor and law enforcement
steps.desc: File a counterfeit-goods report with the OEM's brand protection team and, where warranted, local law enforcement or customs authorities.
steps.guidance: Provide serials, photos, purchase records, and the supplying reseller's identity. Vendor brand-protection teams often coordinate directly with law enforcement.
steps.outcome: Formal counterfeit-goods report is filed and a case/reference number obtained.

steps.title: Validate replacement hardware and restore service
steps.desc: Confirm replacement devices are configured, patched, and performing to baseline before returning the segment to normal operation.
steps.guidance: Run configuration compliance and performance checks against the pre-incident baseline.
steps.outcome: Segment operating normally on verified-genuine hardware.

steps.title: Notify procurement and finance of vendor/reseller risk
steps.desc: Update the approved-vendor list and flag the implicated reseller for suspension pending investigation outcome.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with procurement leadership on any contractual remedies or claims against the reseller.
steps.outcome: Reseller is flagged/suspended and procurement records updated.

steps.title: Review procurement verification controls
steps.desc: Conduct a post-incident review of how the counterfeit unit entered the supply chain and what verification step failed.
steps.guidance: Include procurement, warehouse receiving, and network engineering in the review.
steps.outcome: Root-cause findings and updated receiving-verification procedure are documented.

ITID-63112.def: The introduction of non-genuine server systems or internal components into procurement, deployment, or spares inventory, where the hardware is represented as authentic OEM product.
ITID-63112.purpose: Captures counterfeit server or component-level hardware (CPUs, memory, drives, power supplies, etc.) sold into the supply chain as genuine.
scopeIncludes: Counterfeit or remarked CPUs, memory modules, storage drives, or power supplies
Whole server chassis assembled from harvested or counterfeit parts and sold as new
Components with forged authenticity labels or falsified specification ratings
scopeExcludes: Counterfeit networking equipment such as switches/routers (ITID-63111)
Genuine hardware carrying a deliberately implanted backdoor (ITID-63121)
Firmware-level backdoors in genuine vendor hardware (ITID-61411-61413)
ITID-63112.severity: Medium-High. Counterfeit components carry elevated failure and data-integrity risk, and in server contexts can affect availability of production workloads at scale.
ITID-63112.priority: P2 on discovery in spares/inventory; escalate to P1 if already installed in production infrastructure.
ITID-63112.escalation: Escalate to procurement/supply-chain risk and infrastructure engineering; halt deployment of any remaining units from the same batch pending verification.
indicators: Component fails manufacturer serial/warranty validation
Performance or thermal behavior inconsistent with rated specifications
Packaging or labeling inconsistent with known-genuine samples
Unusually high early-failure rate across a specific purchase batch
vectors: Procurement through unauthorized resellers or secondary markets
Remarking of lower-grade or used components to appear as higher-spec/new
Compromise of a legitimate distributor's own upstream sourcing
rootCauses: No component-level authenticity verification at receiving
Purchasing driven by price/availability outside the approved vendor list
Lack of a component traceability or lot-tracking requirement in procurement contracts
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: Component authenticity verification at receiving
OEM-authorized channel purchasing policy
Batch/lot tracking with supplier traceability requirements
ITID-63112.detection: Detection is primarily a receiving/inventory control; SOC-visible signals are typically indirect (anomalous hardware failure patterns, integrity check failures).
ITID-63112.response: Quarantine affected units, verify authenticity with the OEM, identify and pull all units from the same purchase batch, and replace with verified-genuine hardware.
metrics: Number of counterfeit components identified per quarter
Percentage of server hardware purchased through OEM-authorized channels
Early-failure rate by purchase batch
sops: Hardware Receiving and Authenticity Verification SOP
detections: OEM serial/warranty validation check at receiving
Anomalous hardware failure-rate monitoring by batch
ITID-63112.notes: Differentiator within this Tier-4 group: this leaf is server/component-level hardware, distinct from ITID-63111 (networking equipment) and the ITID-63113 catch-all.

playbook.name: Counterfeit Server/Component Hardware Sold as Genuine
playbook.description: Server systems or internal components (CPUs, memory, drives, power supplies) suspected of being counterfeit have been identified in a data center or asset pool.

steps.title: Document suspect component identifiers
steps.desc: Record part numbers, serials, batch/lot codes, and physical characteristics (weight, markings, connector tolerances) of the suspect component.
steps.guidance: Compare physical characteristics against OEM reference photos; note any performance anomalies reported by operations.
steps.outcome: Component is documented with full identifying detail.

steps.title: Verify with OEM component-authentication program
steps.desc: Submit part/serial data to the OEM's component authentication service to confirm legitimacy.
steps.guidance: Many OEMs run dedicated anti-counterfeit hotlines/portals for server components; use the official channel rather than the supplying vendor.
steps.outcome: OEM confirms counterfeit, genuine, or indeterminate status.
steps.abort: If indeterminate, escalate to physical teardown and lab testing.

steps.title: Correlate with system stability/performance incidents
steps.desc: Check whether the host system has experienced unexplained crashes, thermal events, or data errors that could stem from counterfeit components.
steps.guidance: Review hardware health logs, RAID/SMART data, and helpdesk tickets tied to the affected system.
steps.outcome: Any correlated reliability incidents are identified and linked to the case.

steps.title: Take affected system out of production safely
steps.desc: Drain workloads and remove the affected server from production without abrupt shutdown that could destroy diagnostic state.
steps.guidance: Follow standard change-management/maintenance-window procedures unless immediate risk requires emergency removal.
steps.outcome: System is offline with workloads migrated to trusted hardware.
steps.abort: If workload cannot be migrated immediately, isolate to a segregated network segment as an interim measure.

steps.title: Quarantine same-batch inventory and spares
steps.desc: Pull all spares, replacement parts, and unallocated stock from the same purchase batch or supplier out of circulation.
steps.guidance: Update the CMDB to mark the batch as quarantined pending investigation.
steps.outcome: No further counterfeit components from the batch are deployed.

steps.title: Perform lab teardown and testing of confirmed units
steps.desc: Send confirmed counterfeit components to hardware forensics for teardown, testing, and assessment of any malicious or unsafe modification.
steps.guidance: Include electrical safety testing — counterfeit power supplies and batteries pose fire/safety risk beyond data integrity.
steps.outcome: Lab report on component composition, safety, and any malicious capability.

steps.title: Replace confirmed counterfeit components
steps.desc: Remove and replace all confirmed counterfeit components with parts sourced from OEM-authorized channels.
steps.guidance: Re-verify replacement part serials against OEM database before installation.
steps.outcome: All affected systems running on verified-genuine components.

steps.title: File counterfeit report with OEM and pursue vendor remedy
steps.desc: Report the counterfeit components to the OEM brand-protection team and initiate contractual/legal remedy against the supplying vendor.
steps.guidance: Loop in procurement legal counsel to assess breach-of-contract or fraud claims against the reseller.
steps.outcome: Case filed with OEM; remedy process initiated with vendor.

steps.title: Validate restored system integrity and performance
steps.desc: Run full diagnostics and burn-in testing on the restored system before returning it to production.
steps.guidance: Confirm no residual data corruption or configuration drift from the incident.
steps.outcome: System passes diagnostics and is returned to production.

steps.title: Review component-sourcing and receiving-inspection process
steps.desc: Analyze how the counterfeit component passed receiving inspection and update sourcing/verification controls.
steps.guidance: Consider requiring OEM authentication checks at receiving dock for high-value components going forward.
steps.outcome: Updated receiving-inspection procedure and root-cause report documented.

ITID-63113.def: General or not-yet-classified reports of counterfeit hardware — end-user devices, peripherals, or other equipment types — introduced into procurement or inventory and represented as genuine.
ITID-63113.purpose: Intake bucket for counterfeit hardware entering the supply chain that does not fit the networking-equipment or server/component leaves.
scopeIncludes: Counterfeit peripherals, end-user devices, or accessories not covered by ITID-63111/63112
Reports where the specific hardware category is not yet determined
Mixed or ambiguous counterfeit-hardware reports pending triage
scopeExcludes: Counterfeit networking equipment (ITID-63111)
Counterfeit server/component hardware (ITID-63112)
Deliberately backdoored genuine hardware (ITID-63121)
ITID-63113.severity: Medium by default; adjust based on the criticality of the specific device once triaged.
ITID-63113.priority: P3 pending triage; re-prioritize once the specific hardware category and deployment context are known.
ITID-63113.escalation: Escalate to procurement/supply-chain risk for triage; reclassify to a more specific leaf once the hardware type is confirmed.
indicators: Reported hardware fails authenticity checks
Reseller or purchase channel outside the approved vendor list
Device type not yet mapped to an existing counterfeit-hardware leaf
vectors: Procurement through unauthorized or gray-market channels
Counterfeit goods introduced via a compromised upstream distributor
rootCauses: Gaps in authenticity verification for hardware categories outside networking/servers
Incomplete taxonomy coverage requiring triage before precise classification
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: General hardware authenticity verification program
Approved vendor/distributor purchasing policy
ITID-63113.detection: Varies by hardware type; primarily a procurement/receiving control rather than a SOC telemetry signal.
ITID-63113.response: Triage the report, quarantine the item, and reclassify to a specific leaf (or a new one, if a durable pattern emerges) once the device type is confirmed.
metrics: Count of general counterfeit-hardware reports pending triage
Percentage subsequently reclassified into a specific leaf
sops: Hardware Receiving and Authenticity Verification SOP
detections: OEM serial/warranty validation check at receiving
ITID-63113.notes: Catch-all/intake leaf for the Counterfeit Hardware Tier-4 group; use ITID-63111 or ITID-63112 whenever the hardware category is known.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Counterfeit Hardware
playbook.description: Hardware of unspecified type is suspected to be counterfeit and requires investigation and verification under the standard counterfeit-hardware process.

steps.title: Document the suspect hardware and reporting source
steps.desc: Capture the device type, identifiers, source of suspicion (visual anomaly, performance issue, tip-off), and acquisition chain.
steps.guidance: Interview the reporting staff member or team to understand what triggered suspicion.
steps.outcome: Initial case record with device details and suspicion rationale.

steps.title: Perform initial physical and documentation comparison
steps.desc: Compare the device against known-genuine reference units or OEM documentation for markings, weight, finish, and packaging discrepancies.
steps.guidance: Use OEM-published anti-counterfeiting guides where available.

steps.title: Escalate to OEM/vendor for authoritative verification
steps.desc: Submit identifying information to the OEM or original vendor for a formal authenticity determination.
steps.guidance: Retain the vendor's written response as case evidence.
steps.abort: If OEM verification is unavailable, rely on independent hardware forensics.

steps.title: Remove device from active use
steps.desc: Take the suspect device out of production use or circulation pending investigation outcome.
steps.guidance: Preserve the device's current state for forensic review.
steps.outcome: Device isolated with no further use pending determination.

steps.title: Search inventory for related units
steps.desc: Identify any other units sharing the same source, batch, or purchase order and quarantine them.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference procurement records by vendor and PO number.
steps.outcome: All related inventory is located and quarantined.

steps.title: Conduct forensic inspection of confirmed counterfeit units
steps.desc: Perform teardown/testing to determine functional risk (malicious modification, safety hazard, or purely fraudulent branding).
steps.guidance: Engage internal or third-party hardware forensics as appropriate to the device type.
steps.outcome: Documented risk assessment of the counterfeit hardware.

steps.title: Remove and replace confirmed counterfeit hardware
steps.desc: Dispose of or securely retain (as evidence) confirmed counterfeit units and replace with verified-genuine equipment.
steps.guidance: Coordinate disposal/retention decisions with legal counsel if law enforcement referral is likely.
steps.outcome: No counterfeit hardware remains in active use.

steps.title: Report to vendor brand protection and, if warranted, law enforcement
steps.desc: File a formal counterfeit report with the OEM and consider a law-enforcement or customs referral for fraud investigation.
steps.guidance: Base the law-enforcement referral decision on scale, intent indicators, and legal counsel's advice.

steps.title: Confirm replacement hardware integrity
steps.desc: Verify replacement hardware is genuine and functioning to specification before resuming normal operations.

steps.title: Update procurement and receiving controls
steps.desc: Document root cause and strengthen verification steps to prevent recurrence across hardware categories.
steps.guidance: Share findings with procurement, security, and facilities/receiving teams.

ITID-63121.def: A deliberate physical modification to a device's hardware (an added chip, altered circuit, or implanted component) intended to grant covert access or capability, introduced at some point in the physical supply chain (manufacturing, distribution, or in-transit tampering) rather than through firmware alone.
ITID-63121.purpose: Captures physically implanted hardware backdoors — added or altered circuitry, chips, or components — discovered in devices moving through the physical supply chain, as distinct from vendor-shipped firmware backdoors.
scopeIncludes: An unauthorized chip or circuit added to a board during manufacturing or transit
Physical modification of a device discovered during teardown/inspection that provides covert connectivity or access
Hardware implants introduced by an intermediary (contract manufacturer, distributor, or carrier) without vendor knowledge
scopeExcludes: Firmware-only backdoors in otherwise unmodified genuine hardware, including vendor-mandated or OEM-level firmware backdoors (ITID-61411, ITID-61412, ITID-61413 — a parallel Critical System Disruption category)
Counterfeit hardware with no implanted backdoor capability (ITID-63111-63113)
Nation-state hardware implants specifically tied to an attributed APT campaign (ITID-63611, Nation-State Tampering with Critical Equipment)
ITID-63121.severity: High-Critical. A physical hardware implant is one of the most difficult compromises to detect and remediate, and typically implies deep, sustained access.
ITID-63121.escalation: Escalate immediately to CISO, physical security, and (where nation-state involvement is suspected) law enforcement/national authorities; treat affected devices as compromised pending forensic teardown.
indicators: Unexplained additional component, trace, or connector found during teardown/inspection
Unexpected network beaconing from a device with no legitimate reason to originate traffic
X-ray/imaging inspection revealing a board layout inconsistent with the OEM reference design
vectors: Interdiction of a shipment in transit to implant hardware before final delivery
Insertion during contract manufacturing or assembly outside vendor oversight
Compromise of a lower-tier component supplier to embed the implant upstream
rootCauses: Lack of physical chain-of-custody controls between manufacturing and delivery
No incoming hardware inspection (teardown, X-ray, or board-level verification) for high-risk device categories
Limited visibility into sub-tier manufacturing and assembly locations
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: Chain-of-custody tracking for high-risk hardware shipments
Incoming hardware teardown/X-ray inspection program for sensitive device classes
Tamper-evident packaging and seals with verification at receiving
ITID-63121.detection: Limited technical detection; primarily reliant on physical inspection programs and anomalous network behavior once the device is deployed.
ITID-63121.response: Isolate the affected device, preserve it for forensic teardown, identify and quarantine other units from the same batch/shipment, and notify the OEM.
metrics: Number of confirmed hardware implants per year
Percentage of high-risk hardware categories subject to incoming teardown inspection
Time from suspicion to forensic confirmation
sops: Hardware Receiving and Authenticity Verification SOP
detections: Network beaconing anomaly detection on newly deployed hardware
ITID-63121.notes: This is the sole leaf under Hardware Backdoors and is scoped to the PHYSICAL-INTERDICTION/implant angle. Cross-reference rather than duplicate ITID-61411-61413, which cover firmware-level backdoors shipped by the vendor itself; a device can appear in both if a physical implant and a separate firmware backdoor are both present, but each should be logged against the ITID that matches its mechanism.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Hardware Backdoor (Physical Supply Chain Context)
playbook.description: A hardware component is suspected to contain an intentionally implanted backdoor introduced somewhere in the physical supply chain.

steps.title: Document indicators of a hardware backdoor
steps.desc: Capture the evidence prompting suspicion — unexplained network beaconing, undocumented components on a board, anomalous boot behavior, or a credible tip.
steps.guidance: Correlate with network telemetry (unexpected outbound connections) and physical inspection notes.
steps.outcome: Documented indicator set supporting further investigation.

steps.title: Engage hardware security/forensics team for board-level inspection
steps.desc: Perform X-ray, decapsulation, or circuit-trace analysis to identify undocumented chips, traces, or firmware modifications.
steps.guidance: Compare the suspect board against a known-genuine reference unit of the same revision.
steps.outcome: Forensic determination of whether a backdoor implant is present.
steps.abort: If internal capability is insufficient, engage an accredited third-party hardware security lab.

steps.title: Trace supply chain custody of the affected unit
steps.desc: Reconstruct the chain of custody from manufacturer through distributor, reseller, and internal receiving to identify where tampering could have occurred.
steps.guidance: Request manufacturing and shipping records from the OEM and logistics providers.
steps.outcome: Custody timeline documented with candidate tampering points identified.

steps.title: Isolate the suspect device from all networks
steps.desc: Immediately disconnect the device from network access to prevent further data exfiltration or remote command execution via the backdoor.
steps.guidance: Preserve power state per forensic guidance if live memory analysis is planned before shutdown.
steps.outcome: Device is fully isolated with no network path.

steps.title: Identify and quarantine other units of the same model/batch
steps.desc: Locate all deployed and in-stock units sharing the same model, hardware revision, and supply source.
steps.guidance: Treat all units from the same batch as suspect until individually verified.
steps.outcome: All related units quarantined pending inspection.

steps.title: Review network and data-access logs for exploitation
steps.desc: Determine whether the backdoor was actively used and what data or systems may have been accessed.
steps.guidance: Focus on the timeframe since the device entered service.
steps.outcome: Scope of any actual exploitation is documented.

steps.title: Remove all confirmed backdoored hardware from service
steps.desc: Physically remove and securely store (as evidence) every unit confirmed to contain the implant.
steps.guidance: Coordinate evidence handling with legal counsel given likely law-enforcement/national-security interest.
steps.outcome: No backdoored hardware remains connected to any network.

steps.title: Notify OEM, law enforcement, and relevant government authority
steps.desc: Report the confirmed hardware implant to the OEM, law enforcement, and, if the device supports critical functions, the appropriate national critical-infrastructure or counter-intelligence authority.
steps.guidance: Hardware implants are often treated as a national-security matter; escalate promptly through executive and legal channels.
steps.outcome: Formal reports filed with all relevant authorities.

steps.title: Deploy verified-clean replacement hardware
steps.desc: Source and deploy replacement hardware through a vetted, higher-assurance supply channel, verifying integrity before deployment.
steps.guidance: Consider enhanced receiving inspection (X-ray or trusted-supplier attestation) for the replacement units.
steps.outcome: Replacement hardware is deployed and verified free of implants.

steps.title: Conduct full supply-chain security review
steps.desc: Review sourcing, custody, and receiving-inspection practices for the affected hardware category and implement stronger assurance controls.
steps.guidance: Consider adopting hardware attestation, tamper-evident packaging requirements, or trusted-foundry sourcing for critical hardware.
steps.outcome: Updated supply-chain assurance policy documented and adopted.

ITID-63131.def: Evidence that a shipment's physical security (seals, packaging, chain-of-custody) was compromised in transit, indicating a window of opportunity for tampering, theft, or substitution, regardless of whether a specific hardware modification has yet been confirmed.
ITID-63131.purpose: Captures interdiction and physical tampering with a shipment while it is in transit through the supply chain, prior to any specific implant or counterfeit finding being confirmed.
scopeIncludes: Broken, missing, or inconsistent tamper-evident seals on a shipment at receiving
Chain-of-custody gaps or unexplained handling delays for a sensitive shipment
Packaging showing signs of having been opened and resealed
scopeExcludes: A confirmed hardware implant resulting from the tampering (ITID-63121)
Cargo theft where goods do not arrive at all (ITID-63211, Supply Chain Theft and Fraud)
Contamination/tampering specific to perishable or sensitive goods in transit (ITID-63232)
ITID-63131.severity: Medium-High, pending confirmation; escalate to High if a subsequent inspection confirms tampering with device internals.
ITID-63131.priority: P2 on detection of a broken chain-of-custody or seal anomaly; escalate to P1 if the shipment contains sensitive/critical hardware.
ITID-63131.escalation: Escalate to physical security and supply-chain risk immediately; quarantine the shipment and initiate forensic inspection before deployment.
indicators: Tamper-evident seal broken, mismatched, or missing at receiving
Shipment tracking showing an unexplained stop, delay, or route deviation
Physical inconsistencies between packaging and shipment manifest
vectors: Interdiction of a shipment at a transfer point (port, customs, carrier hub) to gain physical access
Collusion with a logistics employee to create an opportunity for tampering
Exploitation of unmonitored dwell time in a warehouse or transfer facility
rootCauses: No tamper-evident seal verification requirement at receiving
Incomplete chain-of-custody tracking across carrier handoffs
Lack of GPS/route monitoring for high-value or sensitive shipments
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: Tamper-evident seals with verification at every handoff
End-to-end chain-of-custody tracking for sensitive shipments
GPS/route monitoring with alerting on unexpected deviations or dwell time
ITID-63131.detection: Detection relies on physical/logistics controls (seal checks, custody logs, route monitoring) rather than SOC telemetry.
ITID-63131.response: Quarantine the shipment, verify seal/custody records, forensically inspect contents before deployment, and investigate the specific handoff point where the anomaly occurred.
metrics: Number of shipments with broken/anomalous seals per quarter
Percentage of sensitive shipments with full chain-of-custody tracking
Time from anomaly detection to forensic clearance
sops: Hardware Receiving and Authenticity Verification SOP
ITID-63131.notes: This is the sole leaf under Tampered Shipments and functions as the general/unclassified entry point for in-transit tampering evidence; if inspection subsequently confirms a hardware implant, reclassify to ITID-63121.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Tampered Shipment
playbook.description: A shipment of hardware or components shows evidence of physical tampering during transit, raising concern about compromised contents.

steps.title: Document tamper evidence at receiving
steps.desc: Photograph and log broken seals, re-taped packaging, mismatched tamper-evident labels, or other signs of intrusion at the point of receipt.
steps.guidance: Do not open or further disturb suspect packaging beyond what is needed to assess the tamper evidence.
steps.outcome: Tamper evidence is fully documented before any contents are handled.

steps.title: Verify shipment manifest against contents
steps.desc: Reconcile the packing list and manifest against actual contents to identify missing, added, or substituted items.
steps.guidance: Involve two staff members to co-verify the reconciliation for integrity of the record.
steps.outcome: Discrepancies between manifest and actual contents are documented.

steps.title: Request chain-of-custody records from the carrier/logistics provider
steps.desc: Obtain transit logs, handling records, and any GPS/telemetry data from the shipping carrier for the affected shipment.
steps.guidance: Request records covering all handoff points, not just origin and destination.
steps.outcome: Custody trail obtained for the shipment's full transit.
steps.abort: If the carrier cannot produce records, document the gap as an investigative finding.

steps.title: Quarantine the shipment and hold from deployment
steps.desc: Physically segregate the shipment's contents and prevent installation or use until integrity is confirmed.
steps.guidance: Label the quarantine area clearly and restrict access to the investigation team.
steps.outcome: Shipment contents are held with no risk of premature deployment.

steps.title: Check for other shipments in the same transit batch
steps.desc: Identify sibling shipments routed through the same carrier leg, vehicle, or handling point around the same time.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the carrier and internal logistics to trace related shipments.
steps.outcome: Related shipments identified and placed under heightened scrutiny.

steps.title: Forensically inspect shipment contents for tampering or implants
steps.desc: Have hardware forensics inspect the physical goods for signs of tampering, substitution, or implanted devices.
steps.guidance: Prioritize inspection of high-value or security-relevant items in the shipment first.
steps.outcome: Inspection results document whether contents were compromised.

steps.title: Reject or replace compromised contents
steps.desc: Return confirmed-tampered items to the vendor/carrier under claim, and source verified-clean replacements.
steps.guidance: Follow the vendor's RMA process and retain evidence copies before returning items if law enforcement referral is possible.
steps.outcome: Compromised items removed from the supply chain and replacements procured.

steps.title: File incident report with carrier and, where warranted, law enforcement
steps.desc: Report the tampering incident to the logistics provider's security team and to law enforcement if theft, sabotage, or implant activity is confirmed.
steps.guidance: Include the custody trail and forensic findings in the report.
steps.outcome: Formal report filed with a tracked case reference.

steps.title: Deploy verified-clean replacement goods
steps.desc: Confirm replacement items pass integrity checks before releasing them into production use.
steps.outcome: Verified goods released from quarantine into normal use.

steps.title: Review packaging and carrier security requirements
steps.desc: Assess whether tamper-evident packaging standards and carrier security requirements need strengthening.
steps.guidance: Consider requiring tamper-evident seals with serialized verification for high-value shipments going forward.

ITID-63141.def: An attack in which an adversary with physical or close proximity access to a device measures its power consumption during cryptographic operations to statistically infer secret key material, without needing to break the underlying algorithm.
ITID-63141.purpose: Captures power-analysis side-channel attacks (simple or differential power analysis) used to extract cryptographic key material from a physical device.
scopeIncludes: Simple Power Analysis (SPA) or Differential Power Analysis (DPA) performed against a smart card, HSM, IoT device, or embedded cryptographic module
Use of specialized probing equipment to capture power traces during key operations
scopeExcludes: Electromagnetic emission analysis (a distinct side-channel technique, ITID-63143)
Spectre/Meltdown-class microarchitectural speculative-execution attacks (ITID-63142)
Software-only cryptographic attacks with no physical measurement component (out of scope for this Tier-2 category)
ITID-63141.severity: High. Successful key extraction can fully compromise the cryptographic protections of the affected device class.
ITID-63141.priority: P1 on any confirmed or strongly suspected key-extraction attempt against production hardware.
ITID-63141.escalation: Escalate immediately to the cryptographic/security engineering team and CISO; assume key compromise and begin key rotation/revocation planning.
indicators: Physical evidence of probing equipment attached to a device (test clips, shunt resistors, modified enclosures)
Device recovered from a hostile or uncontrolled environment showing signs of tampering
Anomalous behavior consistent with repeated forced cryptographic operations (used to gather traces)
vectors: Physical access to a device (stolen, borrowed, or briefly unattended) to attach measurement probes
Repeated triggering of cryptographic operations on a device to build a statistical power-trace dataset
rootCauses: Cryptographic hardware lacking power-analysis countermeasures (masking, constant-power design)
Insufficient physical security around devices holding high-value key material
No tamper-detection/self-destruct capability on the affected hardware
controls: Use of side-channel-resistant cryptographic hardware (masked/constant-power implementations)
Physical tamper-detection and key-zeroization on intrusion
Restricted physical access and custody controls for devices holding key material
ITID-63141.detection: Hardware side-channel attack — no ATT&CK Enterprise technique applies; this is a physical/microarchitectural attack class documented by CVE and academic literature rather than ATT&CK. Detection is almost entirely physical (tamper evidence, custody controls) rather than log-based.
ITID-63141.response: Treat any suspected exposure as key compromise: revoke and rotate affected keys, forensically examine the device for probing evidence, and review physical custody procedures for the device class.
metrics: Number of devices found with physical tamper/probing evidence
Time from suspected exposure to key rotation completion
Percentage of high-value crypto hardware with tamper-detection enabled
sops: Cryptographic Key Compromise and Rotation SOP
detections: Physical tamper-evidence inspection on returned/recovered devices
ITID-63141.notes: Differentiator within this Tier-4 group: this leaf is the power-measurement side-channel technique specifically, distinct from EM emission analysis (ITID-63143) and Spectre/Meltdown-class microarchitectural attacks (ITID-63142).

playbook.name: Power Analysis Attack Extracting Cryptographic Keys
playbook.description: Evidence indicates an adversary used differential or simple power analysis against a hardware cryptographic module to extract secret key material.

steps.title: Identify the affected cryptographic hardware and key material at risk
steps.desc: Determine which device(s), HSM, smartcard, or embedded crypto module is suspected of being subjected to power analysis, and which keys it protects.
steps.guidance: Correlate with any physical access logs, anomalous device handling, or lab-environment access around the module.
steps.outcome: Affected devices and at-risk keys are identified and listed.

steps.title: Assess cryptographic-anomaly and usage indicators
steps.desc: Review key-usage logs for anomalies consistent with extracted-key misuse (unexpected signing/decryption activity, use from unfamiliar locations).
steps.guidance: Compare against baseline usage patterns for the affected keys.
steps.outcome: Determination of whether extracted keys show signs of active misuse.

steps.title: Engage hardware security lab to confirm side-channel vulnerability
steps.desc: Have hardware security specialists assess the module's susceptibility to power analysis and, where feasible, attempt to reproduce key extraction under controlled conditions.
steps.guidance: This confirms whether the module's countermeasures (masking, power filtering) were actually defeated.
steps.outcome: Technical confirmation of the vulnerability and extraction feasibility.

steps.title: Revoke and rotate the at-risk cryptographic keys
steps.desc: Immediately revoke any keys confirmed or strongly suspected to be exposed and issue replacement keys.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with all systems and partners relying on the affected keys to minimize disruption during rotation.
steps.outcome: Exposed keys are revoked and no longer trusted for authentication or decryption.

steps.title: Isolate the affected hardware module from production use
steps.desc: Remove the vulnerable cryptographic module from active service to prevent further exposure while investigation continues.
steps.outcome: Module is no longer processing production cryptographic operations.
steps.abort: If immediate removal is impossible, restrict physical access to the module to trusted personnel only.

steps.title: Apply firmware or microcode countermeasures where available
steps.desc: Deploy vendor-supplied firmware updates that add or strengthen power-analysis countermeasures (masking, noise injection, randomized timing).
steps.guidance: Confirm with the vendor whether a software/firmware mitigation is sufficient or whether the vulnerability is inherent to the hardware design.
steps.outcome: Available countermeasures are applied and verified.
steps.abort: If no effective firmware mitigation exists, proceed to hardware replacement.

steps.title: Replace hardware that cannot be adequately mitigated
steps.desc: Physically replace cryptographic modules for which no firmware mitigation adequately addresses the power-analysis vulnerability.
steps.guidance: Select replacement hardware with certified side-channel resistance (e.g., FIPS 140-3 Level 3+ or Common Criteria side-channel evaluation).
steps.outcome: Vulnerable hardware is replaced with side-channel-resistant modules.

steps.title: Validate new keys and hardware in production
steps.desc: Confirm rotated keys and replacement/patched hardware are functioning correctly across all dependent systems.
steps.guidance: Run end-to-end cryptographic operation tests before declaring full recovery.
steps.outcome: All dependent systems operating correctly on new keys and secured hardware.

steps.title: Notify affected stakeholders and assess disclosure obligations
steps.desc: Determine whether the key compromise triggers customer, partner, or regulatory notification obligations.
steps.guidance: Consult legal/compliance on breach-notification requirements tied to the compromised keys' use (e.g., data encryption, code signing).
steps.outcome: Notification obligations assessed and, where required, executed.

steps.title: Review cryptographic hardware selection and physical-access controls
steps.desc: Evaluate whether procurement standards for cryptographic hardware need to require certified side-channel resistance, and whether physical access controls around such hardware were adequate.
steps.guidance: Update procurement standards and physical security requirements for future cryptographic hardware deployments.
steps.outcome: Updated hardware procurement and access-control standards documented.

ITID-63142.def: An attack that abuses a CPU's speculative or out-of-order execution behavior (and its measurable timing/cache side effects) to read memory that should be inaccessible to the attacker, such as across process, VM, or privilege boundaries.
ITID-63142.purpose: Captures Spectre/Meltdown-class attacks that exploit CPU speculative execution to leak data across security boundaries via microarchitectural side channels.
scopeIncludes: Exploitation of a Spectre, Meltdown, or related transient-execution CPU vulnerability against production hardware
Cross-VM or cross-tenant memory disclosure in shared/cloud infrastructure attributable to a speculative-execution flaw
scopeExcludes: Power-analysis or EM-emission side-channel attacks against embedded/crypto hardware (ITID-63141, ITID-63143)
Standard software vulnerabilities with no microarchitectural component
ITID-63142.severity: High-Critical, particularly in shared/multi-tenant infrastructure where cross-tenant data disclosure is possible.
ITID-63142.priority: P1 on confirmed exploitation attempt or credible proof-of-concept observed against production systems; P2 for tracking unpatched-CPU exposure.
ITID-63142.escalation: Escalate to infrastructure/platform engineering and CISO; prioritize microcode/OS mitigation deployment and assess cross-tenant blast radius in shared environments.
indicators: CPU/hypervisor telemetry showing anomalous cache-timing access patterns consistent with a known transient-execution exploit
Vulnerability scanner or CPU vendor advisory flagging unpatched/unmitigated microcode on production hardware
Unexplained cross-VM data exposure in a shared hosting environment
vectors: Malicious code (including in a co-located VM or container) executing speculative-execution gadgets to leak adjacent memory
Exploitation of unpatched microcode/OS mitigations in shared cloud or virtualization infrastructure
rootCauses: Microcode and OS/hypervisor mitigations not applied to production hardware
Legacy hardware that cannot receive a full mitigation and remains in service
Insufficient isolation between tenants on shared physical hosts
controls: Microcode and OS/hypervisor mitigation patching program for known transient-execution vulnerabilities
Hardware refresh planning for CPUs that cannot be fully mitigated
Enhanced tenant isolation (dedicated hosts) for the most sensitive workloads
ITID-63142.detection: No ATT&CK Enterprise technique directly captures this microarchitectural class; some analysts loosely associate exploitation-driven system instability with T1499.004 (Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation), but that framing describes a DoS side effect rather than the data-disclosure mechanism itself, so it is not used here as a primary mapping. Detection instead relies on CPU vendor advisories, mitigation-compliance scanning, and (where available) hypervisor-level anomaly monitoring.
ITID-63142.response: Patch microcode/OS mitigations on affected hardware immediately, assess whether any cross-boundary data disclosure occurred, and plan hardware replacement where mitigation is incomplete.
metrics: Percentage of production hardware with current microcode/OS mitigations applied
Number of unmitigated legacy hosts remaining
Time from CPU vendor advisory to mitigation deployment
detections: Mitigation-compliance scanning against known CPU advisories
ITID-63142.notes: Differentiator within this Tier-4 group: this leaf covers CPU microarchitectural speculative-execution side channels specifically, as opposed to power-analysis (ITID-63141) or EM-emission (ITID-63143) hardware side channels.

playbook.name: Spectre/Meltdown-Class CPU Speculative Execution Attack
playbook.description: A speculative-execution side-channel vulnerability (Spectre/Meltdown-class) is being actively exploited or is confirmed exploitable against organizational CPUs.

steps.title: Identify affected CPU models and vulnerable variant
steps.desc: Determine which CPU families/steppings are in use and map them against the specific Spectre/Meltdown-class CVE variant of concern.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference vendor advisories (Intel, AMD, ARM) and internal hardware asset inventory.
steps.outcome: List of affected systems and the applicable vulnerability variant(s).

steps.title: Assess exploitation indicators via timing/cryptographic anomaly analysis
steps.desc: Analyze system and application logs for signs consistent with speculative-execution exploitation (unexpected cross-process data leakage, anomalous timing patterns, unexplained privileged-memory disclosure).
steps.guidance: Engage a specialist if proof-of-concept exploit code matching the variant is publicly known and in the wild.
steps.outcome: Determination of whether active exploitation is occurring versus a theoretical exposure.

steps.title: Determine sensitivity of co-resident workloads
steps.desc: For multi-tenant or virtualized hosts, identify which workloads share physical CPU resources with potentially untrusted code.
steps.guidance: This is critical for cloud/virtualization environments where cross-tenant leakage is the primary risk.
steps.outcome: Risk exposure mapped by host and co-tenancy arrangement.

steps.title: Isolate high-risk co-tenant workloads
steps.desc: Where practical, migrate untrusted or high-risk workloads off shared physical hardware with sensitive workloads pending mitigation.
steps.guidance: Prioritize isolation for hosts running both untrusted third-party code and highly sensitive data processing.
steps.outcome: Sensitive workloads no longer share vulnerable CPU resources with untrusted code.
steps.abort: If migration is not feasible in the short term, apply available OS-level scheduling mitigations as an interim measure.

steps.title: Apply available OS and hypervisor mitigations
steps.desc: Deploy vendor-provided operating system and hypervisor patches implementing available speculative-execution mitigations (e.g., retpoline, KPTI, microcode-assisted mitigations).
steps.guidance: Test for performance impact before broad rollout, particularly on latency-sensitive workloads.
steps.outcome: Available software mitigations are deployed fleet-wide.

steps.title: Apply CPU microcode updates
steps.desc: Deploy manufacturer-issued microcode updates addressing the specific speculative-execution variant.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with hardware vendors for validated microcode packages compatible with the specific server/BIOS revisions in use.
steps.outcome: Microcode updates applied fleet-wide where available.
steps.abort: Note explicitly that software/microcode mitigation is often incomplete for Spectre/Meltdown-class issues; residual risk must be tracked.

steps.title: Plan hardware replacement for unmitigable exposure
steps.desc: For CPU generations where no adequate microcode or software mitigation exists, plan phased hardware replacement for the highest-risk hosts.
steps.guidance: Prioritize replacement based on data sensitivity and co-tenancy risk rather than replacing the entire fleet at once.
steps.outcome: Hardware replacement roadmap approved for unmitigable systems.

steps.title: Validate mitigation effectiveness and performance impact
steps.desc: Confirm mitigations are correctly applied fleet-wide and assess any performance degradation introduced.
steps.guidance: Run both security validation (mitigation presence) and performance benchmarking.
steps.outcome: Mitigations confirmed active with acceptable performance impact.

steps.title: Restore full workload placement flexibility
steps.desc: Once mitigations are validated, restore normal workload scheduling and co-tenancy policies where isolation was applied as a temporary measure.
steps.outcome: Normal operations resumed with mitigations in place.

steps.title: Review hardware procurement and patch-velocity standards
steps.desc: Assess how quickly the organization was able to identify exposure and apply mitigations, and update CPU procurement criteria and microcode/patch SLAs accordingly.
steps.guidance: Consider including speculative-execution resistance and vendor patch responsiveness in future hardware procurement evaluation criteria.
steps.outcome: Updated procurement and patch-management standards documented.

ITID-63143.def: An attack in which an adversary with physical or close proximity access to a device captures and analyzes its electromagnetic emissions during operation to infer secret data, without requiring direct electrical contact with the device.
ITID-63143.purpose: Captures electromagnetic emission analysis attacks used to extract sensitive data (such as cryptographic keys) from a device's unintentional radio-frequency emissions.
scopeIncludes: Use of EM probes or antennas to capture emissions from a device during cryptographic or sensitive processing
TEMPEST-style eavesdropping intended to reconstruct displayed or processed data from emitted signals
scopeExcludes: Power-analysis attacks requiring electrical contact/measurement (ITID-63141)
Spectre/Meltdown-class microarchitectural attacks (ITID-63142)
ITID-63143.severity: High, particularly for devices handling classified, cryptographic, or otherwise highly sensitive data.
ITID-63143.priority: P1 for any confirmed or strongly suspected EM eavesdropping attempt against sensitive infrastructure.
ITID-63143.escalation: Escalate to physical security, cryptographic/security engineering, and CISO; assume potential data or key exposure pending assessment.
indicators: Discovery of unauthorized EM-capture equipment (antennas, receivers) near sensitive facilities or equipment
Facility TEMPEST/emissions-security assessment identifying non-compliant shielding
Device recovered from an uncontrolled environment with no verifiable custody history
vectors: Placement of covert EM-capture equipment within range of a target device or facility
Exploitation of inadequate shielding on devices processing high-value cryptographic or classified data
rootCauses: Absence of TEMPEST/emissions-security shielding on sensitive equipment
Inadequate physical perimeter control allowing close-proximity equipment placement
No periodic emissions-security assessment for high-value facilities
controls: TEMPEST/emissions-security shielding for high-value cryptographic and processing equipment
Physical perimeter controls limiting close-proximity access to sensitive facilities
Periodic emissions-security assessment for facilities handling classified or highly sensitive data
ITID-63143.detection: Hardware side-channel attack — no ATT&CK Enterprise technique applies; this is a physical/microarchitectural attack class documented by CVE and academic literature rather than ATT&CK. Detection is physical (sweep for unauthorized equipment, emissions-security audits) rather than log-based.
ITID-63143.response: Sweep the area for unauthorized capture equipment, assess whether the affected device processed sensitive data during the exposure window, and treat any exposed cryptographic material as compromised.
metrics: Number of emissions-security assessments completed per year
Findings of non-compliant shielding remediated
Incidents of unauthorized EM-capture equipment discovered
detections: Periodic sweep for unauthorized RF/EM capture equipment
ITID-63143.notes: Differentiator within this Tier-4 group: this leaf is the electromagnetic-emission side-channel technique specifically, distinct from power-analysis (ITID-63141) and CPU microarchitectural (ITID-63142) side channels.

playbook.name: Electromagnetic Emission Analysis Attack
playbook.description: An adversary is suspected of using electromagnetic emission (TEMPEST-class) analysis to extract sensitive information or cryptographic key material from hardware.

steps.title: Identify the targeted equipment and physical proximity risk
steps.desc: Determine which devices are suspected targets and assess whether unauthorized personnel or equipment (e.g., an antenna, receiver) had proximity sufficient for EM capture.
steps.guidance: Review physical access logs, visitor records, and CCTV footage for the area around the suspect equipment during the relevant window.
steps.outcome: Documented assessment of proximity-based feasibility and any physical evidence of monitoring equipment.

steps.title: Assess for cryptographic-anomaly or data-exposure indicators
steps.desc: Analyze key-usage and data-access logs for signs that information consistent with EM-derived leakage has been used elsewhere.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the crypto/security engineering team on which keys or data the targeted equipment processes.
steps.outcome: Determination of whether extracted information appears to have been used or disclosed.

steps.title: Engage hardware security specialists to assess emission profile
steps.desc: Have specialists measure the equipment's electromagnetic emission profile and assess its susceptibility to remote or near-field capture.
steps.guidance: Consider engaging a TEMPEST-accredited testing service for a rigorous assessment.
steps.outcome: Technical report on emission risk and feasible capture range.

steps.title: Restrict physical access to the affected area
steps.desc: Tighten physical access controls to the space housing the targeted equipment, and sweep for unauthorized monitoring devices.
steps.guidance: Conduct a technical surveillance countermeasures (TSCM) sweep of the area if covert monitoring equipment is suspected.
steps.outcome: Area secured and swept, with no unauthorized monitoring equipment present.

steps.title: Rotate any keys or data potentially exposed via emission
steps.desc: As a precaution, revoke and rotate cryptographic keys or sensitive data handled by the targeted equipment during the suspected exposure window.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with key management and application owners to minimize disruption.
steps.outcome: Potentially exposed keys/data are rotated or invalidated.

steps.title: Deploy EM shielding or physical countermeasures
steps.desc: Implement shielding (Faraday enclosures, TEMPEST-rated equipment, physical separation) to reduce future emission exposure for the affected equipment.
steps.guidance: Prioritize shielding for equipment handling the most sensitive cryptographic or classified operations.
steps.outcome: Emission risk is reduced to an acceptable level via shielding or physical countermeasures.

steps.title: Replace equipment lacking adequate emission security where required
steps.desc: For the highest-sensitivity use cases, replace equipment with TEMPEST-certified alternatives if shielding is insufficient.
steps.outcome: Highest-sensitivity operations run on emission-hardened equipment.

steps.title: Validate shielding effectiveness and resume normal operations
steps.desc: Re-test emission levels after countermeasures are applied to confirm the risk has been mitigated before resuming normal use.
steps.outcome: Emission levels confirmed within acceptable bounds; equipment returned to normal use.

steps.title: Review physical security and emission-security standards
steps.desc: Assess whether facility physical security and emission-security (TEMPEST) standards are adequate for the sensitivity of equipment housed there, and update standards as needed.
steps.guidance: Consider periodic TSCM sweeps and emission testing for high-sensitivity facilities going forward.

ITID-63144.def: General or not-yet-classified reports of a hardware side-channel attack — such as timing analysis, acoustic cryptanalysis, or fault-injection — used to extract sensitive data from a physical device.
ITID-63144.purpose: Intake bucket for hardware side-channel attacks that do not fit the power-analysis, Spectre/Meltdown, or EM-emission leaves.
scopeIncludes: Timing-analysis, acoustic, or fault-injection side-channel attacks not covered by the more specific leaves
Reports where the specific side-channel technique is not yet determined
scopeExcludes: Power analysis (ITID-63141)
Spectre/Meltdown-class microarchitectural attacks (ITID-63142)
Electromagnetic emission analysis (ITID-63143)
ITID-63144.severity: High by default, pending confirmation of the specific technique and target sensitivity.
ITID-63144.priority: P2 pending triage; re-prioritize to P1 if the target device holds cryptographic or classified material.
ITID-63144.escalation: Escalate to cryptographic/security engineering for triage; reclassify to a specific leaf once the technique is confirmed.
indicators: Physical evidence of measurement/probing equipment inconsistent with the known power-analysis or EM-emission leaves
Device behavior consistent with a side-channel data-extraction attempt not yet categorized
vectors: Physical or close-proximity access used to perform an uncategorized side-channel measurement technique
rootCauses: Cryptographic hardware lacking general side-channel countermeasures
Gaps in physical custody controls for sensitive devices
controls: Use of side-channel-resistant cryptographic hardware
Physical tamper-detection and restricted custody for sensitive devices
ITID-63144.detection: Hardware side-channel attack — no ATT&CK Enterprise technique applies; this is a physical/microarchitectural attack class documented by CVE and academic literature rather than ATT&CK.
ITID-63144.response: Triage the report, assess key/data exposure, and reclassify to a specific leaf (or flag for a new dedicated leaf if a durable new pattern emerges).
metrics: Count of general side-channel reports pending triage
Percentage subsequently reclassified into a specific leaf
sops: Cryptographic Key Compromise and Rotation SOP
detections: Physical tamper-evidence inspection on returned/recovered devices
ITID-63144.notes: Catch-all/intake leaf for the Side-Channel Attacks on Hardware Tier-4 group.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Side-Channel Hardware Attack
playbook.description: A hardware side-channel attack of unspecified technique is suspected against organizational systems, requiring investigation under the general cryptographic/hardware-security IR process.

steps.title: Characterize the suspected side-channel technique and target
steps.desc: Gather available evidence to determine the likely side-channel vector (timing, power, EM, acoustic, cache-based) and the targeted hardware or cryptographic function.
steps.guidance: Consult with cryptographic engineering and hardware security specialists early to properly classify the attack type.
steps.outcome: The suspected technique and target hardware are documented.

steps.title: Analyze for cryptographic-anomaly or timing indicators
steps.desc: Review key-usage logs and, where feasible, timing/behavioral telemetry for anomalies consistent with side-channel exploitation.
steps.outcome: Determination of whether exploitation indicators are present.

steps.title: Engage hardware security specialists for technical confirmation
steps.desc: Have specialists test or analyze the suspect hardware/function to confirm the vulnerability and assess exploitability.
steps.outcome: Technical confirmation of vulnerability and exploitability.

steps.title: Isolate the affected hardware from sensitive operations
steps.desc: Remove or restrict the affected hardware from processing sensitive cryptographic operations or data pending remediation.
steps.outcome: Affected hardware no longer exposes sensitive operations to the side-channel risk.

steps.title: Rotate any potentially exposed keys or credentials
steps.desc: As a precaution, rotate cryptographic keys or credentials that may have been exposed via the side-channel.
steps.outcome: Potentially exposed keys/credentials are invalidated and replaced.

steps.title: Apply available firmware/software countermeasures
steps.desc: Deploy vendor-supplied patches, microcode, or configuration changes that mitigate the specific side-channel vulnerability.
steps.guidance: Confirm with the vendor whether the mitigation is complete or partial.
steps.abort: If mitigation is incomplete, proceed to hardware replacement for the highest-risk systems.

steps.title: Replace hardware where mitigation is inadequate
steps.desc: Physically replace hardware that cannot be adequately protected via firmware or software countermeasures.
steps.guidance: Select replacements with documented side-channel resistance certifications where available.

steps.title: Validate mitigations and resume normal operations
steps.desc: Confirm mitigations are effective and restore normal use of the affected hardware and cryptographic functions.
steps.outcome: Operations resumed with confirmed mitigations in place.

steps.title: Review hardware security evaluation criteria
steps.desc: Update procurement and security-evaluation criteria to include side-channel resistance testing for future hardware acquisitions handling sensitive functions.

ITID-63211.def: The physical theft of goods — an entire shipment, container, or portion of cargo — while in the custody of a carrier, at a transfer point, or in transit between supply chain nodes.
ITID-63211.purpose: Captures outright physical theft of cargo or freight while it is in transit through the logistics chain.
scopeIncludes: Hijacking of a truck, container, or rail shipment
Theft from an unattended or inadequately secured vehicle/yard during transit
Organized cargo-theft rings targeting high-value shipments
scopeExcludes: Fraudulent redirection of a shipment via deception rather than physical seizure (ITID-63212)
Theft facilitated by a logistics employee acting as an insider (ITID-63221)
Theft from a warehouse/storage facility rather than in transit (Warehouse and Storage Facility Attacks category)
ITID-63211.severity: Medium-High, scaled to the value and criticality of the stolen cargo.
ITID-63211.priority: P2 by default; escalate to P1 for high-value or mission-critical shipments (e.g., cryptographic hardware, critical infrastructure components).
ITID-63211.escalation: Escalate to physical security, logistics partner, and law enforcement immediately; notify affected business units of shipment loss.
indicators: Shipment tracking shows loss of GPS signal or unexplained route deviation followed by non-delivery
Carrier reports a hijacking or theft incident
Discrepancy between manifest and delivered quantity
vectors: Organized criminal interception of a vehicle or container in transit
Theft during an unmonitored stop, rest period, or yard dwell
rootCauses: Lack of GPS/route monitoring on high-value shipments
Inadequate physical security at rest stops, yards, or transfer points
No requirement for tamper-evident, high-security seals on high-value cargo
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: GPS/route monitoring with real-time alerting for high-value shipments
High-security locks and tamper-evident seals
Vetted, monitored rest/transfer points for high-value cargo routes
ITID-63211.detection: Physical logistics crime — no ATT&CK Enterprise technique applies; tracked via physical security and logistics-partner coordination.
ITID-63211.response: Report to law enforcement and the logistics partner immediately, assess business impact of the lost shipment, and review whether the specific route/carrier requires additional controls.
metrics: Number of cargo theft incidents per quarter
Value of goods lost to cargo theft
Percentage of high-value shipments under GPS/route monitoring
ITID-63211.notes: Differentiator within this Tier-4 group: this leaf is outright physical seizure of cargo, as opposed to deception-based diversion (ITID-63212) or broker fraud (ITID-63213).

playbook.name: Cargo/Freight Theft During Transit
playbook.description: A shipment of cargo or freight was stolen while in transit between origin and destination.

steps.title: Confirm theft and establish shipment status
steps.desc: Verify with the carrier and tracking systems that the shipment is confirmed missing or diverted rather than delayed.
steps.guidance: Check GPS/telematics data, delivery confirmations, and driver check-in records.
steps.outcome: Theft is confirmed and last-known location/time established.
steps.abort: If the shipment reappears as delayed rather than stolen, close as a logistics delay rather than a security incident.

steps.title: Determine contents and value at risk
steps.desc: Identify the specific goods, quantities, and value of the stolen shipment, and whether contents include sensitive or regulated items.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference the bill of lading and purchase/sales order.
steps.outcome: Full inventory and value of stolen goods documented.

steps.title: Gather transit and handling records
steps.desc: Collect route history, handoff points, driver/vehicle assignment, and any anomalies noted en route.
steps.guidance: Request records from the carrier promptly before they age out of retention.
steps.outcome: Transit history compiled to support the theft investigation.

steps.title: Notify law enforcement and file a theft report
steps.desc: File a police report in the relevant jurisdiction covering the theft, including all available shipment and route details.
steps.guidance: Cargo theft often crosses jurisdictions; confirm which agency has primary responsibility (local police, state police, or a dedicated cargo theft task force).
steps.outcome: Police report filed with a case number.

steps.title: Notify carrier/logistics provider security team
steps.desc: Formally notify the carrier's security or loss-prevention team to trigger their internal investigation and insurance process.
steps.outcome: Carrier's security team engaged and investigation opened on their side.

steps.title: Flag stolen goods to prevent resale/reuse
steps.desc: Where goods carry serial numbers or unique identifiers, distribute alerts to resellers, marketplaces, or industry theft-reporting databases.
steps.guidance: Use industry cargo-theft databases (e.g., CargoNet or regional equivalents) where applicable.
steps.outcome: Stolen goods are flagged in relevant tracking/alert systems.

steps.title: Assess and close any exploited process gap
steps.desc: Determine whether the theft exploited a specific weakness (route predictability, unsecured parking, insider tip) and address it.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the carrier on route/security changes if the gap is on their side.

steps.title: File insurance claim and pursue replacement goods
steps.desc: Submit an insurance claim for the stolen goods and arrange replacement shipment to fulfill the original order.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with finance/insurance teams to ensure documentation supports the claim.
steps.outcome: Claim filed and replacement shipment arranged.

steps.title: Notify affected customer/recipient of delay
steps.desc: Communicate with the intended recipient about the theft, expected delay, and remediation plan.

steps.title: Review high-value shipment security requirements
steps.desc: Evaluate whether high-value or high-risk shipments need enhanced security measures (covert tracking, security escorts, varied routing) going forward.
steps.guidance: Share findings with procurement and logistics partners.

ITID-63212.def: The rerouting of a legitimate shipment to an unauthorized delivery address through falsified delivery instructions, impersonation, or manipulation of shipping records, resulting in the goods being delivered into the adversary's control rather than the intended recipient's.
ITID-63212.purpose: Captures fraudulent redirection of a shipment to a location controlled by the adversary, achieved through deception rather than physical seizure.
scopeIncludes: Falsified change-of-address instructions submitted to a carrier or shipper
Impersonation of an authorized party to redirect a shipment
Manipulation of shipping labels or manifests to divert goods
scopeExcludes: Physical hijacking or theft of a shipment (ITID-63211)
A logistics employee facilitating theft from the inside (ITID-63221)
A fictitious freight broker inserting itself into the transaction (ITID-63213)
ITID-63212.severity: Medium-High, scaled to the value of the diverted shipment.
ITID-63212.priority: P2 by default; escalate to P1 for high-value or sensitive-hardware shipments.
ITID-63212.escalation: Escalate to logistics security, procurement/vendor management, and (if a compromised account or email is the vector) the SOC's business-email-compromise process; notify the carrier immediately to attempt an in-transit recall.
indicators: Delivery confirmation to an address inconsistent with the original order
Last-minute change-of-address or delivery-instruction request received outside normal channels
Carrier confirms delivery but the intended recipient reports non-receipt
vectors: Social engineering or impersonation of an authorized employee/vendor contact to request a delivery change
Compromise of a shipping-notification or purchase-order email thread to insert fraudulent redirect instructions
rootCauses: No verification requirement for last-minute delivery-address changes
Lack of out-of-band confirmation for shipment redirection requests
Insufficient monitoring of purchase-order/shipping-notification email threads for tampering
mitreTechniques: T1195.003 Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
controls: Out-of-band verification required for any shipment address change
Carrier-level alerting on delivery-instruction changes for high-value shipments
Vendor/procurement process hardening against email-thread manipulation
ITID-63212.detection: Physical logistics crime — no ATT&CK Enterprise technique applies; tracked via physical security and logistics-partner coordination. Where a compromised email account is the enabling vector, that portion of the incident should also be logged and investigated under the organization's Business Email Compromise ITID.
ITID-63212.response: Contact the carrier immediately to attempt recall/redirection, notify the affected business unit and vendor, and investigate the origin of the fraudulent redirect instruction.
metrics: Number of fraudulent diversion attempts per quarter
Value of goods diverted
Percentage of high-value shipments with out-of-band redirect verification
ITID-63212.notes: Differentiator within this Tier-4 group: this leaf is deception-based redirection of a real shipment, as opposed to outright physical theft (ITID-63211) or a fabricated broker entity (ITID-63213). Any email-compromise component should also be cross-logged under the Business Email Compromise ITID.

playbook.name: Fraudulent Shipment Diversion (Fake Delivery Address Redirect)
playbook.description: An attacker fraudulently redirected a shipment to an unauthorized delivery address, typically via social engineering of the carrier or a compromised order system.

steps.title: Confirm the redirect and identify the fraudulent address
steps.desc: Verify with the carrier that a delivery address change occurred and was not authorized by the legitimate shipper/recipient.
steps.guidance: Obtain the redirect request record (who requested it, via what channel, from what account/contact).
steps.outcome: Fraudulent redirect confirmed with the diverted address identified.
steps.abort: If the change is confirmed legitimate, close the case.

steps.title: Determine how the redirect request was authorized
steps.desc: Investigate whether the redirect was enabled via a compromised account, social-engineered carrier representative, or intercepted communication.
steps.guidance: Review authentication logs on the shipping/order account and any correspondence with the carrier.
steps.outcome: Attack vector for the fraudulent redirect is identified.

steps.title: Determine shipment status and recoverability
steps.desc: Establish whether the shipment has already been delivered to the fraudulent address or can still be intercepted in transit.
steps.guidance: Contact the carrier immediately for real-time tracking status.

steps.title: Request emergency intercept or hold from carrier
steps.desc: Immediately request the carrier hold or intercept the shipment before delivery to the fraudulent address.
steps.guidance: Use the carrier's security/fraud escalation line rather than standard customer service for faster action.
steps.outcome: Shipment is held or redirected back if still in transit.
steps.abort: If the shipment has already been delivered, proceed directly to law-enforcement and recovery steps.

steps.title: Lock down the compromised account or channel used for the redirect
steps.desc: If a compromised account or communication channel enabled the redirect, secure it immediately (reset credentials, revoke sessions).
steps.guidance: Coordinate with IT security if the shipping/order platform account was compromised.
steps.outcome: The exploited account/channel is secured against further misuse.

steps.title: Report fraud to carrier security and law enforcement
steps.desc: File formal fraud reports with the carrier's security team and law enforcement, including all evidence of the fraudulent redirect.
steps.outcome: Reports filed with tracked case numbers.

steps.title: Verify no additional shipments were diverted
steps.desc: Check other pending or recent shipments tied to the same account, customer, or carrier relationship for similar diversion attempts.
steps.outcome: Confirmation that no other shipments were fraudulently diverted.

steps.title: Arrange replacement shipment and recover diverted goods where possible
steps.desc: Ship a replacement to the correct recipient and pursue recovery of diverted goods through law enforcement or the carrier's claims process.
steps.outcome: Correct recipient receives goods; recovery process initiated for diverted shipment.

steps.title: Strengthen shipment change-authorization controls
steps.desc: Review and strengthen verification requirements for delivery address changes with carriers and internal order systems (e.g., callback verification, MFA on shipping accounts).
steps.outcome: Updated address-change verification procedure documented and communicated to carriers.
