ITID-64141.def: An adversary uses social media platforms to research, befriend, or otherwise manipulate an employee into disclosing information or taking an action that furthers a later trust-exploitation attack, distinct from a direct phishing or impersonation attempt.
ITID-64141.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for adversaries using social media to build false trust with employees as a precursor to a supply-chain-relevant compromise.
scopeIncludes: Fake recruiter or professional-networking profiles used to elicit organizational information
Long-term rapport-building on social platforms preceding a request for access or information
Social media reconnaissance feeding a later spear phishing or impersonation attack
scopeExcludes: The resulting spear phishing or executive impersonation attempt itself once launched (ITID-64121, ITID-64111)
Purely passive OSINT gathering with no direct employee interaction (tracked under reconnaissance elsewhere in the taxonomy)
ITID-64141.severity: Low-Medium at the engagement stage; escalates only if disclosure of sensitive information is confirmed.
ITID-64141.priority: P3 at report; P2 if sensitive information disclosure is confirmed.
ITID-64141.escalation: Escalate to SOC and HR/security awareness if an employee reports having disclosed information; assess blast radius of what was shared.
indicators: Unsolicited, persistent contact from an unverifiable professional profile
Requests for organizational details disguised as networking or recruitment
Employee reports of an unusually inquisitive online contact
vectors: Fake recruiter outreach on professional networking platforms
Long-con rapport building via direct messaging
rootCauses: Limited employee awareness of social-engineering reconnaissance via social media
No policy on verifying unsolicited professional/social contacts before information sharing
controls: Security awareness training on social-media-based social engineering
Employee reporting channel for suspicious online contact
ITID-64141.detection: Minimal technical telemetry; detection relies almost entirely on employee self-reporting.
ITID-64141.response: Debrief the employee to determine what, if anything, was disclosed, and assess whether it enables a follow-on attack.
metrics: Count of reported social-media engineering attempts
Count resulting in confirmed information disclosure
ITID-64141.notes: Lone-child cross-reference stub. Tracks the reconnaissance/rapport-building stage; the downstream attack it enables is tracked under the specific ITID for that attack type.

playbook.name: Social Media Engineering of Employees
playbook.description: An attacker uses social media platforms to build rapport with or deceive employees, extracting sensitive information or gaining access by exploiting perceived personal or professional trust.

steps.title: Intake report of suspicious social media contact
steps.desc: Collect details of the social-media interaction (platform, profile, messages) reported by the employee as suspicious or that led to information/access disclosure.
steps.guidance: Note whether the profile impersonates a real person/company (recruiter, colleague, industry contact) and what was requested.
steps.outcome: Incident logged with platform, profile details, and content of interaction.

steps.title: Assess what information or access was disclosed
steps.desc: Interview the employee to determine exactly what information, credentials, or access was shared during the interaction.
steps.guidance: Common targets: org-chart details, internal project names, credentials via a fake job/survey link, or malware via a shared document.

steps.title: Investigate the attacking profile/infrastructure
steps.desc: Review the attacker's social media profile, connected accounts, and any links/files shared for further indicators.
steps.guidance: Check whether the profile is part of a known campaign (e.g. fake recruiter operations).
steps.outcome: Attacker infrastructure and campaign context documented.

steps.title: Isolate any compromised endpoint or credentials
steps.desc: If a malicious link/file was accessed or credentials disclosed, isolate the affected endpoint and reset the credentials immediately.
steps.abort: Not applicable if disclosure was informational only (no credential/malware exposure).

steps.title: Report and request takedown of the malicious profile
steps.desc: Report the fraudulent/malicious social media profile to the platform for takedown and block it organization-wide where feasible.

steps.title: Search for other employees targeted by same actor
steps.desc: Determine whether other employees were contacted by the same or similar profiles as part of a broader campaign.
steps.guidance: Send a discreet advisory to relevant teams (e.g. those with public LinkedIn presence) to check for similar contact attempts.
steps.outcome: Full scope of targeted employees identified.

steps.title: Update social media awareness guidance
steps.desc: Update employee guidance on social-media engineering tactics, especially around unsolicited professional contact and information requests.

steps.title: Confirm no lasting access or data exposure remains
steps.desc: Verify no persistent access, malware, or ongoing data exposure resulted from the interaction.
steps.outcome: Environment confirmed clean; disclosure impact contained.

steps.title: Conduct awareness review and share indicators
steps.desc: Review the incident with security-awareness stakeholders and share attacker indicators/tactics broadly for detection.

ITID-64211.def: An adversary obtains a legitimate organization's code-signing certificate (via theft, breach, or unauthorized issuance) and uses it to sign malicious code, exploiting the trust that operating systems, security tools, and users place in a valid digital signature.
ITID-64211.purpose: Captures cases where an adversary uses a stolen, legitimate code-signing certificate to make malware appear as trusted, signed software.
scopeIncludes: Malware signed with a stolen legitimate vendor code-signing certificate
Detection of a certificate later revoked due to confirmed theft and abuse for signing
scopeExcludes: Use of a fraudulently issued (not stolen) certificate obtained by deceiving a CA (ITID-64312)
Spoofing via a lookalike publisher name rather than a genuine stolen certificate (ITID-64342)
ITID-64211.severity: High, given that a validly signed binary bypasses most signature-based trust controls.
ITID-64211.priority: P1 upon confirmation that a certificate under the organization's control has signed unauthorized code.
ITID-64211.escalation: Escalate immediately to the certificate issuer for revocation and to threat intelligence to identify scope of malware distributed under the certificate.
indicators: Signed binary flagged by threat intelligence as malicious despite a valid signature
Unexplained code-signing activity in build/release logs
CA or vendor notification of certificate misuse
vectors: Theft of a private signing key from a build server or HSM
Compromise of a developer or release-engineering workstation holding signing credentials
rootCauses: Signing keys not stored in a hardware security module with strict access control
Inadequate separation between build infrastructure and signing infrastructure
mitreTechniques: T1553.002 Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing
controls: HSM-backed signing key storage
Signing event logging and anomaly alerting
Least-privilege access to signing infrastructure
ITID-64211.detection: Strong technical signal via signing-log monitoring and threat-intelligence feeds on abused certificates; weak signal for the initial key theft itself.
ITID-64211.response: Revoke the compromised certificate, notify affected downstream consumers, and re-sign legitimate releases under a new key.
metrics: Time from theft to revocation
Number of malicious binaries identified under the abused certificate
ITID-64211.notes: Differentiated from its sibling (ITID-64212) by asset type: this leaf is code-signing trust, not TLS/transport trust. Cross-referenced against ITID-12633 (stolen device certificate/token impersonation), which concerns device identity rather than software-supply-chain signing trust.

playbook.name: Stolen Code-Signing Certificate Used to Sign Malware
playbook.description: An attacker has stolen an organization's code-signing certificate and private key and is using it to sign malicious software, lending it false trust and evading signature-based defenses.

steps.title: Confirm malicious use of organization's code-signing certificate
steps.desc: Validate reports or threat-intel alerts that malware has been observed signed with the organization's code-signing certificate.
steps.guidance: Obtain sample malware/hashes and confirm the signing certificate serial number and thumbprint match the organization's issued certificate.
steps.outcome: Confirmed match between malware signature and the organization's certificate.
steps.abort: If thumbprint does not match any organization-issued cert, redirect to standard malware-analysis workflow.

steps.title: Determine how the private key was exfiltrated
steps.desc: Investigate build servers, HSMs, or key-storage locations for evidence of compromise leading to private key theft.
steps.guidance: Review access logs on signing infrastructure, HSM audit logs, and build pipeline integrity.
steps.outcome: Root cause of key theft identified.

steps.title: Identify all software signed with the compromised key
steps.desc: Inventory every binary/build signed with the certificate since the estimated compromise window to determine legitimate vs. malicious signings.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference build system logs against release records.
steps.outcome: Full list of signed artifacts categorized as legitimate or suspect.

steps.title: Revoke the compromised certificate immediately
steps.desc: Request immediate revocation of the code-signing certificate from the issuing CA and publish to CRL/OCSP.
steps.guidance: This is the highest-priority containment action; coordinate directly with the CA's emergency revocation process.
steps.outcome: Certificate revoked and revocation propagated via CRL/OCSP.

steps.title: Isolate compromised signing infrastructure
steps.desc: Isolate the build server, HSM, or key-storage system where the theft occurred to prevent further misuse or reissuance abuse.

steps.title: Notify CA, security vendors, and affected customers
steps.desc: Notify the issuing CA of the compromise, alert AV/EDR vendors to blocklist the certificate thumbprint, and notify customers who may have installed the malicious signed software.
steps.guidance: Provide malware hashes and certificate details to accelerate vendor blocklisting.
steps.outcome: CA, vendors, and customers notified with actionable indicators.

steps.title: Rebuild signing infrastructure and rotate keys
steps.desc: Rebuild the compromised signing environment from a known-good state and generate a new code-signing key pair, ideally in a hardware security module.
steps.guidance: Do not reuse any component of the compromised signing chain.
steps.outcome: New signing infrastructure established with a fresh, properly protected key.

steps.title: Harden key-storage and signing access controls
steps.desc: Implement stricter access controls, HSM-backed key storage, and signing-request approval workflows to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Hardened signing process documented and implemented.

steps.title: Reissue legitimate software with new certificate
steps.desc: Re-sign and redistribute legitimate software builds using the new certificate, and update customer-facing advisories.
steps.outcome: Legitimate software properly re-signed and distributed.

steps.title: Conduct post-incident review of signing key security
steps.desc: Review the full incident with engineering, security, and legal to capture root cause and validate hardening measures.
steps.outcome: Root cause and remediation documented; process improvements tracked to completion.

ITID-64212.def: An adversary obtains the private key associated with a legitimate organization's TLS certificate and uses it to stand up a spoofed, seemingly-valid endpoint or to decrypt/inject into intercepted traffic, exploiting the trust clients place in the certificate's validity.
ITID-64212.purpose: Captures cases where a stolen TLS private key is used to impersonate a trusted endpoint and intercept traffic.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed theft of a TLS private key from a server, key vault, or CI/CD secret store
A rogue server presenting a stolen-but-valid certificate to conduct man-in-the-middle interception
scopeExcludes: MitM conducted via a rogue certificate authority-issued or self-signed certificate rather than a stolen legitimate key (ITID-64322)
Corporate TLS inspection using organization-issued interception certificates (ITID-64321)
ITID-64212.severity: High, since a valid stolen key defeats standard certificate-pinning-free TLS trust checks.
ITID-64212.priority: P1 upon confirmed key theft or observed misuse.
ITID-64212.escalation: Escalate immediately to revoke the certificate and rotate the key; notify any parties relying on certificate pinning to the compromised key.
indicators: Certificate transparency log entries for unexpected re-issuance
Anomalous TLS endpoint presenting the organization's certificate from an unrecognized IP range
Key vault or secrets-store access anomaly
vectors: Theft of a private key from an improperly secured secrets store
Compromise of a server or load balancer holding the TLS key material
rootCauses: Private keys stored outside a hardware security module or managed key vault
Overly broad access to key material across engineering teams
controls: Key vault / HSM-backed private key storage
Certificate transparency log monitoring
Certificate pinning where feasible
ITID-64212.detection: Certificate transparency monitoring and key-access logging provide meaningful technical signal.
ITID-64212.response: Revoke and reissue the certificate, rotate the key, and investigate the scope of the underlying key-storage compromise.
metrics: Time from key theft detection to revocation
Number of anomalous certificate-transparency entries investigated
ITID-64212.notes: Differentiated from ITID-64211 by asset type (TLS/transport trust vs. code-signing trust). MITRE mapping intentionally uses T1552.004 (Private Keys) rather than T1557, since this leaf concerns the theft that enables MitM, not the interception technique itself (see ITID-64321/64322 for the interception leaves).

playbook.name: Stolen TLS Certificate Private Key Used for MITM
playbook.description: An attacker has obtained the private key for an organization's TLS certificate and is using it to conduct man-in-the-middle interception of traffic believed to be secured.

steps.title: Confirm private key compromise and active MITM use
steps.desc: Validate evidence (e.g. certificate transparency log anomalies, threat-intel report, unexpected certificate observed in the wild) that the TLS private key is compromised and in use for interception.
steps.guidance: Check Certificate Transparency logs for unexpected reissuance or duplicate certificate usage.
steps.outcome: Confirmed compromise and active misuse of the TLS private key.

steps.title: Determine source of key exposure
steps.desc: Investigate the server, load balancer, or key-management system where the private key was stored for evidence of compromise.
steps.guidance: Check for unauthorized access to key vaults, misconfigured backups, or exposed configuration files.
steps.outcome: Root cause of key exposure identified.

steps.title: Identify scope of affected services and traffic
steps.desc: Determine which domains/services use the compromised certificate and estimate the volume/sensitivity of traffic potentially intercepted.
steps.outcome: Affected services and potential data-exposure scope documented.

steps.title: Revoke the compromised TLS certificate
steps.desc: Immediately request revocation of the certificate through the issuing CA (CRL/OCSP) and disable it on affected servers.
steps.outcome: Certificate revoked and no longer trusted by browsers/clients enforcing revocation checks.

steps.title: Deploy replacement certificate on affected services
steps.desc: Issue and deploy a new TLS certificate with a newly generated private key on all affected services immediately.
steps.guidance: Ensure the new private key is generated and stored securely, distinct from the compromised storage location.
steps.outcome: Affected services running with a trusted, non-compromised certificate.

steps.title: Secure key storage and rotate related secrets
steps.desc: Harden the key-storage mechanism (e.g. move to HSM or managed key vault) and rotate any other secrets that may have been exposed alongside the key.
steps.outcome: Key storage hardened; related secrets rotated.

steps.title: Notify affected users/customers if data interception is likely
steps.desc: If sensitive data was likely intercepted, notify affected users/customers and legal/compliance as required.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with legal for breach-notification obligations.
steps.abort: Not applicable if traffic exposure was minimal/non-sensitive.

steps.title: Validate new certificate deployment and monitor for further misuse
steps.desc: Confirm all affected services are serving the new certificate correctly and monitor CT logs for further unauthorized certificate issuance.
steps.outcome: Services confirmed secure; no further unauthorized certificates observed.

steps.title: Review key-management practices and update policy
steps.desc: Conduct post-incident review of key-management practices and update policy to prevent recurrence (e.g. mandatory HSM use, access reviews).

ITID-64213.def: A generalized case of a stolen digital certificate or signing credential being misused to exploit trust, where the specific certificate type or usage does not yet map to a more specific leaf.
ITID-64213.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for stolen certificate or digital signature cases that do not fit the code-signing or TLS-specific leaves.
scopeIncludes: Stolen document-signing, email-signing (S/MIME), or other non-code/non-TLS certificate misuse
Cases pending classification before routing to ITID-64211 or ITID-64212
scopeExcludes: Confirmed code-signing certificate theft (ITID-64211)
Confirmed TLS private key theft (ITID-64212)
ITID-64213.severity: Medium-High pending classification of the specific certificate type and usage.
ITID-64213.priority: P2 at report; reclassify and adjust priority once certificate type is confirmed.
ITID-64213.escalation: Escalate to the relevant PKI/certificate management team for immediate revocation assessment.
indicators: Unexplained certificate usage inconsistent with its intended purpose
Certificate authority or vendor notification of anomalous use
vectors: Theft of certificate material from an inadequately secured store
rootCauses: Insufficient inventory and lifecycle management of issued certificates
mitreTechniques: T1553.002 Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing
controls: Centralized certificate inventory and lifecycle management
Anomaly alerting on certificate usage
ITID-64213.detection: Variable; depends heavily on the specific certificate type once classified.
ITID-64213.response: Classify the certificate type and usage promptly, then route to the applicable specific leaf and follow its response guidance.
metrics: Count of general certificate-theft reports pending classification
ITID-64213.notes: Catch-all intake leaf for the Stolen Certificates and Digital Signatures group; expect most confirmed cases to reclassify into ITID-64211 or ITID-64212.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Stolen Certificate or Digital Signature
playbook.description: A general or not-yet-classified incident involving a stolen certificate or digital signature being misused to establish false trust.

steps.title: Confirm certificate/signature theft and misuse
steps.desc: Validate the report of a stolen certificate or digital signature and confirm evidence of unauthorized use.
steps.guidance: Identify certificate type (code-signing, TLS, document-signing, email/S-MIME) to route to the correct specific playbook if warranted.
steps.outcome: Theft and misuse confirmed with initial classification.
steps.abort: If evidence does not support theft/misuse, close as false positive.

steps.title: Determine source and scope of the compromise
steps.desc: Investigate how the certificate/private key was obtained and what has been signed or authenticated using it.
steps.outcome: Compromise source and scope of misuse documented.

steps.title: Revoke the compromised certificate
steps.desc: Request immediate revocation from the issuing CA/authority and publish to CRL/OCSP.

steps.title: Isolate compromised systems and notify stakeholders
steps.desc: Isolate any system involved in the theft and notify the CA, affected vendors, or customers as appropriate.

steps.title: Assess and remediate everything signed with the compromised credential
steps.desc: Inventory and validate all artifacts/transactions signed with the compromised certificate to distinguish legitimate from malicious use.
steps.outcome: Full inventory reviewed and remediated as needed.

steps.title: Reissue certificate and harden key protection
steps.desc: Generate and deploy a replacement certificate with proper key protection (HSM or equivalent) and review access controls on the signing process.
steps.outcome: New, properly protected certificate in use.

steps.title: Confirm restored trust and normal operations
steps.desc: Confirm the replacement certificate functions correctly and dependent systems/services operate normally.
steps.outcome: Normal operations confirmed with the new certificate.

steps.title: Document findings and update certificate-management policy
steps.desc: Capture root cause and update certificate lifecycle/key-management policy to prevent recurrence.

ITID-64221.def: An adversary leverages access, credentials, or a connection that was legitimately extended to a trusted third party (vendor, contractor, managed service provider) to reach the organization's environment or data, exploiting the trust relationship itself rather than a separate technical vulnerability.
ITID-64221.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for cases where an adversary abuses access legitimately granted to a trusted third party.
scopeIncludes: Attacker pivoting into the organization through a compromised MSP or vendor with legitimate remote access
Misuse of a vendor's standing VPN or API access to exfiltrate data or move laterally
scopeExcludes: A vendor impersonation scam with no genuine access relationship (ITID-64131)
Software dependency trust abuse (ITID-64431)
ITID-64221.severity: High, given the typically broad access trusted third parties are granted.
ITID-64221.priority: P1 upon confirmed misuse of third-party access.
ITID-64221.escalation: Escalate immediately to revoke or restrict the third party's access pending investigation; notify the third party and assess shared blast radius.
indicators: Anomalous activity on a third-party access path outside its normal scope or hours
Third-party credential used from an unexpected location or for an unexpected purpose
vectors: Compromise of an MSP's own environment used as a pivot
Overprivileged standing access granted to a vendor beyond its operational need
rootCauses: Third-party access not scoped to least privilege
Lack of continuous monitoring on third-party access paths
controls: Least-privilege, time-bound third-party access
Continuous monitoring of third-party access paths
Vendor security assessment program
ITID-64221.detection: Good, where third-party access is instrumented and baselined; weak where it is not.
ITID-64221.response: Suspend the third-party access path immediately upon suspicion, then investigate scope before restoring.
metrics: Count of third-party access anomalies detected
Mean time to suspend compromised third-party access
ITID-64221.notes: Lone-child cross-reference stub for the broader Third-Party Trust Exploitation category (644xx); this leaf specifically tracks identity/credential-level misuse of granted access rather than business-process fraud.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Misuse of Trusted Third-Party Access
playbook.description: A general or not-yet-classified incident involving a third party's legitimately granted access being misused beyond its intended scope or purpose.

steps.title: Intake report of suspected third-party access misuse
steps.desc: Collect details of the suspected misuse of vendor/partner/contractor access, including the account, systems touched, and observed anomalous behavior.
steps.guidance: Compare activity against the documented scope of the third party's access agreement/contract.
steps.outcome: Incident logged with initial scope of suspected misuse.

steps.title: Review third-party access logs and permissions
steps.desc: Pull authentication and activity logs for the third-party account(s) to establish a timeline and confirm activity outside authorized scope.
steps.guidance: Check VPN/remote-access logs, application audit trails, and any privileged-access-management session recordings.
steps.outcome: Timeline of activity established; out-of-scope actions confirmed or ruled out.
steps.abort: If activity is within authorized scope, close as false positive.

steps.title: Suspend or restrict the third-party access
steps.desc: Immediately suspend or restrict the third party's access pending investigation.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the business owner of the vendor relationship before full suspension if it risks disrupting critical services.

steps.title: Notify the third-party organization
steps.desc: Notify the vendor/partner organization's designated security contact of the suspected misuse and request their cooperation in the investigation.
steps.guidance: Use the contractually designated security contact, not the individual account holder if they are the suspect.

steps.title: Determine root cause and remediate access model
steps.desc: Determine whether the misuse was intentional, accidental, or due to overly broad access grants, and remediate accordingly.
steps.guidance: Review whether least-privilege was applied to the original access grant.
steps.outcome: Root cause determined and access model corrected.

steps.title: Re-scope or terminate third-party access per contract terms
steps.desc: Work with legal/procurement to re-scope, restrict, or terminate the third party's access consistent with contractual terms.
steps.outcome: Access re-scoped or terminated per agreed terms.

steps.title: Restore appropriately-scoped access and verify controls
steps.desc: Restore third-party access at the corrected scope, if continued access is needed, and verify monitoring controls are in place.
steps.outcome: Access restored at appropriate scope with monitoring in place.

steps.title: Review third-party access governance process
steps.desc: Review the incident with vendor-management and security governance stakeholders and update onboarding/access-review processes for third parties.

ITID-64231.def: An adversary exploits an established cross-domain trust configuration (e.g., federated identity, cross-forest Active Directory trust, cross-tenant application trust) to escalate privilege or move from a lower-trust domain into a higher-trust one.
ITID-64231.purpose: Captures privilege escalation achieved by abusing a configured trust relationship between separate security domains.
scopeIncludes: Abuse of a cross-forest AD trust to escalate from a compromised subsidiary domain into the parent domain's privileged accounts
Abuse of federated identity trust configuration to gain elevated access in a partner tenant
scopeExcludes: Escalation specifically via a parent/subsidiary corporate ownership relationship rather than a technical domain trust (ITID-64232)
Escalation with no cross-domain trust element (tracked under general privilege escalation elsewhere in the taxonomy)
ITID-64231.severity: High, given the potential for domain-wide or tenant-wide compromise.
ITID-64231.priority: P1 upon confirmed cross-domain privilege escalation.
ITID-64231.escalation: Escalate immediately to identity/directory services teams; consider severing the trust relationship as a containment measure.
indicators: Unexpected privileged authentication events crossing a domain or tenant trust boundary
Modification of trust or federation configuration outside change control
vectors: Compromise of a lower-security domain used as a stepping stone across an established trust
Abuse of an over-permissioned federation/trust configuration
rootCauses: Overly broad or unaudited cross-domain trust configurations
Lack of tiered administration separating domains by trust level
mitreTechniques: T1484.002 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Trust Modification
controls: Tiered administration model
Regular audit of cross-domain trust configurations
Alerting on trust/federation configuration changes
ITID-64231.detection: Strong where directory/identity change auditing is enabled; weak in environments without trust-configuration monitoring.
ITID-64231.response: Contain by restricting or severing the abused trust path, then investigate the full extent of cross-domain access achieved.
metrics: Count of cross-domain trust abuse incidents
Time to contain a compromised trust path
ITID-64231.notes: Differentiated from ITID-64232 by mechanism: this leaf is a technical domain/tenant trust configuration; ITID-64232 is a corporate-ownership-structure trust relationship.

playbook.name: Cross-Domain Trust Relationship Abused for Privilege Escalation
playbook.description: An attacker leverages an established cross-domain (e.g. AD forest/domain trust or federated identity) trust relationship to escalate privileges from a lower-trust domain into a higher-trust environment.

steps.title: Identify anomalous cross-domain authentication activity
steps.desc: Investigate alerts of unexpected authentication or access originating from a trusted external/lower-trust domain into the higher-trust domain.
steps.guidance: Review domain/forest trust configuration and authentication logs (e.g. Kerberos referral tickets, SID history) for anomalies.
steps.outcome: Suspicious cross-domain access confirmed and initial scope identified.

steps.title: Map the abused trust path and affected accounts
steps.desc: Trace the specific trust relationship (domain, forest, or federation) and identify all accounts/groups that gained unauthorized privilege through it.
steps.guidance: Check for SID history abuse, unconstrained delegation, or federation trust misconfiguration.
steps.outcome: Full trust path and affected accounts documented.

steps.title: Determine extent of privileged access obtained
steps.desc: Assess what privileged resources, systems, or data the attacker accessed after escalation.
steps.outcome: Full scope of privileged access obtained documented.

steps.title: Disable or restrict the abused trust relationship
steps.desc: Immediately disable or tightly restrict the specific cross-domain/forest trust path being abused.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with domain admins; a full trust removal may require careful planning to avoid business disruption.
steps.outcome: Abused trust path disabled or restricted, halting further escalation.

steps.title: Disable compromised/escalated accounts
steps.desc: Disable any accounts confirmed to have obtained unauthorized elevated privilege through the abused trust.
steps.outcome: Escalated accounts disabled; further misuse prevented.

steps.title: Remove unauthorized privileges and rogue trust configuration
steps.desc: Strip any unauthorized group memberships, SID history entries, or delegation settings created via the abuse, and correct trust configuration.
steps.outcome: Trust configuration and privileges restored to intended, least-privilege state.

steps.title: Review and harden cross-domain trust architecture
steps.desc: Review all cross-domain/forest trust relationships for necessity and scope; apply selective authentication and least-privilege trust design.
steps.outcome: Trust architecture reviewed and hardened; unnecessary trusts removed.

steps.title: Re-enable trust relationship under corrected configuration
steps.desc: If the trust is required for business operations, re-enable it under corrected, monitored configuration and validate no residual abuse path exists.
steps.outcome: Trust relationship restored securely with monitoring in place.

steps.title: Document trust-abuse findings and update architecture review process
steps.desc: Capture root cause and update the process for reviewing and approving cross-domain trust relationships going forward.

ITID-64232.def: An adversary exploits the implicit or configured trust extended between a parent company and its subsidiary (or between merged/acquired entities) to escalate privilege from the less-secure entity into the more-secure one, distinct from a purely technical cross-domain trust configuration.
ITID-64232.purpose: Captures privilege escalation achieved by abusing the implicit trust extended between a parent company and a subsidiary.
scopeIncludes: Compromise of a recently acquired subsidiary used to pivot into parent-company systems via inherited network or identity trust
Abuse of a parent/subsidiary shared-services relationship to gain elevated access
scopeExcludes: Escalation via a purely technical cross-forest or federation trust with no corporate-ownership element (ITID-64231)
ITID-64232.severity: High, particularly during merger/acquisition integration windows when trust boundaries are least mature.
ITID-64232.priority: P1 upon confirmed escalation via a parent/subsidiary trust path.
ITID-64232.escalation: Escalate to both entities' security teams; treat integration-period incidents as high urgency given typically immature controls.
indicators: Unusual access from subsidiary infrastructure into parent-company systems
Shared-services accounts used outside their expected pattern following an acquisition
vectors: Compromise of a subsidiary with weaker security posture prior to full security integration
Abuse of shared-services or shared-identity infrastructure set up during M&A integration
rootCauses: Incomplete security due diligence or integration following M&A
Premature or overly broad network/identity integration between parent and subsidiary
mitreTechniques: T1484.002 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Trust Modification
controls: Segmented, phased M&A security integration
Independent security assessment of acquired entities prior to trust extension
ITID-64232.detection: Moderate; dependent on whether logging/monitoring has been unified across parent and subsidiary at the time of the incident.
ITID-64232.response: Segment the compromised subsidiary from the parent environment pending investigation; do not assume integration-period trust is fully vetted.
metrics: Count of M&A-related trust abuse incidents
Average security integration maturity score at time of incident
sops: M&A Security Integration Incident Response SOP
detections: Cross-entity access monitoring during integration windows
ITID-64232.notes: Differentiated from ITID-64231 by axis: this leaf is the corporate-ownership trust relationship (parent/subsidiary, M&A); ITID-64231 is a purely technical domain/tenant trust configuration.

playbook.name: Inherited Trust from Parent Company/Subsidiary Relationship Abused
playbook.description: An attacker exploits the implicit trust relationship between a parent company and subsidiary (e.g. shared network access, federated identity, or inherited privileges) to move laterally into the higher-value environment.

steps.title: Identify anomalous activity traversing parent/subsidiary boundary
steps.desc: Investigate alerts showing unexpected access from a subsidiary (or parent) environment into the other's network or systems.
steps.guidance: Review shared VPN links, federated SSO configurations, and inter-company network peering for anomalies.
steps.outcome: Cross-entity intrusion confirmed and entry point identified.

steps.title: Determine the specific inherited-trust mechanism abused
steps.desc: Identify the exact mechanism (shared identity provider, network trust, shared credentials, M&A-era leftover access) enabling the traversal.
steps.guidance: Corporate M&A integrations often leave overly broad trust in place after initial integration.

steps.title: Assess scope of access gained in the target entity
steps.desc: Determine what systems, data, or privileges the attacker reached in the parent or subsidiary environment via the inherited trust.
steps.outcome: Full scope of impact across both entities documented.

steps.title: Sever or restrict the inter-entity trust path
steps.desc: Immediately restrict or sever the specific network/identity trust link being abused between parent and subsidiary.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with both entities' IT/security teams to avoid unplanned business disruption.

steps.title: Disable compromised accounts across both entities
steps.desc: Disable any accounts used to traverse the trust boundary in either the parent or subsidiary environment.
steps.outcome: Compromised accounts disabled organization-wide across both entities.

steps.title: Remove excess inherited privileges and stale integration access
steps.desc: Audit and remove overly broad access grants left over from the corporate integration that enabled the abuse.
steps.outcome: Excess/stale access removed; trust scoped to business need.

steps.title: Formalize least-privilege inter-entity access model
steps.desc: Work with both entities' security/IT leadership to formalize a least-privilege, monitored model for parent/subsidiary trust going forward.
steps.outcome: Documented, approved inter-entity access model in place.

steps.title: Restore necessary business connectivity under new model
steps.desc: Restore required business connectivity under the corrected, least-privilege trust model and validate the fix.
steps.outcome: Business operations restored with reduced attack surface.

steps.title: Review M&A/integration security process
steps.desc: Review how the excessive trust was established during integration and update the M&A security-integration playbook to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Integration security process updated with findings incorporated.

ITID-64233.def: A generalized case of privilege escalation achieved by abusing some form of established trust relationship, where the specific trust mechanism does not yet map to a more specific leaf.
ITID-64233.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for trust-based privilege escalation that does not fit the cross-domain or parent/subsidiary leaves.
scopeIncludes: Escalation via a trust relationship type not yet enumerated (e.g., franchise/licensee relationships, joint-venture shared infrastructure)
Cases pending classification before routing to ITID-64231 or ITID-64232
scopeExcludes: Confirmed cross-domain technical trust abuse (ITID-64231)
Confirmed parent/subsidiary trust abuse (ITID-64232)
ITID-64233.severity: High pending classification of the specific trust mechanism abused.
ITID-64233.priority: P1 at confirmation; reclassify once the specific trust mechanism is identified.
ITID-64233.escalation: Escalate to identity/directory services and the relevant business relationship owner.
indicators: Privilege escalation crossing an organizational trust boundary not yet categorized
vectors: Abuse of an uncommon or newly established inter-organizational trust relationship
rootCauses: Trust relationships established without a standardized security review process
mitreTechniques: T1484.002 Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Trust Modification
controls: Standardized security review for any new inter-organizational trust relationship
ITID-64233.detection: Variable; depends on the specific trust mechanism once classified.
ITID-64233.response: Classify the trust mechanism promptly and route to the applicable specific leaf.
metrics: Count of general trust-based escalation reports pending classification
ITID-64233.notes: Catch-all intake leaf for the Trust-Based Privilege Escalation group; expect most confirmed cases to reclassify into ITID-64231 or ITID-64232.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Trust-Based Privilege Escalation
playbook.description: A general or not-yet-classified incident in which an attacker exploits an established trust relationship between systems, domains, or organizations to escalate privileges.

steps.title: Confirm privilege escalation via abused trust relationship
steps.desc: Validate the report of unauthorized privilege escalation and identify the trust relationship (technical or organizational) that enabled it.
steps.outcome: Escalation confirmed and enabling trust relationship identified.
steps.abort: If no trust-based mechanism is involved, redirect to standard privilege-escalation playbook.

steps.title: Map scope of privileges and systems affected
steps.desc: Determine all accounts, systems, and data affected by the escalation.

steps.title: Restrict or disable the abused trust relationship
steps.desc: Immediately restrict, disable, or otherwise contain the trust relationship/mechanism being exploited.

steps.title: Disable affected privileged accounts
steps.desc: Disable any accounts confirmed to hold unauthorized escalated privileges.

steps.title: Remove unauthorized privileges and correct trust configuration
steps.desc: Strip unauthorized privileges granted via the trust abuse and correct the underlying configuration that allowed it.
steps.outcome: Configuration corrected; privileges restored to intended state.

steps.title: Review and harden trust relationship governance
steps.desc: Review the broader set of trust relationships of the same type for similar exposure and apply least-privilege hardening.
steps.outcome: Trust governance hardened across similar relationships.

steps.title: Restore normal operations and verify controls
steps.desc: Restore any legitimately needed access under corrected configuration and verify monitoring is in place.

steps.title: Document findings and update trust-relationship review process
steps.desc: Capture root cause and update the periodic review process for trust relationships to catch similar issues proactively.

ITID-64241.def: An adversary exploits a zero-day flaw in a SAML or OIDC implementation (e.g., signature validation bypass, assertion replay, token confusion) to forge or manipulate authentication assertions, defeating the trust that relying parties place in the identity provider's signed tokens.
ITID-64241.purpose: Captures exploitation of a previously unknown vulnerability in a SAML or OIDC authentication protocol implementation to forge trusted authentication assertions.
scopeIncludes: Forged SAML assertions or OIDC tokens exploiting a previously unknown implementation flaw
Exploitation of a zero-day in an identity provider's or service provider's SAML/OIDC library
scopeExcludes: Exploitation of a known, previously patched SAML/OIDC vulnerability (tracked under general exploitation domains elsewhere in the taxonomy)
Kerberos protocol zero-days (ITID-64242)
ITID-64241.severity: Critical, given that a successful forgery can grant broad, cross-application authenticated access.
ITID-64241.priority: P1 immediately upon suspicion of assertion/token forgery.
ITID-64241.escalation: Escalate to identity provider vendor and all relying-party application owners immediately; consider emergency key rotation.
indicators: Authentication events with signature validation anomalies
Token or assertion reuse outside expected replay windows
Vendor advisory on a SAML/OIDC implementation zero-day matching observed behavior
vectors: Exploitation of a signature-validation logic flaw in an identity provider or service provider library
Assertion replay exploiting weak or absent audience/timestamp validation
rootCauses: Reliance on a single identity provider/library implementation with no defense-in-depth validation
Delayed patching of identity infrastructure due to its criticality and complexity
controls: Rapid patch management for identity infrastructure
Signing-key rotation capability
Anomaly detection on authentication assertion patterns
ITID-64241.detection: Weak until the specific zero-day is disclosed and detection signatures are available; strong retroactively via log review once known.
ITID-64241.response: Apply vendor emergency patch or mitigation immediately; rotate signing keys and invalidate active sessions issued during the exposure window.
metrics: Time to patch identity infrastructure zero-days
Number of sessions invalidated post-incident
ITID-64241.notes: The 'zero-day in the protocol itself' framing does not map perfectly to T1606, which describes the outcome (forged credentials) rather than the zero-day exploitation mechanism; this is the closest real ATT&CK fit and is used with that caveat noted for analyst awareness.

playbook.name: Zero-Day in SAML/OIDC Authentication Protocol Implementation
playbook.description: An attacker exploits a previously unknown vulnerability in a SAML or OIDC authentication implementation to forge assertions/tokens or bypass authentication, abusing the trust federated systems place in the identity provider.

steps.title: Confirm exploitation of SAML/OIDC zero-day
steps.desc: Validate evidence (anomalous assertions/tokens, vendor advisory, threat-intel report) indicating exploitation of an unpatched SAML/OIDC implementation flaw.
steps.guidance: Check for signature-wrapping attacks, assertion replay, or malformed token acceptance in IdP/SP logs.
steps.outcome: Zero-day exploitation confirmed with technical evidence.

steps.title: Identify affected identity provider and service providers
steps.desc: Determine which IdP implementation/version is vulnerable and which downstream service providers/relying parties trust it.
steps.outcome: Full list of affected IdP/SP components documented.

steps.title: Determine scope of forged authentication events
steps.desc: Identify all sessions/accounts that may have been accessed via forged or replayed assertions/tokens.
steps.outcome: Scope of unauthorized access via forged auth documented.

steps.title: Apply interim compensating controls
steps.desc: Since a vendor patch may not yet exist, implement compensating controls: reduce session/token lifetimes, require step-up MFA, and tighten assertion validation where configurable.
steps.guidance: Work with the IdP vendor for recommended interim mitigations.
steps.outcome: Attack surface reduced pending a permanent patch.

steps.title: Revoke active sessions and force re-authentication
steps.desc: Invalidate all active sessions/tokens issued during the suspected exploitation window and force full re-authentication with MFA.

steps.title: Engage vendor for emergency patch coordination
steps.desc: Report the zero-day to the IdP/SP vendor and coordinate on emergency patch development and deployment timeline.

steps.title: Apply vendor patch once available
steps.desc: Deploy the vendor's official patch or configuration fix across all affected IdP/SP instances as soon as it is available and validated.
steps.abort: If patch is delayed, maintain compensating controls and document risk acceptance with leadership.

steps.title: Audit for persistence established via forged authentication
steps.desc: Review accounts and systems accessed via the exploit for any persistence mechanisms (new accounts, tokens, backdoors) established during the compromise window.
steps.outcome: No residual persistence confirmed, or persistence removed.

steps.title: Restore normal session lifetimes and validate protocol integrity
steps.desc: Restore standard session/token lifetime settings once the patch is confirmed effective, and validate SAML/OIDC assertion integrity checks are functioning correctly.
steps.outcome: Normal operations restored with validated protocol security.

steps.title: Document zero-day response and update federation hardening standards
steps.desc: Capture the timeline, vendor coordination, and compensating controls used; update standards for federated authentication hardening.

ITID-64242.def: An adversary exploits a zero-day flaw in a Kerberos implementation (e.g., ticket validation bypass, encryption downgrade) to forge or misuse Kerberos tickets, defeating the trust the domain places in properly issued tickets.
ITID-64242.purpose: Captures exploitation of a previously unknown vulnerability in the Kerberos authentication protocol or its implementation to forge or steal trusted tickets.
scopeIncludes: Forged or manipulated Kerberos tickets exploiting a previously unknown implementation flaw
Zero-day exploitation of the KDC or a Kerberos library used by relying services
scopeExcludes: Exploitation of known, previously patched Kerberos vulnerabilities or well-documented technique variants (e.g., standard Golden/Silver Ticket abuse using stolen but non-zero-day methods, tracked elsewhere)
SAML/OIDC protocol zero-days (ITID-64241)
ITID-64242.severity: Critical, given Kerberos's central role in domain authentication.
ITID-64242.priority: P1 immediately upon suspicion of ticket forgery via an unpatched vulnerability.
ITID-64242.escalation: Escalate to directory services team immediately; consider krbtgt account key rotation as containment.
indicators: Anomalous ticket-granting activity inconsistent with normal authentication patterns
KDC behavior inconsistent with a documented, patched vulnerability, suggesting a novel flaw
vectors: Exploitation of a flaw in ticket validation or encryption negotiation logic
Exploitation of an unpatched KDC implementation vulnerability
rootCauses: Complexity of the Kerberos protocol implementation increasing the attack surface for subtle flaws
Delayed patching of domain controllers due to operational criticality
mitreTechniques: T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
controls: Rapid domain controller patch management
krbtgt key rotation capability
Kerberos authentication anomaly monitoring
ITID-64242.detection: Weak until the zero-day is disclosed; ticket-anomaly monitoring can retroactively surface abuse once indicators are known.
ITID-64242.response: Apply emergency patch or mitigation, rotate the krbtgt key, and invalidate outstanding tickets issued during the exposure window.
metrics: Time to patch domain controller zero-days
Number of tickets invalidated post-incident
ITID-64242.notes: As with ITID-64241, the 'zero-day in the protocol' framing is broader than any single ATT&CK technique; T1558 is used as the closest real fit for the ticket-forgery outcome, with the caveat noted.

playbook.name: Zero-Day in Kerberos Authentication Protocol
playbook.description: An attacker exploits a previously unknown vulnerability in a Kerberos authentication implementation to forge tickets or bypass authentication controls, abusing the trust the domain places in ticket-granting mechanisms.

steps.title: Confirm exploitation of Kerberos zero-day
steps.desc: Validate evidence of exploitation of an unpatched Kerberos implementation vulnerability (e.g. forged tickets not detected by standard Golden/Silver ticket heuristics, vendor advisory).
steps.guidance: Review domain controller security logs and ticket-granting-service anomalies.
steps.outcome: Zero-day exploitation confirmed with technical evidence.

steps.title: Identify affected domain controllers and realms
steps.desc: Determine which domain controllers/KDC implementations are vulnerable and which realms/trusts are affected.

steps.title: Determine scope of forged ticket usage
steps.desc: Identify accounts/services accessed via forged or manipulated Kerberos tickets during the exploitation window.

steps.title: Apply interim compensating controls
steps.desc: Implement interim mitigations: reduce Kerberos ticket lifetimes, enable additional monitoring/alerting on ticket anomalies, and restrict high-privilege account usage where possible.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the OS/KDC vendor for recommended mitigations pending a patch.
steps.outcome: Attack surface reduced pending permanent patch.

steps.title: Reset krbtgt account and invalidate outstanding tickets
steps.desc: Reset the krbtgt account password (twice, per standard procedure) to invalidate all outstanding Kerberos tickets and force re-authentication.
steps.guidance: Follow the double-reset procedure with appropriate replication delay to avoid disrupting authentication.

steps.title: Engage vendor for emergency patch coordination
steps.desc: Report the zero-day to the OS/KDC vendor and coordinate on emergency patch development and deployment timeline.

steps.title: Apply vendor patch once available
steps.desc: Deploy the vendor's official patch across all affected domain controllers/KDC instances as soon as it is available and validated.
steps.abort: If patch is delayed, maintain compensating controls and document risk acceptance with leadership.

steps.title: Audit for persistence established via forged tickets
steps.desc: Review accounts and systems accessed during the compromise window for persistence mechanisms established via the forged tickets.
steps.outcome: No residual persistence confirmed, or persistence removed.

steps.title: Restore normal ticket lifetimes and validate authentication integrity
steps.desc: Restore standard Kerberos ticket lifetime settings once the patch is confirmed effective and validate authentication is functioning normally.
steps.outcome: Normal operations restored with validated authentication security.

steps.title: Document zero-day response and update authentication hardening standards
steps.desc: Capture the timeline, vendor coordination, and compensating controls used; update standards for authentication protocol hardening.

ITID-64243.def: A generalized case of a previously unknown authentication-protocol vulnerability being exploited to defeat trust in an authentication assertion or ticket, where the specific protocol does not yet map to a more specific leaf.
ITID-64243.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for zero-day exploits in authentication protocols that do not fit the SAML/OIDC or Kerberos leaves.
scopeIncludes: Zero-day exploitation of other authentication protocols (e.g., RADIUS, OAuth device flow, WS-Federation) not yet enumerated as their own leaf
Cases pending classification before routing to ITID-64241 or ITID-64242
scopeExcludes: Confirmed SAML/OIDC zero-day (ITID-64241)
Confirmed Kerberos zero-day (ITID-64242)
ITID-64243.severity: Critical pending classification of the specific protocol affected.
ITID-64243.priority: P1 at confirmation; reclassify once the specific protocol is identified.
ITID-64243.escalation: Escalate to identity infrastructure owners and the relevant protocol vendor immediately.
indicators: Authentication anomaly inconsistent with any known, patched vulnerability
vectors: Exploitation of an unpatched flaw in an authentication protocol implementation not yet enumerated
rootCauses: Broad diversity of authentication protocols in use, each carrying independent zero-day risk
mitreTechniques: T1558 Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
controls: Rapid patch management across all authentication infrastructure
Broad authentication anomaly monitoring
ITID-64243.detection: Weak until the zero-day is disclosed and classified into a more specific leaf.
ITID-64243.response: Classify the affected protocol promptly and route to the applicable specific leaf; apply emergency mitigations in the interim.
metrics: Count of general authentication zero-day reports pending classification
ITID-64243.notes: Catch-all intake leaf for the Zero-Day Exploits in Authentication Protocols group; as noted on its siblings, the 'protocol zero-day' framing does not map cleanly to any single ATT&CK technique.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Zero-Day Exploit in Authentication Protocol
playbook.description: A general or not-yet-classified incident involving exploitation of a previously unknown vulnerability in an authentication protocol implementation.

steps.title: Confirm zero-day exploitation of authentication protocol
steps.desc: Validate evidence of exploitation of an unpatched authentication protocol vulnerability and identify the specific protocol involved.
steps.outcome: Zero-day exploitation confirmed and protocol identified.
steps.abort: If a known/patched vulnerability, redirect to standard vulnerability-response playbook.

steps.title: Determine scope of affected systems and accounts
steps.desc: Identify affected authentication infrastructure and any accounts/sessions compromised via the exploit.

steps.title: Apply interim compensating controls
steps.desc: Implement compensating controls such as reduced session lifetimes, additional MFA requirements, or restricted access pending a vendor patch.
steps.outcome: Attack surface reduced pending permanent fix.

steps.title: Invalidate potentially compromised sessions/credentials
steps.desc: Force re-authentication and invalidate sessions/tokens issued during the suspected exploitation window.

steps.title: Engage vendor for patch coordination
steps.desc: Report the vulnerability to the affected vendor and coordinate on patch timeline.

steps.title: Apply vendor patch once available
steps.desc: Deploy the vendor's patch across affected infrastructure once available and validated.

steps.title: Audit for persistence from the exploitation window
steps.desc: Review systems accessed during the exploitation window for persistence mechanisms.
steps.outcome: No residual persistence confirmed, or persistence removed.

steps.title: Restore normal authentication settings and validate integrity
steps.desc: Restore standard authentication settings once patch is confirmed effective and validate normal operation.

steps.title: Document findings and update authentication hardening standards
steps.desc: Capture findings and update authentication protocol hardening standards.

ITID-64311.def: An adversary technically compromises and exfiltrates or gains unauthorized use of a Certificate Authority's intermediate signing key, enabling them to mint certificates that inherit the CA's root of trust, exploiting the trust every relying party places in that CA's chain.
ITID-64311.purpose: Captures the direct theft or compromise of a Certificate Authority's intermediate signing key.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed theft of an intermediate CA private key from a CA's signing infrastructure
Unauthorized use of a properly secured intermediate key following an insider or external technical breach
scopeExcludes: Certificates fraudulently obtained by deceiving CA staff rather than stealing key material (ITID-64312)
Broad CA infrastructure breach enabling mass unauthorized issuance without isolated key theft (ITID-64313)
ITID-64311.severity: Critical, given the scale of downstream trust a single intermediate key underpins.
ITID-64311.priority: P1 immediately upon confirmed or suspected key compromise.
ITID-64311.escalation: Escalate to the CA, browser/OS root program operators, and all relying applications for emergency revocation and distrust.
indicators: Certificate transparency log entries for certificates the CA did not knowingly issue
CA-reported anomaly in signing infrastructure access
Threat intelligence reporting on certificates chaining to the compromised intermediate
vectors: Technical breach of CA signing infrastructure (network intrusion, insider access abuse)
Inadequate HSM access controls at the CA
rootCauses: Insufficient isolation and access control around CA signing infrastructure
Delayed detection of anomalous signing activity at the CA
mitreTechniques: T1553.004 Subvert Trust Controls: Install Root Certificate
controls: CA-side HSM key isolation
Certificate transparency monitoring
Emergency revocation and distrust procedures
ITID-64311.detection: Strong via certificate transparency monitoring once misuse begins; weak for the initial key theft absent CA-side detection.
ITID-64311.response: Coordinate emergency revocation with the CA and root program operators; assess and remediate all certificates issued under the compromised key.
metrics: Time from compromise to revocation
Number of fraudulently issued certificates identified
ITID-64311.notes: Differentiated from siblings by mechanism: this leaf is technical key theft. Distinct from ITID-43631 (fraudulently issued certificate via compromised CA), which tracks the downstream fraudulent-certificate exploitation domain; this leaf tracks the supply-chain trust-anchor compromise itself.

playbook.name: CA Intermediate Signing Key Compromised
playbook.description: An attacker has compromised an intermediate Certificate Authority's private signing key, enabling issuance of fraudulent certificates trusted by the CA's entire chain of trust.

steps.title: Confirm intermediate CA key compromise
steps.desc: Validate reports/evidence (CT log anomalies, unauthorized certificate issuance, CA breach notification) that an intermediate CA signing key has been compromised.
steps.guidance: Coordinate closely with the CA operator (internal PKI team or external CA vendor).

steps.title: Identify all certificates issued under the compromised intermediate
steps.desc: Enumerate every certificate signed by the compromised intermediate CA, distinguishing legitimate issuances from fraudulent ones.
steps.guidance: Use CA issuance logs and CT logs to build a complete inventory.
steps.outcome: Full inventory of issued certificates compiled and categorized.

steps.title: Assess downstream trust impact
steps.desc: Determine which systems, browsers, and relying parties trust the compromised intermediate and the potential blast radius.

steps.title: Revoke the compromised intermediate CA certificate
steps.desc: Immediately revoke the compromised intermediate certificate and publish revocation via CRL/OCSP; notify the root CA if externally operated.
steps.guidance: This is the highest-priority action — every certificate under this intermediate becomes untrustworthy.

steps.title: Revoke fraudulently issued certificates en masse
steps.desc: Revoke all certificates identified as fraudulently issued under the compromised intermediate.

steps.title: Isolate compromised CA infrastructure
steps.desc: Isolate the HSM, signing server, or CA infrastructure component where the key compromise occurred.
steps.outcome: Compromised CA infrastructure isolated and secured.

steps.title: Rebuild CA infrastructure and issue new intermediate
steps.desc: Rebuild the CA signing infrastructure from a known-good state, generate a new intermediate key pair in a properly secured HSM, and obtain re-signing from the root CA.
steps.outcome: New, properly secured intermediate CA operational.

steps.title: Reissue legitimate certificates under new intermediate
steps.desc: Re-issue all legitimate certificates that were under the compromised intermediate using the new, trusted intermediate.
steps.outcome: All legitimate certificate holders migrated to the new intermediate.

steps.title: Harden CA key protection and issuance controls
steps.desc: Review and strengthen HSM protection, dual-control issuance procedures, and audit logging for the CA.
steps.outcome: Hardened CA controls documented and implemented.

steps.title: Validate trust restoration across relying parties
steps.desc: Confirm relying parties (browsers, OS trust stores, internal systems) correctly trust the new intermediate and reject the revoked one.
steps.outcome: Trust chain validated as correctly restored.

steps.title: Conduct post-incident review with CA governance stakeholders
steps.desc: Review the full incident with PKI/CA governance stakeholders, external auditors if applicable, and document root cause and remediation.
steps.outcome: Root cause and remediation documented; governance improvements tracked.

ITID-64312.def: An adversary manipulates Certificate Authority staff or its validation process (e.g., forged domain-control evidence, impersonated requester, deceived validation reviewer) into issuing a certificate for a domain or identity the adversary does not legitimately control, exploiting trust in the CA's human validation process.
ITID-64312.purpose: Captures cases where a rogue certificate is issued because CA staff were socially engineered rather than because key material was stolen.
scopeIncludes: Certificate issued after a validation reviewer was deceived by forged ownership evidence
Social engineering of CA support staff to bypass domain validation controls
scopeExcludes: Certificates issued via direct technical compromise of signing key material (ITID-64311)
Mass unauthorized issuance via a broad infrastructure breach (ITID-64313)
ITID-64312.severity: High, scoped typically to the specific domain(s) fraudulently validated rather than CA-wide trust.
ITID-64312.priority: P1 upon confirmation of a fraudulently validated certificate.
ITID-64312.escalation: Escalate to the CA for immediate revocation and process review of the validation failure.
indicators: Certificate transparency log entry for a domain the organization does not recognize as requested
CA notification of a validation process irregularity
vectors: Forged domain-control validation evidence submitted to the CA
Social engineering of a CA support representative
rootCauses: Weak or manual domain-validation processes susceptible to social engineering
Insufficient CA staff training on validation-fraud tactics
mitreTechniques: T1553.004 Subvert Trust Controls: Install Root Certificate
controls: Automated, cryptographic domain validation (e.g., ACME) in preference to manual review
Certificate transparency monitoring for the organization's own domains
ITID-64312.detection: Good via certificate transparency monitoring; the social-engineering step itself is typically invisible to the victim organization until the fraudulent certificate surfaces.
ITID-64312.response: Request emergency revocation from the CA and monitor for use of the fraudulent certificate in the wild.
metrics: Time from fraudulent issuance to revocation
Count of unauthorized certificates detected via CT monitoring
detections: Certificate transparency monitoring for organization domains
ITID-64312.notes: Differentiated from ITID-64311 by axis: this leaf is process/human (social engineering of validation), not a technical key breach.

playbook.name: Rogue CA Certificate Issued via Social Engineering of CA Staff
playbook.description: An attacker social-engineers Certificate Authority staff into issuing a fraudulent certificate for a domain or entity they do not control, abusing the human trust boundary within the CA's issuance process.

steps.title: Confirm rogue certificate issuance via social engineering
steps.desc: Validate reports (CT log anomaly, domain owner complaint, CA internal audit) that a certificate was issued to an unauthorized party via deception of CA validation staff.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the CA operator's incident response team to review the issuance case file.
steps.outcome: Fraudulent issuance confirmed with supporting evidence.

steps.title: Identify the deceived validation process and staff involved
steps.desc: Determine which domain-validation or identity-verification step was bypassed or deceived (e.g. forged authorization letter, spoofed email approval).
steps.outcome: Specific process gap and social-engineering method documented.

steps.title: Determine scope of the rogue certificate's use
steps.desc: Investigate whether the rogue certificate has been used in the wild (e.g. for phishing sites or MITM) and the scope of impact.
steps.outcome: Usage and impact of the rogue certificate documented.

steps.title: Revoke the fraudulently issued certificate
steps.desc: Immediately revoke the rogue certificate through the CA and publish to CRL/OCSP.

steps.title: Notify the legitimate domain/entity owner
steps.desc: Notify the legitimate owner of the domain/entity that was impersonated so they can monitor for and report abuse.

steps.title: Review and remediate the CA's validation process gap
steps.desc: Work with the CA to identify and close the specific process gap that allowed staff to be deceived (e.g. add secondary verification, require call-back confirmation).

steps.title: Retrain or audit CA staff involved in validation
steps.desc: Coordinate with the CA to review staff training and internal controls around identity/domain validation to prevent recurrence.

steps.title: Confirm no further rogue certificates outstanding
steps.desc: Confirm via CT log monitoring that no additional rogue certificates were issued through the same method.
steps.outcome: Environment confirmed clear of related rogue certificates.

steps.title: Document findings and share with CA/browser trust community if warranted
steps.desc: Document the incident and, if broadly relevant, share findings with the CA/Browser Forum community for wider industry hardening.
steps.outcome: Findings documented and shared as appropriate.

ITID-64313.def: An adversary breaches a Certificate Authority's broader infrastructure (issuance systems, databases, automation pipelines) beyond a single key or a single social-engineered validation, enabling issuance of unauthorized certificates across many domains or identities at scale.
ITID-64313.purpose: Captures a broad technical breach of CA infrastructure enabling unauthorized certificate issuance at scale.
scopeIncludes: Large-scale breach of CA issuance systems resulting in numerous unauthorized certificates across unrelated domains
Compromise of CA automation/orchestration infrastructure enabling bulk fraudulent issuance
scopeExcludes: A single stolen intermediate signing key with no broader infrastructure compromise (ITID-64311)
A single fraudulently validated certificate via social engineering (ITID-64312)
ITID-64313.severity: Critical, given the multi-organization blast radius of a CA-wide infrastructure breach.
ITID-64313.priority: P1 immediately upon confirmation of scale beyond a single certificate or key.
ITID-64313.escalation: Escalate to industry-wide notification channels (CA/Browser Forum, root program operators) given the multi-tenant impact.
indicators: Certificate transparency log anomalies spanning many unrelated domains from the same CA
Public CA incident disclosure describing an infrastructure breach
vectors: Network intrusion into CA issuance/orchestration infrastructure
Compromise of CA automation pipeline credentials
rootCauses: Insufficient segmentation between CA issuance infrastructure and general corporate IT
Inadequate monitoring of CA automation pipelines
mitreTechniques: T1553.004 Subvert Trust Controls: Install Root Certificate
controls: Segmentation of CA issuance infrastructure
Industry-wide certificate transparency monitoring and coordinated disclosure processes
ITID-64313.detection: Strong at industry level via certificate transparency; the organization's own exposure depends on whether any of its own domains were among those affected.
ITID-64313.response: Assess whether the organization's own domains or certificates are affected by the disclosed breach; participate in coordinated revocation if so.
metrics: Number of organization-affiliated certificates identified as affected
Time to confirm organizational exposure following a public CA breach disclosure
sops: Industry CA Breach Exposure Assessment SOP
ITID-64313.notes: Differentiated from ITID-64311/64312 by scale and mechanism: this leaf is a broad infrastructure breach with mass, cross-domain impact rather than a single key or single fraudulent validation.

playbook.name: CA Infrastructure Breached to Issue Unauthorized Certificates at Scale
playbook.description: An attacker breaches Certificate Authority infrastructure directly (systems, not just a single key) to issue unauthorized certificates at scale, abusing the CA's core issuance trust.

steps.title: Confirm CA infrastructure breach and scaled unauthorized issuance
steps.desc: Validate evidence of a breach into CA issuance infrastructure resulting in unauthorized certificates issued at volume.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the CA's incident response team and review issuance system audit logs.
steps.outcome: Breach confirmed with scale of unauthorized issuance established.

steps.title: Determine breach vector into CA infrastructure
steps.desc: Investigate how the attacker gained access to the CA's issuance systems (e.g. compromised admin credentials, vulnerable issuance API, insider access).

steps.title: Inventory all unauthorized certificates issued
steps.desc: Compile a complete list of certificates issued through the breached infrastructure that were not legitimately requested.
steps.guidance: Cross-reference issuance logs against legitimate customer requests.
steps.outcome: Full inventory of unauthorized certificates compiled.

steps.title: Isolate breached CA issuance infrastructure
steps.desc: Immediately isolate and take offline the compromised issuance systems to stop further unauthorized issuance.

steps.title: Revoke all unauthorized certificates at scale
steps.desc: Bulk-revoke every certificate identified as unauthorized and publish updated CRL/OCSP responses.

steps.title: Notify root CA, browsers, and OS trust-store maintainers
steps.desc: If the breach threatens the integrity of the broader trust chain, notify root CA operators and browser/OS trust-store maintainers per CA/Browser Forum incident procedures.
steps.outcome: Relevant trust-store maintainers notified and engaged.

steps.title: Rebuild CA issuance infrastructure from known-good state
steps.desc: Rebuild all breached issuance systems from verified clean images/backups with hardened configuration.

steps.title: Reissue legitimate certificates affected by revocation
steps.desc: Coordinate reissuance of certificates for legitimate customers whose certificates were caught up in bulk revocation.
steps.outcome: Legitimate customers restored to valid certificates.

steps.title: Implement enhanced issuance monitoring and access controls
steps.desc: Deploy enhanced anomaly detection on issuance volume/patterns and tighten administrative access controls to the issuance systems.

steps.title: Validate restored trust and monitor for residual abuse
steps.desc: Confirm trust-store maintainers and relying parties correctly reject revoked certificates, and monitor for any residual unauthorized issuance.
steps.outcome: Trust confirmed restored; no residual unauthorized issuance detected.

steps.title: Conduct full post-incident review with external auditors
steps.desc: Conduct a comprehensive post-incident review, likely including external audit (e.g. WebTrust), and document remediation for the industry trust community.
steps.outcome: Root cause and remediation documented and validated externally.

ITID-64314.def: A generalized case of a Certificate Authority compromise undermining certificate trust, where the specific mechanism does not yet map to a more specific leaf.
ITID-64314.purpose: Serves as the intake bucket for Certificate Authority compromise cases that do not fit the key-theft, social-engineering, or infrastructure-breach leaves.
scopeIncludes: Reports of CA compromise pending determination of mechanism (key theft, staff deception, or infrastructure breach)
Third-party notification of a CA-related trust incident with insufficient initial detail to classify
scopeExcludes: Confirmed intermediate key theft (ITID-64311)
Confirmed social-engineering-based fraudulent issuance (ITID-64312)
Confirmed broad infrastructure breach (ITID-64313)
ITID-64314.severity: Critical pending classification of the specific compromise mechanism.
ITID-64314.priority: P1 at report; reclassify once the mechanism is confirmed.
ITID-64314.escalation: Escalate to PKI/certificate management team and the CA immediately regardless of classification status.
indicators: Any CA-related trust anomaly not yet attributable to a specific mechanism
vectors: Unclassified CA compromise vector pending investigation
rootCauses: Insufficient initial detail available to attribute root cause
mitreTechniques: T1553.004 Subvert Trust Controls: Install Root Certificate
controls: PKI incident response readiness
Certificate transparency monitoring
ITID-64314.detection: Variable; depends on the mechanism once classified.
ITID-64314.response: Classify the compromise mechanism promptly and route to the applicable specific leaf.
metrics: Count of general CA compromise reports pending classification
ITID-64314.notes: Catch-all intake leaf for the Certificate Authority (CA) Compromise group.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Certificate Authority Compromise
playbook.description: A general or not-yet-classified incident involving compromise of Certificate Authority infrastructure, keys, or issuance processes.

steps.title: Confirm CA compromise and initial classification
steps.desc: Validate the report of CA compromise and determine which component (signing key, infrastructure, or issuance process) is affected.
steps.outcome: Compromise confirmed and preliminary classification made.
steps.abort: If evidence does not support compromise, close as false positive.

steps.title: Determine scope of unauthorized certificate activity
steps.desc: Identify certificates issued or otherwise affected as a result of the compromise.

steps.title: Revoke affected certificates/keys
steps.desc: Revoke any compromised certificates or keys and publish via CRL/OCSP.

steps.title: Isolate affected CA infrastructure and notify stakeholders
steps.desc: Isolate any breached systems and notify root CA, browser/OS trust-store maintainers, or affected customers as appropriate to the scope.

steps.title: Rebuild/re-secure CA infrastructure or keys
steps.desc: Rebuild compromised infrastructure or generate replacement keys from a verified clean state.
steps.outcome: CA infrastructure/keys restored to a secure state.

steps.title: Reissue legitimate certificates
steps.desc: Coordinate reissuance for legitimate certificate holders affected by revocation.
steps.outcome: Legitimate holders restored to valid certificates.

steps.title: Harden CA controls
steps.desc: Review and strengthen the specific control gap that led to compromise (key protection, access control, or issuance validation).

steps.title: Validate restored trust chain
steps.desc: Confirm relying parties trust the restored/replacement CA components and reject revoked material.

steps.title: Document findings and update CA governance
steps.desc: Document root cause and remediation and update CA governance/security standards.

ITID-64321.def: An adversary (external attacker or malicious insider) abuses a legitimately deployed, organization-operated TLS inspection/interception proxy to decrypt and access traffic outside the proxy's authorized policy scope, exploiting the trust employees and systems place in the corporate network.
ITID-64321.purpose: Captures cases where an organization's own authorized TLS inspection proxy is abused to intercept traffic beyond its sanctioned scope.
scopeIncludes: Insider misuse of TLS inspection logs or decrypted traffic beyond authorized business purpose
External compromise of the TLS inspection proxy itself, exposing decrypted traffic to the attacker
scopeExcludes: A rogue, unauthorized certificate installed to enable interception outside any sanctioned proxy (ITID-64322)
Theft of a TLS private key used to stand up a spoofed endpoint (ITID-64212)
ITID-64321.severity: High, given that a compromised inspection point exposes the plaintext of a large volume of otherwise-encrypted traffic.
ITID-64321.priority: P1 upon confirmed misuse or compromise of the inspection proxy.
